# Changelog

Study items added from source documents. Each entry gives the verbatim quote it was checked against.

## 2026-11-01: DOE-HDBK-1019 (Nuclear Physics and Reactor Theory)

- **Card** (Decay): What is internal conversion?
  - Answer: A gamma ray emitted by an excited nucleus interacts with one of the innermost electrons of the same atom, and that electron is ejected.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93, Modes of Radioactive Decay, NP-01 p. 29 (PDF page 53)
  - Quote: "Internal conversion occurs when a gamma ray, emitted by the nucleus as it goes from the excited state to the ground state, interacts with one of the innermost electrons of the same atom. The electron is ejected from the atom."
  - Why: The handbook defines internal conversion as the nucleus's own gamma interacting with an inner electron of the same atom, which is then ejected. Supporting text: "interacts with one of the innermost electrons of the same atom. The electron is ejected from the atom."
- **Quiz** (Radiation physics): On the Chart of the Nuclides, nuclides that lie below and to the right of the line of stability typically undergo:
  - Answer: A. Beta-minus decay
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93, Modes of Radioactive Decay, NP-01 p. 29 (PDF page 53)
  - Quote: "Nuclides that lie below and to the right of the line of stability will typically beta minus decay. Nuclides above and to the left of the line will typically either beta plus decay or electron capture. Most alpha emitters are found in the upper, right-hand corner of the chart."
  - Why: The handbook says nuclides below and to the right of the line of stability typically beta-minus decay, while beta-plus decay and electron capture belong above and to the left, and alpha emitters sit in the upper right corner. Supporting text: "Nuclides that lie below and to the right of the line of stability will typically beta minus decay."
- **Card** (Radiation): What is pair production, and what gamma energy does it require?
  - Answer: A gamma ray interacts with the electric field of a nucleus and is converted into an electron-positron pair. The gamma must have more than 1.02 MeV.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93, Interaction of Radiation with Matter, NP-01 p. 67 (PDF page 91)
  - Quote: "In pair-production, a gamma interacts with the electric field of a nucleus and is converted into an electron-positron pair. The gamma must have an energy greater than 1.02 MeV for this to occur."
  - Why: The handbook describes pair production as a gamma converting to an electron-positron pair in a nucleus's field, and sets the 1.02 MeV threshold. Supporting text: "a gamma interacts with the electric field of a nucleus and is converted into an electron-positron pair. The gamma must have an energy greater than 1.02 MeV"
- **Quiz** (Radiation physics): In Compton scattering, a gamma ray:
  - Answer: B. Transfers part of its energy to an orbital electron and scatters off at a lower energy
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93, Interaction of Radiation with Matter, NP-01 p. 67 (PDF page 91)
  - Quote: "Photoelectric effect is where a gamma interacts with an electron orbiting an atom. The entire energy of the gamma is transferred to the electron, and the electron is ejected from its orbit. In Compton scattering a gamma interacts with an orbital electron, but only part of the gamma energy is transferred to the electron. The electron is ejected from its orbit, and the gamma is scattered off at a lower energy."
  - Why: The handbook says Compton scattering transfers only part of the gamma's energy to an orbital electron and the gamma scatters at lower energy; full transfer is the photoelectric effect, pair conversion is pair production, and capture in orbital shells describes a slowed beta particle. Supporting text: "In Compton scattering a gamma interacts with an orbital electron, but only part of the gamma energy is transferred to the electron. The electron is ejected from its orbit, and the gamma is scattered off at a lower energy."
- **Card** (Fission): What is critical energy in fission?
  - Answer: The minimum excitation energy a nucleus must have before it can fission.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93, Nuclear Fission, NP-01 p. 55 (PDF page 79)
  - Quote: "Critical energy is the minimum excitation energy that a nucleus must have before it can fission."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's definition of critical energy. Supporting text: "Critical energy is the minimum excitation energy that a nucleus must have before it can fission."
- **Quiz** (Fission): Breeding differs from conversion in that, during breeding:
  - Answer: A. More fissile material is produced than is consumed
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93, Nuclear Fission, NP-01 p. 55 (PDF page 79)
  - Quote: "Conversion is the process of transmuting fertile material into fissile material in a reactor, where the amount of fissile material produced is less than the amount of fissile material consumed. Breeding is the same as conversion, except the amount of fissile material produced is more than the amount of fissile material consumed."
  - Why: The handbook defines breeding as conversion in which more fissile material is produced than consumed; producing less is conversion, both transmute fertile into fissile material, and an equal amount fits neither definition. Supporting text: "Breeding is the same as conversion, except the amount of fissile material produced is more than the amount of fissile material consumed."
- **Card** (Fission): What is fertile material?
  - Answer: Material that can undergo transmutation to become fissile material.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93, Nuclear Fission, NP-01 p. 55 (PDF page 79)
  - Quote: "Fertile material is material that can undergo transmutation to become fissile material."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's definition of fertile material. Supporting text: "Fertile material is material that can undergo transmutation to become fissile material."
- **Card** (Fission): Why does uranium-235 fission with thermal neutrons while uranium-238 does not?
  - Answer: For U-235, the binding energy released by absorbing a neutron is greater than the critical energy for fission. For U-238 it is less, so the neutron must also bring kinetic energy.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93, Nuclear Fission, NP-01 p. 55 (PDF page 79)
  - Quote: "Uranium-235 fissions with thermal neutrons because the binding energy released by the absorption of a neutron is greater than the critical energy for fission. The binding energy released by uranium-238 absorbing a neutron is less than the critical energy, so additional kinetic energy must be possessed by the neutron for fission to be possible."
  - Why: The handbook compares the binding energy released on absorption with the critical energy: greater for U-235, less for U-238, which then needs neutron kinetic energy. Supporting text: "the binding energy released by the absorption of a neutron is greater than the critical energy for fission. The binding energy released by uranium-238 absorbing a neutron is less than the critical energy"
- **Card** (Neutrons): What is self-shielding?
  - Answer: Depression of the local neutron flux inside a material because neutrons are absorbed near its surface.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93, Nuclear Cross Sections and Neutron Flux, NP-02 p. 17 (PDF page 121)
  - Quote: "Self-shielding is where the local neutron flux is depressed within a material due to neutron absorption near the surface of the material."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's definition of self-shielding. Supporting text: "the local neutron flux is depressed within a material due to neutron absorption near the surface of the material."
- **Quiz** (Reactor kinetics): Compared with uranium-235, the fraction of plutonium-239 fission neutrons born as delayed neutrons is:
  - Answer: A. Smaller: about 0.0021 versus 0.0065
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93, Prompt and Delayed Neutrons, NP-02 p. 32 (PDF page 136)
  - Quote: "The fraction of neutrons born as delayed neutrons is different for different fuel materials. Following are values for some common fuel materials. Uranium-235 0.0065 Plutonium-239 0.0021"
  - Why: The handbook lists delayed neutron fractions of 0.0065 for uranium-235 and 0.0021 for plutonium-239, so plutonium's is smaller, not equal, larger, or zero. Supporting text: "Uranium-235 0.0065 Plutonium-239 0.0021"
- **Quiz** (Radiation physics): Radioactive equilibrium exists when:
  - Answer: A. The production rate of a material equals its removal rate
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93, Radioactivity, NP-01 p. 42 (PDF page 66)
  - Quote: "Radioactive equilibrium exists when the production rate of a material is equal to the removal rate."
  - Why: The handbook defines radioactive equilibrium as production rate equal to removal rate; in the same summary, equal parent and daughter decay rates define transient equilibrium, halving of activity defines half-life, and the straight semi-log line describes decay plots. Supporting text: "Radioactive equilibrium exists when the production rate of a material is equal to the removal rate."
- **Quiz** (Reactivity): A grey neutron absorber may be preferred to a black absorber in control rods because the grey absorber:
  - Answer: B. Causes smaller depressions in neutron flux and power near the rod
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93, Control Rods, NP-03 p. 58 (PDF page 82)
  - Quote: "A grey neutron-absorbing material may be preferable to a black neutron- absorbing material in the construction of control rods because the grey absorber causes smaller depressions in neutron flux and power in the vicinity of the rod."
  - Why: The handbook says a grey absorber is preferable because it causes smaller flux and power depressions near the rod; absorbing essentially all neutrons describes a black absorber, a larger area of influence and flatter profile is the reverse of what it says about resonance absorbers, and constant absorption over core life describes a non-burnable poison. Supporting text: "the grey absorber causes smaller depressions in neutron flux and power in the vicinity of the rod."
- **Card** (Reactivity): What is differential control rod worth, and where in the core is it highest?
  - Answer: The reactivity change per unit movement of a control rod. It is highest at the center of the core, where neutron flux is highest, giving a bell-shaped curve.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93, Control Rods, NP-03 p. 58 (PDF page 82)
  - Quote: "Differential control rod worth is the reactivity change per unit movement of a control rod. The typical differential control rod worth curve has a bell shape. It has very low values at the top and bottom of the core and a maximum value at the center of the core. The curve has this shape because rod worth is related to neutron flux, and flux is highest in the center of the core."
  - Why: The handbook defines differential worth as reactivity change per unit movement and says it peaks at the core center because flux is highest there. Supporting text: "a maximum value at the center of the core. The curve has this shape because rod worth is related to neutron flux, and flux is highest in the center of the core."
- **Quiz** (Reactivity): The typical integral control rod worth curve has:
  - Answer: B. An "S" shape, with a flat slope at the top and bottom and the steepest slope at the center of the core
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93, Control Rods, NP-03 p. 58 (PDF page 82)
  - Quote: "The typical integral control rod worth curve has an "S" shape. It has a relatively flat slope at the top and bottom of the core and a maximum slope at the center of the core."
  - Why: The handbook says the integral worth curve is S-shaped with flat slopes at the top and bottom and maximum slope at the center; the bell shape belongs to the differential curve, and a constant slope or flattest center contradicts it. Supporting text: "an "S" shape. It has a relatively flat slope at the top and bottom of the core and a maximum slope at the center of the core."
- **Quiz** (Reactor kinetics): Prompt critical is the condition in which the reactor is:
  - Answer: A. Critical on prompt neutrons alone
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93, Reactor Kinetics, NP-04 p. 22 (PDF page 114)
  - Quote: "Prompt critical is the condition when the reactor is critical on prompt neutrons alone."
  - Why: The handbook defines prompt critical as critical on prompt neutrons alone; the immediate power increase and decrease are its definitions of prompt jump and prompt drop. Supporting text: "Prompt critical is the condition when the reactor is critical on prompt neutrons alone."
- **Card** (Kinetics): How much positive reactivity, in dollars, makes a reactor prompt critical?
  - Answer: One dollar. That is why measuring reactivity in dollars is useful for judging whether a reactor is prompt critical.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93, Reactor Kinetics, NP-04 p. 22 (PDF page 114)
  - Quote: "Measuring reactivity in units of dollars is useful when determining if a reactor is prompt critical. A reactor that contains one dollar of positive reactivity is prompt critical"
  - Why: The handbook states that one dollar of positive reactivity makes a reactor prompt critical, which is why dollars are useful for this judgment. Supporting text: "A reactor that contains one dollar of positive reactivity is prompt critical"
- **Card** (Kinetics): What is prompt jump?
  - Answer: The small, immediate power increase after a positive reactivity insertion, caused by the increase in the prompt neutron population.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93, Reactor Kinetics, NP-04 p. 22 (PDF page 114)
  - Quote: "Prompt jump is the small, immediate power increase that follows a positive reactivity insertion related to an increase in the prompt neutron population."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's definition of prompt jump. Supporting text: "the small, immediate power increase that follows a positive reactivity insertion related to an increase in the prompt neutron population."
- **Quiz** (Reactivity): When calculating shutdown margin, all control rods are assumed fully inserted except:
  - Answer: A. The single rod with the highest integral worth, which is assumed fully withdrawn
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93, Reactor Operation, NP-04 p. 28 (PDF page 120)
  - Quote: "Shutdown margin is the instantaneous amount of reactivity by which a reactor is subcritical or would be subcritical from its present condition assuming all control rods are fully inserted except for the single rod with the highest integral worth, which is assumed to be fully withdrawn."
  - Why: The handbook's definition assumes every rod inserted except the single rod with the highest integral worth, which is assumed fully withdrawn. Supporting text: "assuming all control rods are fully inserted except for the single rod with the highest integral worth, which is assumed to be fully withdrawn."
- **Card** (Reactivity): Why is the stuck rod criterion applied to shutdown margin?
  - Answer: To ensure that the failure of a single control rod will not prevent the control rod system from shutting down the reactor.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93, Reactor Operation, NP-04 p. 34 (PDF page 126)
  - Quote: "The stuck rod criterion is applied to the shutdown margin to ensure that the failure of a single control rod will not prevent the control rod system from shutting down the reactor."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's stated purpose of the stuck rod criterion. Supporting text: "to ensure that the failure of a single control rod will not prevent the control rod system from shutting down the reactor."
- **Quiz** (Decay heat): Approximately how much decay heat is present immediately after shutdown, and one hour later, as a share of pre-shutdown power?
  - Answer: A. About 5-6% immediately, falling to about 1% within one hour
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93, Reactor Operation, NP-04 p. 34 (PDF page 126)
  - Quote: "Decay heat immediately after shutdown is approximately 5-6% of the pre- shutdown power level. Decay heat will decrease to approximately 1% of the pre-shutdown power level within one hour of reactor shutdown."
  - Why: The handbook gives about 5-6% of pre-shutdown power right after shutdown and about 1% within one hour, and states elsewhere in the same summary that decay heat is always present after operation. Supporting text: "approximately 5-6% of the pre- shutdown power level. Decay heat will decrease to approximately 1% of the pre-shutdown power level within one hour"
- **Card** (Reactivity): What three methods are used to shape or flatten core power distribution?
  - Answer: Reflectors, neutron poisons, and axial or radial variation of fuel enrichment.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93, Reactor Operation, NP-04 p. 34 (PDF page 126)
  - Quote: "Three methods are used to shape or flatten the core power distribution. Use of reflectors Installation of neutron poisons Axial or radial variation of fuel enrichment"
  - Why: The handbook lists exactly these three methods. Supporting text: "Use of reflectors Installation of neutron poisons Axial or radial variation of fuel enrichment"
- **Card** (Reactivity): What is power tilt?
  - Answer: A non-symmetrical variation of core power in one quadrant of the core relative to the other quadrants.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93, Reactor Operation, NP-04 p. 34 (PDF page 126)
  - Quote: "Power tilt is a non-symmetrical variation of core power in one quadrant of the core relative to the other quadrants."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's definition of power tilt. Supporting text: "a non-symmetrical variation of core power in one quadrant of the core relative to the other quadrants."
- **Quiz** (Reactivity): Doppler broadening of resonance absorption peaks occurs because:
  - Answer: A. Nuclei may be moving toward or away from the neutron at the moment of interaction
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93, Reactivity Coefficients, NP-03 p. 28 (PDF page 52)
  - Quote: "The Doppler broadening of resonance peaks occurs because the nuclei may be moving either toward or away from the neutron at the time of interaction."
  - Why: The handbook attributes Doppler broadening to nuclear motion toward or away from the neutron; moderator-to-fuel ratio, void volume, and pressure belong to the moderator, void, and pressure coefficients in the same summary. Supporting text: "the nuclei may be moving either toward or away from the neutron at the time of interaction."
- **Card** (Reactivity): Why are resonance absorbers sometimes preferred to thermal absorbers for control rods?
  - Answer: They have a larger area of influence and give a flatter flux profile.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93, Control Rods, NP-03 p. 58 (PDF page 82)
  - Quote: "Resonance absorbers are sometimes preferred to thermal absorbers as control rod materials because they have a larger area of influence and result in a flatter flux profile."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's reason. Supporting text: "they have a larger area of influence and result in a flatter flux profile."

## 2026-11-01: DOE-HDBK-1012 (Thermodynamics, Heat Transfer, and Fluid Flow)

- **Quiz** (Thermodynamics): A throttling process is one in which:
  - Answer: A. Enthalpy is constant, no work is done, and there is no heat transfer
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92, Thermodynamic Systems and Processes, HT-01 p. 30 (PDF page 56)
  - Quote: "Throttling process - a process in which enthalpy is constant h1 = h2, work = 0, and which is adiabatic, Q=0."
  - Why: The handbook defines throttling as constant enthalpy with zero work and no heat transfer; unchanged entropy, returning to the original state, and a straight Log P-Log V line are its definitions of isentropic, cyclic, and polytropic processes. Supporting text: "a process in which enthalpy is constant h1 = h2, work = 0, and which is adiabatic, Q=0."
- **Card** (Thermo): What is an adiabatic process?
  - Answer: A process in which there is no heat transfer across the system boundaries.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92, Thermodynamic Systems and Processes, HT-01 p. 30 (PDF page 56)
  - Quote: "Adiabatic process - a process in which there is no heat transfer across the system boundaries"
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's definition. Supporting text: "a process in which there is no heat transfer across the system boundaries"
- **Card** (Thermo): What is a control volume?
  - Answer: A fixed region of space that is studied as a thermodynamic system.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92, Thermodynamic Systems and Processes, HT-01 p. 30 (PDF page 56)
  - Quote: "A control volume is a fixed region of space that is studied as a thermodynamic system."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's definition. Supporting text: "A control volume is a fixed region of space that is studied as a thermodynamic system."
- **Quiz** (Thermodynamics): On a T-s or h-s diagram, a real (non-ideal) expansion or compression process appears as:
  - Answer: B. A line similar to vertical but slanted slightly to the right
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92, Second Law of Thermodynamics, HT-01 p. 96 (PDF page 122)
  - Quote: "An isentropic expansion or compression process will be represented as a vertical line on a T-s or h-s diagram. A real expansion or compression process will look similar, but will be slanted slightly to the right."
  - Why: The handbook says a real process looks like the isentropic vertical line but slanted slightly to the right; the vertical line is the ideal isentropic case, and a left slant or horizontal line contradicts it. Supporting text: "A real expansion or compression process will look similar, but will be slanted slightly to the right."
- **Card** (Thermo): State Planck's statement of the Second Law of Thermodynamics.
  - Answer: It is impossible to build an engine that works in a complete cycle and produces no other effect except raising a weight and cooling a heat reservoir.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92, Second Law of Thermodynamics, HT-01 p. 70 (PDF page 96)
  - Quote: "It is impossible to construct an engine that will work in a complete cycle and produce no other effect except the raising of a weight and the cooling of a heat reservoir."
  - Why: The card answer paraphrases the handbook's wording of Planck's statement. Supporting text: "It is impossible to construct an engine that will work in a complete cycle and produce no other effect except the raising of a weight and the cooling of a heat reservoir."
- **Card** (Heat transfer): What does the Second Law of Thermodynamics imply about the direction of heat transfer?
  - Answer: Heat will not transfer from a colder body to a hotter body without some external source of energy.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92, Heat Transfer Terminology, HT-02 p. 5 (PDF page 27)
  - Quote: "The Second Law of Thermodynamics implies that heat will not transfer from a colder to a hotter body without some external source of energy."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's sentence. Supporting text: "heat will not transfer from a colder to a hotter body without some external source of energy."
- **Quiz** (Heat transfer): The overall heat transfer coefficient must be used to solve problems when:
  - Answer: B. Both convection and conduction heat transfer occur
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92, Convection Heat Transfer, HT-02 p. 25 (PDF page 47)
  - Quote: "When both convection and conduction heat transfer occurs, the overall heat transfer coefficient must be used to solve problems."
  - Why: The handbook says the overall coefficient is required when convection and conduction occur together; a stagnant film layer is what the local coefficient measures, and radiation alone is not the case it names. Supporting text: "When both convection and conduction heat transfer occurs, the overall heat transfer coefficient must be used"
- **Card** (Heat transfer): What is the bulk temperature of a fluid?
  - Answer: The temperature that best represents the majority of the fluid, which is not physically connected to the heat transfer site.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92, Heat Transfer Terminology, HT-02 p. 5 (PDF page 27)
  - Quote: "The bulk temperature is the temperature of the fluid that best represents the majority of the fluid which is not physically connected to the heat transfer site."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's definition. Supporting text: "the temperature of the fluid that best represents the majority of the fluid which is not physically connected to the heat transfer site."
- **Quiz** (Heat generation): The thermal power produced by a reactor is directly related to:
  - Answer: A. The reactor coolant mass flow rate and the temperature difference across the core
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92, Heat Generation, HT-02 p. 45 (PDF page 67)
  - Quote: "The thermal power produced by a reactor is directly related to the mass flow rate of the reactor coolant and the temperature difference across the core."
  - Why: The handbook ties thermal power to coolant mass flow rate and core temperature difference; pressure and outlet temperature alone are altered versions of that fact, and active fuel length is part of its separate linear power density definition. Supporting text: "directly related to the mass flow rate of the reactor coolant and the temperature difference across the core."
- **Card** (Heat generation): What is the average volumetric thermal source strength?
  - Answer: The heat generation rate divided by the volume of fuel.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92, Heat Generation, HT-02 p. 50 (PDF page 72)
  - Quote: "The heat generation rate divided by the volume of fuel will give the average volumetric thermal source strength."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's sentence. Supporting text: "The heat generation rate divided by the volume of fuel will give the average volumetric thermal source strength."
- **Card** (Heat transfer): What does the radiation configuration factor account for?
  - Answer: The emittance and relative geometry of two objects.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92, Radiant Heat Transfer, HT-02 p. 29 (PDF page 51)
  - Quote: "Radiation configuration factor takes into account the emittance and relative geometry of two objects."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's sentence. Supporting text: "takes into account the emittance and relative geometry of two objects."
- **Card** (Heat transfer): What does the local heat transfer coefficient measure?
  - Answer: The ability to transfer heat through a stagnant film layer.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92, Heat Transfer Terminology, HT-02 p. 5 (PDF page 27)
  - Quote: "The local heat transfer coefficient represents a measure of the ability to transfer heat through a stagnant film layer."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's definition. Supporting text: "a measure of the ability to transfer heat through a stagnant film layer."
- **Card** (Fluid flow): What does Pascal's law state?
  - Answer: Pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout the confining vessel of a system.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92, Continuity Equation, HT-03 p. 16 (PDF page 38)
  - Quote: "Pascal’s law states that pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout the confining vessel of a system."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's statement of Pascal's law. Supporting text: "pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout the confining vessel of a system."
- **Quiz** (Fluid flow): By the principle of conservation of mass, all mass flow rates into a control volume equal:
  - Answer: A. All mass flow rates out, plus the rate of change of mass within the control volume
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92, Continuity Equation, HT-03 p. 16 (PDF page 38)
  - Quote: "The principle of conservation of mass states that all mass flow rates into a control volume are equal to all mass flow rates out of the control volume plus the rate of change of mass within the control volume."
  - Why: The handbook states mass in equals mass out plus the rate of change of stored mass; volumetric flow out, a minus sign, and velocity times area (its definition of volumetric flow rate) are altered versions of that statement. Supporting text: "all mass flow rates into a control volume are equal to all mass flow rates out of the control volume plus the rate of change of mass within the control volume."
- **Card** (Fluid flow): What is an ideal fluid?
  - Answer: A fluid that is incompressible and has no viscosity.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92, Laminar and Turbulent Flow, HT-03 p. 19 (PDF page 41)
  - Quote: "An ideal fluid is one that is incompressible and has no viscosity."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's definition. Supporting text: "An ideal fluid is one that is incompressible and has no viscosity."
- **Quiz** (Fluid flow): An increasing Reynolds number indicates:
  - Answer: A. Increasing turbulence of flow
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92, Laminar and Turbulent Flow, HT-03 p. 20 (PDF page 42)
  - Quote: "An increasing Reynolds number indicates an increasing turbulence of flow."
  - Why: The handbook says a rising Reynolds number means increasing turbulence; a parabolic profile is its description of laminar flow, and viscosity is a separate fluid property in the same summary. Supporting text: "An increasing Reynolds number indicates an increasing turbulence of flow."
- **Card** (Fluid flow): In fluid systems, what is head?
  - Answer: The term used to describe pressure exerted on or by a fluid.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92, Bernoulli’s Equation, HT-03 p. 30 (PDF page 52)
  - Quote: "Head is the term used to describe pressure exerted on or by a fluid."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's definition. Supporting text: "Head is the term used to describe pressure exerted on or by a fluid."
- **Quiz** (Fluid flow): The length of pipe that causes the same head loss as a valve or fitting is found by:
  - Answer: A. Multiplying the component's L/D value by the pipe diameter
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92, Head Loss, HT-03 p. 36 (PDF page 58)
  - Quote: "The length of pipe that would cause the same head loss as a valve or fitting can be determined by multiplying the value of L/D for the component found in handbooks or vendor manuals by the diameter of the pipe."
  - Why: The handbook says to multiply the component's L/D by the pipe diameter; dividing is an altered version, and the Moody Chart and relative roughness are its method for the friction factor, not equivalent length. Supporting text: "multiplying the value of L/D for the component found in handbooks or vendor manuals by the diameter of the pipe."
- **Card** (Fluid flow): What is frictional loss?
  - Answer: The part of the total head loss that occurs as fluid flows through straight pipes.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92, Head Loss, HT-03 p. 31 (PDF page 53)
  - Quote: "Frictional loss is that part of the total head loss that occurs as the fluid flows through straight pipes."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's definition. Supporting text: "that part of the total head loss that occurs as the fluid flows through straight pipes."
- **Quiz** (Natural circulation): Generally, as the temperature difference between the heat source and heat sink increases, natural circulation flow rate:
  - Answer: A. Increases
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92, Natural Circulation, HT-03 p. 40 (PDF page 62)
  - Quote: "Generally, the greater the temperature difference, the higher the natural circulation flow rate."
  - Why: The handbook says a greater temperature difference generally gives a higher natural circulation flow rate, and defines natural circulation as flow without mechanical devices, so pump speed does not apply. Supporting text: "the greater the temperature difference, the higher the natural circulation flow rate."
  - Context outside the quote: The quote says "the temperature difference" without naming between what; the question names the heat source and sink, which is how the handbook's chapter frames it.
- **Card** (Heat transfer): What is thermal driving head?
  - Answer: The driving force for natural circulation, caused by the difference in density between two areas of fluid.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92, Natural Circulation, HT-03 p. 40 (PDF page 62)
  - Quote: "Thermal driving head is the driving force for natural circulation caused by the difference in density between two areas of fluid."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's definition. Supporting text: "the driving force for natural circulation caused by the difference in density between two areas of fluid."
- **Quiz** (Pumps): How is the operating point (head and flow) of a pump and piping system determined?
  - Answer: A. From the intersection of the pump curve and the system head loss curve plotted on the same axes
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92, Centrifugal Pumps, HT-03 p. 56 (PDF page 78)
  - Quote: "The operating point (head and flow) of a system can be determined by plotting the pump curve and the system head loss curve on the same axes. The system will operate at the intersection of the two curves."
  - Why: The handbook places the operating point at the intersection of the pump and system head loss curves; adding flows or heads is how it builds combined curves for parallel or series pumps, and zero flow is not the intersection it describes. Supporting text: "The system will operate at the intersection of the two curves."
- **Card** (Fluid flow): How do density changes in a fluid relate to temperature changes?
  - Answer: They are inversely proportional: as temperature rises, density falls.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92, Continuity Equation, HT-03 p. 16 (PDF page 38)
  - Quote: "Density changes in a fluid are inversely proportional to temperature changes."
  - Why: The handbook states the inverse proportionality directly. Supporting text: "Density changes in a fluid are inversely proportional to temperature changes."

## 2026-11-01: DOE-HDBK-1018 (Mechanical Science)

- **Quiz** (Pumps): Gas binding of a centrifugal pump is a condition in which:
  - Answer: A. The casing fills with gases or vapors until the impeller can no longer contact enough fluid to function correctly
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93, Centrifugal Pump Operation, ME-03 p. 15 (PDF page 109)
  - Quote: "Gas binding of a centrifugal pump is a condition where the pump casing is filled with gases or vapors to the point where the impeller is no longer able to contact enough fluid to function correctly."
  - Why: The handbook defines gas binding as a gas- or vapor-filled casing that leaves the impeller unable to contact enough fluid; bubble formation and collapse is its definition of cavitation, maximum head at set speed is shutoff head, and discharge-to-suction leakage is slippage. Supporting text: "the pump casing is filled with gases or vapors to the point where the impeller is no longer able to contact enough fluid to function correctly."
- **Card** (Pumps): What is the shutoff head of a centrifugal pump?
  - Answer: The maximum head the pump can develop while operating at a set speed.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93, Centrifugal Pump Operation, ME-03 p. 14 (PDF page 108)
  - Quote: "Shutoff head is the maximum head that can be developed by a centrifugal pump operating at a set speed."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's definition. Supporting text: "the maximum head that can be developed by a centrifugal pump operating at a set speed."
- **Quiz** (Pumps): Which action helps stop cavitation in a centrifugal pump?
  - Answer: C. Reduce the temperature of the liquid being pumped
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93, Centrifugal Pump Operation, ME-03 p. 16 (PDF page 110)
  - Quote: "Steps that can be taken to stop pump cavitation include: Increase the pressure at the suction of the pump. Reduce the temperature of the liquid being pumped. Reduce head losses in the pump suction piping. Reduce the flow rate through the pump. Reduce the speed of the pump impeller."
  - Why: The handbook lists reducing liquid temperature as a step to stop cavitation; the other options reverse its listed steps of reducing flow rate, reducing impeller speed, and reducing suction head losses. Supporting text: "Reduce the temperature of the liquid being pumped."
- **Card** (Pumps): What are three indications that a centrifugal pump is cavitating?
  - Answer: Noise, fluctuating discharge pressure and flow, and fluctuating pump motor current.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93, Centrifugal Pump Operation, ME-03 p. 16 (PDF page 110)
  - Quote: "There are three indications that a centrifugal pump is cavitating. Noise Fluctuating discharge pressure and flow Fluctuating pump motor current"
  - Why: The handbook lists exactly these three indications. Supporting text: "Noise Fluctuating discharge pressure and flow Fluctuating pump motor current"
- **Quiz** (Pumps): On a graph of head versus flow, the characteristic curve of a positive displacement pump operating at a set speed is:
  - Answer: A. A vertical line
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93, Positive Displacement Pumps, ME-03 p. 28 (PDF page 122)
  - Quote: "The characteristic curve for a positive displacement pump operating at a certain speed is a vertical line on a graph of head versus flow."
  - Why: The handbook says the curve is a vertical line, because the pump delivers a definite volume per cycle regardless of head; flow that falls with head describes a centrifugal pump in the same summary, and the other two shapes contradict the definite-volume behavior. Supporting text: "is a vertical line on a graph of head versus flow."
- **Card** (Pumps): What is slippage in a positive displacement pump?
  - Answer: The rate at which liquid leaks from the pump discharge back to the pump suction.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93, Positive Displacement Pumps, ME-03 p. 28 (PDF page 122)
  - Quote: "Slippage is the rate at which liquid leaks from the discharge of the pump back to the pump suction."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's definition. Supporting text: "the rate at which liquid leaks from the discharge of the pump back to the pump suction."
- **Card** (Pumps): How is a positive displacement pump protected from overpressurization?
  - Answer: By a relief valve on the upstream side of the pump discharge valve.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93, Positive Displacement Pumps, ME-03 p. 28 (PDF page 122)
  - Quote: "Positive displacement pumps are protected from overpressurization by a relief valve on the upstream side of the pump discharge valve."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's sentence. Supporting text: "by a relief valve on the upstream side of the pump discharge valve."
- **Quiz** (Pumps): As the viscosity of the pumped liquid increases, the maximum speed at which a reciprocating positive displacement pump can properly operate:
  - Answer: A. Decreases, so the maximum flow rate through the pump decreases
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93, Positive Displacement Pumps, ME-03 p. 28 (PDF page 122)
  - Quote: "As the viscosity of a liquid increases, the maximum speed at which a reciprocating positive displacement pump can properly operate decreases. Therefore, as viscosity increases, the maximum flow rate through the pump decreases."
  - Why: The handbook says higher viscosity lowers both the maximum proper operating speed and the maximum flow rate. Supporting text: "the maximum speed at which a reciprocating positive displacement pump can properly operate decreases. Therefore, as viscosity increases, the maximum flow rate through the pump decreases."
- **Card** (Pumps): What does the volute of a centrifugal pump do?
  - Answer: It collects liquid leaving the impeller at high velocity and slows it by increasing the flow area, converting velocity head to static head.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93, Centrifugal Pumps, ME-03 p. 10 (PDF page 104)
  - Quote: "The volute collects the liquid discharged from the impeller at high velocity and gradually causes a reduction in fluid velocity by increasing the flow area, converting the velocity head to a static head."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's description of the volute. Supporting text: "gradually causes a reduction in fluid velocity by increasing the flow area, converting the velocity head to a static head."
- **Card** (Components): What protective alarms and trips do most mid-sized to large diesel engines have, as a minimum?
  - Answer: Engine overspeed alarm/trip, high water jacket temperature alarm, high exhaust temperature alarm, low lube oil pressure alarm and/or trip, and high crankcase pressure alarm.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93, Diesel Engine Speed, Fuel Controls, and Protection, ME-01 p. 40 (PDF page 60)
  - Quote: "Most mid-sized to large diesel engines have (as a minimum) the following protective alarms and trips. Engine overspeed alarm/trip High water jacket temperature alarm High exhaust temperature alarm Low lube oil pressure (alarm and/or trip) High crankcase pressure alarm"
  - Why: The handbook lists exactly these five alarms and trips. Supporting text: "Engine overspeed alarm/trip High water jacket temperature alarm High exhaust temperature alarm Low lube oil pressure (alarm and/or trip) High crankcase pressure alarm"
- **Quiz** (Components): A mechanical-hydraulic governor controls diesel engine speed by balancing:
  - Answer: A. Engine speed (mechanical flyweights) against hydraulic pressure
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93, Diesel Engine Speed, Fuel Controls, and Protection, ME-01 p. 40 (PDF page 60)
  - Quote: "A mechanical-hydraulic governor controls engine speed by balancing engine speed (mechanical flyweights) against hydraulic pressure."
  - Why: The handbook says the governor balances flyweight engine speed against hydraulic pressure; the other pairs mix parameters from its list of protective alarms and its description of the fuel rack, which the governor positions rather than balances against. Supporting text: "by balancing engine speed (mechanical flyweights) against hydraulic pressure."
- **Card** (Heat exchangers): How do regenerative and non-regenerative heat exchangers differ in the fluids they use?
  - Answer: Regenerative heat exchangers use the same fluid for heating and cooling. Non-regenerative heat exchangers use separate fluids.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93, Types of Heat Exchangers, ME-02 p. 11 (PDF page 79)
  - Quote: "Regenerative heat exchangers use the same fluid for heating and cooling. Non-regenerative heat exchangers use separate fluids for heating and cooling."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's two definitions. Supporting text: "Regenerative heat exchangers use the same fluid for heating and cooling. Non-regenerative heat exchangers use separate fluids for heating and cooling."
- **Quiz** (Valves): Ball valves are characterized by:
  - Answer: A. Quick, quarter-turn on-off operation and poor throttling characteristics
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93, Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 43 (PDF page 63)
  - Quote: "Ball valves allow quick, quarter turn on-off operation and have poor throttling characteristics."
  - Why: The handbook says ball valves give quick quarter-turn operation with poor throttling, which rules out good throttling; an isolated operating mechanism and automatic one-way opening are its descriptions of diaphragm or pinch valves and check valves. Supporting text: "Ball valves allow quick, quarter turn on-off operation and have poor throttling characteristics."
- **Card** (Valves): What is a stop check valve?
  - Answer: A combination of a lift check valve and a globe valve that has the characteristics of both.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93, Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 43 (PDF page 63)
  - Quote: "A stop check valve is a combination of a lift check valve and a globe valve and incorporates the characteristics of both."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's definition. Supporting text: "a combination of a lift check valve and a globe valve and incorporates the characteristics of both."
- **Card** (Valves): When are diaphragm and pinch valves used?
  - Answer: In systems where the entire operating mechanism should be completely isolated from the fluid.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93, Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 43 (PDF page 63)
  - Quote: "Diaphragm valves and pinch valves are used in systems where it is desirable for the entire operating mechanism to be completely isolated from the fluid."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's sentence. Supporting text: "where it is desirable for the entire operating mechanism to be completely isolated from the fluid."
- **Card** (Valves): What advantages do butterfly valves offer?
  - Answer: Significant advantages in weight, space, and cost for large valve applications.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93, Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 43 (PDF page 63)
  - Quote: "Butterfly valves provide significant advantages over other valve designs in weight, space, and cost for large valve applications."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's sentence. Supporting text: "significant advantages over other valve designs in weight, space, and cost for large valve applications."
- **Card** (Valves): How is valve stem leakage usually controlled?
  - Answer: By properly compressing the packing around the valve stem.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93, Valve Functions and Basic Parts, ME-04 p. 7 (PDF page 27)
  - Quote: "Valve stem leakage is usually controlled by properly compressing the packing around the valve stem."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's sentence. Supporting text: "properly compressing the packing around the valve stem."
- **Quiz** (Valves): In an electric motor valve actuator, the gear train between the motor and the valve stem:
  - Answer: A. Reduces rotational speed and increases torque
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93, Valve Actuators, ME-04 p. 50 (PDF page 70)
  - Quote: "Electric motor actuators consist of reversible electric motors connected to the valve stem through a gear train that reduces rotational speed and increases torque."
  - Why: The handbook says the gear train reduces speed and increases torque; the reverse contradicts it, and air on a diaphragm and magnetic attraction are its descriptions of pneumatic and solenoid actuators. Supporting text: "a gear train that reduces rotational speed and increases torque."
- **Card** (Components): What are the advantages of cooling compressed air?
  - Answer: Cool air takes less space and holds less moisture, which reduces corrosion and allows more air to be compressed into a given volume.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93, Air Compressors, ME-05 p. 9 (PDF page 91)
  - Quote: "The advantages to cooling the compressed air are that cool air takes less space and holds less moisture. This reduces corrosion and allows more air to be compressed into a given volume."
  - Why: The card answer restates the handbook's two advantages and their effects. Supporting text: "cool air takes less space and holds less moisture. This reduces corrosion and allows more air to be compressed into a given volume."
- **Quiz** (Components): What is the safe way to open a closed valve in a compressed air system?
  - Answer: A. Crack it open slowly and let pressure equalize before opening it further
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93, Air Compressors, ME-05 p. 9 (PDF page 91)
  - Quote: "Closed valves in a compressed air system should be slowly cracked open and the pressure should be allowed to equalize prior to opening the valve further. Systems should be depressurized prior to opening for maintenance. Oil should be kept out of air systems to prevent possible explosions."
  - Why: The handbook says to crack the valve open slowly and let pressure equalize first; it also says oil must be kept out of air systems and systems depressurized before maintenance, which rules out the other options. Supporting text: "Closed valves in a compressed air system should be slowly cracked open and the pressure should be allowed to equalize prior to opening the valve further."
- **Quiz** (Components): In a hydraulic piston, the force developed equals:
  - Answer: A. Pressure times area
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93, Hydraulics, ME-05 p. 13 (PDF page 95)
  - Quote: "The relationship between pressure and force in a hydraulic piston is expressed mathematically as: F = PxA"
  - Why: The handbook gives F = P x A for a hydraulic piston, so force is pressure times area and none of the other combinations. Supporting text: "F = PxA"
- **Card** (Components): What is a duplex strainer, and why is it used in fuel oil and lube oil lines?
  - Answer: Two sides with a basket in each, only one in service at a time. Flow can be shifted to the other basket while one is cleaned, so oil flow is never interrupted.
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93, Filters and Strainers, ME-05 p. 48 (PDF page 130)
  - Quote: "A duplex strainer is a strainer consisting of two sides with a basket in each side. Only one side is placed in service at a time. These are commonly used in fuel oil and lubricating oil lines, where it is essential to maintain an uninterrupted flow of oil. The flow may be diverted from one basket to the other, while one is being cleaned."
  - Why: The handbook describes the two-basket design and says it keeps oil flow uninterrupted by switching baskets during cleaning. Supporting text: "where it is essential to maintain an uninterrupted flow of oil. The flow may be diverted from one basket to the other, while one is being cleaned."
- **Quiz** (Components): During a backwash of a strainer or filter, liquid flows:
  - Answer: A. Opposite to normal flow, entering at the outlet and leaving at the inlet to a drain or waste tank
  - Source: DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93, Filters and Strainers, ME-05 p. 46 (PDF page 128)
  - Quote: "The intent of a backwash is to flow liquid in the opposite direction of normal flow, creating a pressure that pushes the debris off the strainer or filter."
  - Why: The handbook says a backwash flows liquid opposite to normal flow, and its lineup sends flush water into the outlet and out the inlet to the drain, so normal-direction flow and a bypass are wrong. Supporting text: "flow liquid in the opposite direction of normal flow"
  - Context outside the quote: The detail that flow enters the outlet and leaves the inlet comes from the next paragraph of the same summary, not from the quoted sentence.

## 2026-11-01: ML24088A065 (Kemmerer Unit 1 PSAR, Rev. 0) (PSAR design basis)

Design application document; content may change before the operating license stage.

- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Energy storage): In the Natrium design, why can steam generation and thermal energy storage operations (for example, ramp rates) be independent of reactor power operations?
  - Answer: A. Because of the molten salt energy storage tanks
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 1, Sec. 1.1.4.2 Secondary Systems and Components, p. 1.1-10 (PDF page 40)
  - Quote: "Similarly, steam generation and thermal energy storage operations (e.g., ramp rates) are independent from reactor power operations due to the presence of the molten salt energy storage tanks."
  - Why: The PSAR attributes the independence to the molten salt storage tanks; the PSAR places heat storage in the salt system and the steam generators in the Energy Island, and says the plant maintains constant reactor power while varying grid supply. Supporting text: "independent from reactor power operations due to the presence of the molten salt energy storage tanks."
- **Card** (PSAR design basis; flashcard): How are Natrium Energy Island SSCs (salt storage tanks, steam generator, turbine) safety-classified?
  - Answer: Non-safety-related with no special treatment (NST).
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 1, Sec. 1.1.3 Overall Configuration, p. 1.1-2 (PDF page 32)
  - Quote: "The EI structures, systems, and components (SSCs) are classified as non-safety-related with no special treatment (NST)."
  - Why: The PSAR states this classification for EI SSCs. Supporting text: "classified as non-safety-related with no special treatment (NST)."
- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Safety functions): The Fundamental Safety Functions (FSFs) defined for Kemmerer Unit 1 are:
  - Answer: A. Retaining radionuclides, controlling heat generation, and controlling heat removal
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 1, Sec. 1.3.2 Fundamental Safety Functions, p. 1.3-1 (PDF page 71)
  - Quote: "The FSFs are retaining radionuclides, controlling heat generation, and controlling heat removal."
  - Why: The PSAR lists exactly these three FSFs; the other options swap one in for a function the PSAR does not list. Supporting text: "The FSFs are retaining radionuclides, controlling heat generation, and controlling heat removal."
- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Safety functions): The Fundamental Safety Function of controlling heat generation is performed by:
  - Answer: A. Inserting control rods into the reactor core
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 1, Sec. 1.3.2 Fundamental Safety Functions, p. 1.3-2 (PDF page 72)
  - Quote: "The FSF of controlling heat generation is performed via insertion of control rods into the reactor core and is described in Section 1.3.2.2."
  - Why: The PSAR assigns heat generation control to control rod insertion; RAC and IAC perform heat removal, and the Sodium Processing System purifies sodium. Supporting text: "performed via insertion of control rods into the reactor core"
- **Card** (PSAR design basis; flashcard): For the fuel, what is the first safety-related radionuclide retention barrier in the Natrium functional containment strategy?
  - Answer: The fuel cladding.
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 1, Sec. 1.3.2.1 Retaining Radionuclides, p. 1.3-2 (PDF page 72)
  - Quote: "For the fuel, the cladding provides the first safety-related (SR) radionuclide retention barrier."
  - Why: The PSAR names the cladding as the first SR barrier. Supporting text: "the cladding provides the first safety-related (SR) radionuclide retention barrier."
- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Safety functions): In the Natrium functional containment strategy, which barrier comes next after the fuel cladding?
  - Answer: A. The Reactor Enclosure System (reactor head, reactor vessel, and component interfaces)
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 1, Sec. 1.3.2.1 Retaining Radionuclides, p. 1.3-2 (PDF page 72)
  - Quote: "The Reactor Enclosure System provides the next radionuclide retention barrier following the fuel cladding. The SR portion of this boundary includes the reactor head, reactor vessel, and associated component interfaces."
  - Why: The PSAR says the Reactor Enclosure System is the next barrier after the cladding; the Reactor Building, Sodium Cover Gas System, and IHT are other SSCs it lists in the functional containment strategy, not the next barrier. Supporting text: "The Reactor Enclosure System provides the next radionuclide retention barrier following the fuel cladding."
- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Coolant): Why does a postulated intermediate coolant leak result in sodium entering the primary system rather than primary coolant being released to the intermediate system?
  - Answer: A. Intermediate coolant pressure is greater than primary coolant pressure
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 1, Sec. 1.3.2.1 Retaining Radionuclides, p. 1.3-3 (PDF page 73)
  - Quote: "The intermediate coolant pressure is greater than primary coolant pressure, therefore postulated leaks of intermediate coolant result in an ingress of sodium to the primary system rather than a release of primary coolant to the intermediate system."
  - Why: The PSAR says the intermediate side is at higher pressure, so leakage flows into the primary; the reverse pressure contradicts it, the PSAR describes the primary as near atmospheric pressure, and it places the IHXs in the reactor pool. Supporting text: "The intermediate coolant pressure is greater than primary coolant pressure"
- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Sodium hazards): If a sodium-salt heat exchanger (SHX) leaks during normal operation, which way does the fluid flow?
  - Answer: A. Salt flows from the Nuclear Island Salt System into the intermediate sodium loop
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 7, Sec. 7.1.4.3 System Design and Performance Evaluation, p. 7.1-78 (PDF page 1275)
  - Quote: "During normal operation, IHT pressure is maintained at a lower pressure than NSS so that, in the event of an SHX leak, NSS coolant flows from the NSS to the intermediate loop."
  - Why: The PSAR keeps the IHT below NSS pressure so an SHX leak sends salt into the intermediate loop, not sodium into the salt; equal pressure contradicts that, and primary sodium does not pass through the SHX. Supporting text: "IHT pressure is maintained at a lower pressure than NSS so that, in the event of an SHX leak, NSS coolant flows from the NSS to the intermediate loop."
- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Sodium hazards): How does the Sodium Cover Gas System detect a sodium-salt reaction between the Nuclear Island Salt System and the IHT?
  - Answer: A. By continuously monitoring the intermediate cover gas for nitrogen, a reaction byproduct
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 7, Sec. 7.2.3.2.1 Compliance with Principal Design Criteria, p. 7.2-28 (PDF page 1307)
  - Quote: "The SCG detects sodium-salt reactions between the Nuclear Island Salt System (NSS) and the IHT by continuously monitoring for reaction byproducts, specifically nitrogen gas, in the Intermediate SCG."
  - Why: The PSAR says sodium-salt reactions are detected by nitrogen in the intermediate cover gas; the other options are real PSAR monitoring functions (sodium impurities, cesium, and the RV-GV annulus) aimed at different conditions. Supporting text: "by continuously monitoring for reaction byproducts, specifically nitrogen gas, in the Intermediate SCG."
- **Card** (PSAR design basis; flashcard): What protects the Natrium reactor from sodium-air reactions if the reactor vessel leaks?
  - Answer: The inert gas-filled annulus between the reactor vessel and the guard vessel.
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 1, Sec. 1.1.4.1.2 Reactor Enclosure System, p. 1.1-3 (PDF page 33)
  - Quote: "while the inert gas-filled annulus between the RV and Guard Vessel (GV) protects the system from sodium-air reactions in the highly unlikely event of a RV leak."
  - Why: The PSAR credits the inert RV-GV annulus with this protection. Supporting text: "the inert gas-filled annulus between the RV and Guard Vessel (GV) protects the system from sodium-air reactions"
- **Card** (PSAR design basis; flashcard): How is sodium leakage from the reactor vessel into the guard vessel detected?
  - Answer: Argon in the RV-GV annulus is recirculated and monitored for sodium buildup through absolute filter differential pressure changes, oxygen concentration, and radiation levels.
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 7, Sec. 7.2.3.2.1 Compliance with Principal Design Criteria, p. 7.2-28 (PDF page 1307)
  - Quote: "Argon gas is supplied to the RV-GV annulus to provide an inert environment that mitigates the effects of a sodium leak. Annulus gas is recirculated and monitored for sodium buildup via absolute filter differential pressure changes, oxygen concentrations, and radiation levels."
  - Why: The PSAR lists these three monitored indications for annulus sodium buildup. Supporting text: "Annulus gas is recirculated and monitored for sodium buildup via absolute filter differential pressure changes, oxygen concentrations, and radiation levels."
- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Sodium hazards): What is the design basis strategy of the Sodium Leak Detection, Collection, and Containment System (NNA)?
  - Answer: A. Mitigate the effects of a sodium fire once a leak has occurred
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 7, Sec. 7.5.2.1 Summary Description, p. 7.5-10 (PDF page 1420)
  - Quote: "The design basis strategy for NNA is to mitigate the effects of a sodium fire once a leak has occurred. Leak prevention is outside the scope of NNA and is addressed by other systems."
  - Why: The PSAR states NNA mitigates sodium fires after a leak and that leak prevention is outside its scope; smoke detection and fire water distribution belong to other fire protection subsystems it describes. Supporting text: "The design basis strategy for NNA is to mitigate the effects of a sodium fire once a leak has occurred."
- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Coolant): What keeps primary and intermediate sodium from freezing, and what takes over when that is not enough?
  - Answer: A. Decay heat; then operation of the primary and intermediate sodium pumps adds sufficient heat
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 5, Sec. 5.3.6.3 PDC 72 - Sodium Heating Systems, p. 5.3-25 (PDF page 1109)
  - Quote: "During normal operation, decay heat prevents sodium freezing. When decay heat is insufficient to maintain adequate sodium temperatures, operation of the Primary Sodium Pumps and Intermediate Sodium Pumps provides sufficient heat to the primary and intermediate sodium to prevent freezing."
  - Why: The PSAR names decay heat first and pump operation as the backup heat source; the other options reverse that order or name air cooling and salt storage systems that do not serve this function. Supporting text: "decay heat prevents sodium freezing. When decay heat is insufficient to maintain adequate sodium temperatures, operation of the Primary Sodium Pumps and Intermediate Sodium Pumps provides sufficient heat"
- **Card** (PSAR design basis; flashcard): What inherent property keeps the Natrium core covered by subcooled sodium during licensing basis events?
  - Answer: The high boiling point of sodium, which keeps the core covered by subcooled sodium at near-atmospheric pressure.
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 1, Sec. 1.3.2.1 Retaining Radionuclides, p. 1.3-3 (PDF page 73)
  - Quote: "the high boiling point of sodium, which ensures that the reactor core remains covered by subcooled sodium at near atmospheric pressure during LBEs."
  - Why: The PSAR credits sodium's high boiling point for this. Supporting text: "the high boiling point of sodium, which ensures that the reactor core remains covered by subcooled sodium at near atmospheric pressure"
- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Decay heat): Which two diverse residual heat removal systems satisfy the Fundamental Safety Function of controlling heat removal?
  - Answer: A. The Intermediate Air Cooling System (IAC) and the Reactor Air Cooling System (RAC)
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 1, Sec. 1.3.2.3 Controlling Heat Removal, p. 1.3-4 (PDF page 74)
  - Quote: "Two diverse residual heat removal systems, the Intermediate Air Cooling System (IAC) and Reactor Air Cooling (RAC), perform functions that satisfy the FSF of controlling heat removal."
  - Why: The PSAR names IAC and RAC as the two diverse residual heat removal systems; the other options pair one with systems the PSAR assigns to sodium purification, normal power heat transfer, or reactivity control. Supporting text: "the Intermediate Air Cooling System (IAC) and Reactor Air Cooling (RAC), perform functions that satisfy the FSF of controlling heat removal."
- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Natural circulation): In the Intermediate Air Cooling System's passive mode, how are intermediate sodium and cooling air moved?
  - Answer: A. Natural circulation of sodium and natural convection of air
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 1, Sec. 1.1.4.1.6 Intermediate Air Cooling System, p. 1.1-5 (PDF page 35)
  - Quote: "In active mode, there is forced circulation of the sodium in the intermediate loop provided by the ISP and forced air flow across the AHX provided by the IAC air blower. In blower mode, there is natural circulation of the sodium in the intermediate loop and forced air flow across the AHX provided by the IAC air blower. In passive mode, there is natural circulation of the sodium in the intermediate loop and natural convection flow of the air across the AHX."
  - Why: The PSAR defines passive mode as natural circulation of sodium with natural convection of air; forced sodium with forced air is active mode, natural sodium with blower air is blower mode, and forced sodium with natural air is not one of its three modes. Supporting text: "In passive mode, there is natural circulation of the sodium in the intermediate loop and natural convection flow of the air across the AHX."
- **Card** (PSAR design basis; flashcard): What actuation or operator action does the Reactor Air Cooling System need to remove decay heat?
  - Answer: None. It is continuously in operation and needs no automatic or manual actuation or operator action.
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 7, Sec. 7.2.1.1 Summary Description, p. 7.2-1 (PDF page 1280)
  - Quote: "The RAC is continuously in operation and requires no automatic or manual actuations or operator action to perform the heat removal safety function."
  - Why: The PSAR states this directly. Supporting text: "continuously in operation and requires no automatic or manual actuations or operator action"
- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Natural circulation): What drives air flow through the Reactor Air Cooling System?
  - Answer: A. Buoyancy from heating the air in the riser annulus
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 7, Sec. 7.2.1.1 Summary Description, p. 7.2-2 (PDF page 1281)
  - Quote: "Natural convection air flow within the RAC is induced by the buoyancy forces resulting from heating the air within the riser annulus."
  - Why: The PSAR says RAC air flow comes from buoyancy of air heated in the riser annulus; it also says RAC needs no moving parts, which rules out fans and blowers, and the cover gas is not part of the RAC air path. Supporting text: "induced by the buoyancy forces resulting from heating the air within the riser annulus."
- **Card** (PSAR design basis; flashcard): How does heat get from the reactor vessel into the Reactor Air Cooling System air?
  - Answer: The reactor vessel radiates heat across the argon gap to the guard vessel. The guard vessel convects heat to the air and also radiates to the collector cylinder, which convects heat to the air.
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 1, Sec. 1.1.4.1.3 Reactor Air Cooling System, p. 1.1-4 (PDF page 34)
  - Quote: "The RV is designed to thermally radiate heat across the argon gas space to the GV. The GV transfers a portion of the heat through convection directly into the RAC air flow path. To enhance total heat transferred, heat is thermally radiated to the collector cylinder which through convection transfers heat to the RAC air flow path."
  - Why: The card answer follows the PSAR's description of the heat path. Supporting text: "radiate heat across the argon gas space to the GV. The GV transfers a portion of the heat through convection directly into the RAC air flow path. To enhance total heat transferred, heat is thermally radiated to the collector cylinder"
- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Natural circulation): Why are the Reactor Air Cooling System stack outlets at a higher elevation than the stack inlets?
  - Answer: A. To separate the air flow streams and limit the potential for recirculation
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 7, Sec. 7.2.1.1 Summary Description, p. 7.2-1 (PDF page 1280)
  - Quote: "The stack outlets are at a higher elevation than the stack inlets to provide separation of the air flow streams to limit the potential for recirculation."
  - Why: The PSAR gives separation of air streams to limit recirculation as the reason; it states the RAC has no moving parts, the stacks are not supported by the superstructure, and rain is handled by louvers, cowls, and drains. Supporting text: "to provide separation of the air flow streams to limit the potential for recirculation."
- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Reactivity): Which statement describes the Natrium Control Rod Drive System scram function?
  - Answer: A. It is gravity-driven, fails safe on loss of electrical power, and is backed up by motor drive-in of the control rods
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 1, Sec. 1.1.4.1.9 Control Rod Drive System, p. 1.1-6 (PDF page 36)
  - Quote: "The CRD scram function is gravity-driven and is fail safe on a loss of electrical power. The CRD gravity scram is backed up by CRDM motor drive-in of the CRAs for defense-in-depth."
  - Why: The PSAR describes a gravity-driven, fail-safe scram backed up by motor drive-in, which rules out spring or hydraulic drive and the reversed primary/backup order. Supporting text: "The CRD scram function is gravity-driven and is fail safe on a loss of electrical power. The CRD gravity scram is backed up by CRDM motor drive-in of the CRAs"
- **Card** (PSAR design basis; flashcard): How many control rod drive mechanisms and control rod assemblies does the Natrium Control Rod Drive System have?
  - Answer: Thirteen CRDMs, controlling nine primary and four secondary control rod assemblies.
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 1, Sec. 1.1.4.1.9 Control Rod Drive System, p. 1.1-6 (PDF page 36)
  - Quote: "The CRD consists of thirteen CRDMs that control the position of nine primary CRAs and four secondary CRAs that are used to ensure reactor shutdown when required in response to an off-normal condition."
  - Why: The PSAR states these numbers. Supporting text: "thirteen CRDMs that control the position of nine primary CRAs and four secondary CRAs"
- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Reactivity): What does the Natrium power runback feature do?
  - Answer: A. Inserts control rods with the drive motors on abnormal conditions, preventing a scram for a variety of upset conditions
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 1, Sec. 1.3.2.2 Controlling Heat Generation, p. 1.3-4 (PDF page 74)
  - Quote: "The power runback feature is an active means of achieving the FSF of controlling heat generation and prevents a scram for a variety of upset conditions during power operation. The power runback is performed by the CRD and Nuclear Island Rod Monitoring and Control System, which use control rod drive motors to insert control rods upon detection of abnormal conditions."
  - Why: The PSAR describes runback as motor-driven rod insertion on abnormal conditions that prevents a scram; gravity insertion is the scram itself, motor drive-in coincident with a scram is the separate scram follow feature, and rod withdrawal is the opposite action. Supporting text: "prevents a scram for a variety of upset conditions during power operation. The power runback is performed by the CRD and Nuclear Island Rod Monitoring and Control System, which use control rod drive motors to insert control rods upon detection of abnormal conditions."
- **Card** (PSAR design basis; flashcard): Under PDC 11, what must the net effect of prompt inherent nuclear feedback do in the power operating range?
  - Answer: Tend to compensate for a rapid increase in reactivity.
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 3, Sec. 3.12.2 Design Basis, p. 3.12-3 (PDF page 1042)
  - Quote: "the reactor core and associated systems that contribute to reactivity feedback are designed so that, in the power operating range, the net effect of the prompt inherent nuclear feedback characteristics tends to compensate for a rapid increase in reactivity."
  - Why: The card answer restates the PSAR's statement of PDC 11. Supporting text: "the net effect of the prompt inherent nuclear feedback characteristics tends to compensate for a rapid increase in reactivity."
- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Reactivity): According to the PSAR, how does the Natrium core respond as core temperatures rise?
  - Answer: A. Net negative feedback reduces power to a stable level where heat production and heat removal balance
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 1, Sec. 1.3.2.2 Controlling Heat Generation, p. 1.3-4 (PDF page 74)
  - Quote: "As temperatures rise, the net negative feedback of the core reduces power. The natural feedbacks are self-regulating, inherent in the fuel design, and result in a safe and stable power level at which heat production and heat removal are in balance."
  - Why: The PSAR says net negative feedback reduces power to a safe, stable level where production and removal balance, which rules out positive feedback, zero feedback, or a complete shutdown. Supporting text: "the net negative feedback of the core reduces power. The natural feedbacks are self-regulating, inherent in the fuel design, and result in a safe and stable power level at which heat production and heat removal are in balance."
- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Instrumentation): How many Reactor Protection System divisions must vote on the same input parameter for an RPS division to generate a scram or ESF actuation output?
  - Answer: A. Two or more of the four divisions
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 7, Sec. 7.6.3.1 Reactor Protection System Description, Architecture, and Equipment Locations, p. 7.6-18 (PDF page 1446)
  - Quote: "When a given RPS division senses that two or more of the four RPS divisions has voted in favor of a particular reactor scram or ESF actuation based on the same input parameter, then that division automatically generates an output signal to the appropriate reactor or ESF actuation interface circuit to initiate that reactor scram or ESF actuation function."
  - Why: The PSAR's logic generates the output when two or more of four divisions vote on the same parameter, not one, three, or all four. Supporting text: "two or more of the four RPS divisions has voted in favor of a particular reactor scram or ESF actuation based on the same input parameter"
- **Card** (PSAR design basis; flashcard): Are the Natrium RPS manual scram and ESF actuation functions credited in the safety analysis?
  - Answer: No. They can be initiated from the Main Control Room and are diverse from the automatic RPS logic, but they are not credited in the safety analysis.
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 7, Sec. 7.6.3.1 Reactor Protection System Description, Architecture, and Equipment Locations, p. 7.6-18 (PDF page 1446)
  - Quote: "The RPS also provides the capability to manually initiate each reactor scram and ESF actuation function from the Main Control Room (MCR), although these manual functions are not credited in the safety analysis. These manual reactor scram and ESF control circuits are diverse from the RPS automatic logic."
  - Why: The PSAR states both points. Supporting text: "although these manual functions are not credited in the safety analysis. These manual reactor scram and ESF control circuits are diverse from the RPS automatic logic."
- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Instrumentation): How does the Nuclear Instrumentation System (XIS) provide a reactor power indication?
  - Answer: A. It senses neutron flux leakage from the core, which is proportional to reactor flux
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 1, Sec. 1.1.4.1.12 Nuclear Instrumentation System, p. 1.1-7 (PDF page 37)
  - Quote: "The Nuclear Instrumentation System (XIS) provides instrumentation to sense neutron flux leakage from the core during fuel movement, reactor startup, power operations, shutdown, and accident conditions. Neutron leakage is proportional to reactor flux and thus can be converted into a power indication."
  - Why: The PSAR says XIS senses neutron leakage, which is proportional to flux and converted to power; pool temperatures and pump speed are Reactor Instrumentation System parameters, and radiation monitoring is a separate system. Supporting text: "sense neutron flux leakage from the core"
- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Instrumentation): Why does an abnormal temperature condition in the primary cold pool trip the intermediate sodium pumps?
  - Answer: A. To reduce the heat load that ISP operation places on the primary system, keeping RAC heat removal requirements within limits
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 7, Sec. 7.1.4.3 System Design and Performance Evaluation, p. 7.1-78 (PDF page 1275)
  - Quote: "The ISP trip initiated by abnormal temperature condition in the PHT cold pool reduces the heat load to the PHT caused by ISP operation in order to maintain heat removal requirements for the RAC within limits."
  - Why: The PSAR says the temperature-initiated ISP trip reduces ISP heat load to keep RAC heat removal requirements within limits; overfill protection is the purpose of the level-initiated trips, the RAC is always in operation, and SHX leak handling is a separate design feature. Supporting text: "reduces the heat load to the PHT caused by ISP operation in order to maintain heat removal requirements for the RAC within limits."
- **Card** (PSAR design basis; flashcard): What protects the reactor vessel from overfill if an intermediate heat exchanger leaks?
  - Answer: An intermediate sodium pump trip initiated by abnormal level in the IHT expansion tank or in the primary sodium pool.
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 7, Sec. 7.1.4.3 System Design and Performance Evaluation, p. 7.1-78 (PDF page 1275)
  - Quote: "The ISP trip initiated by abnormal level conditions in the IHT expansion tank or in the PHT sodium pool provides protection against Reactor Vessel overfill in the unlikely event of leakage within the IHX."
  - Why: The PSAR states this purpose for the level-initiated ISP trip. Supporting text: "provides protection against Reactor Vessel overfill in the unlikely event of leakage within the IHX."
- **Card** (PSAR design basis; flashcard): What sources of decay heat does the Natrium decay heat generation rate methodology include?
  - Answer: Fission products, activated non-fissionable materials, and actinides produced within the fuel.
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 3, Sec. 3.12.1.5 Decay Heat Generation Rate, p. 3.12-2 (PDF page 1041)
  - Quote: "The decay heat generation rate methodology predicts the heat produced due to the decay of radioactive isotopes within the reactor. These include fission products, activated non-fissionable materials, and actinides produced within the fuel."
  - Why: The PSAR lists these three sources. Supporting text: "These include fission products, activated non-fissionable materials, and actinides produced within the fuel."
- **Card** (PSAR design basis; flashcard): In the primary Sodium Processing System, what do the cold traps and the cesium trap remove?
  - Answer: Cold traps remove oxides and hydrogen impurities. The cesium trap removes cesium released to the coolant from fuel pin failures.
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 1, Sec. 1.1.4.1.8 Sodium Processing System, p. 1.1-6 (PDF page 36)
  - Quote: "The purification equipment consists of cold traps, which remove oxides and hydrogen impurities, and a cesium trap, which removes cesium released to the coolant from fuel pin failures."
  - Why: The PSAR states what each trap removes. Supporting text: "cold traps, which remove oxides and hydrogen impurities, and a cesium trap, which removes cesium released to the coolant from fuel pin failures."
- **Quiz** (PSAR design basis; Coolant): How is cesium concentration in the primary sodium monitored?
  - Answer: A. With a radiation monitor
  - Source: ML24088A065, Ch. 1, Sec. 1.1.4.1.8 Sodium Processing System, p. 1.1-6 (PDF page 36)
  - Quote: "The sodium is continuously monitored for oxygen and hydrogen using a plugging temperature indicator, multi-purpose sampler and direct-measurement oxygen and hydrogen sensors. Cesium concentration is monitored using a radiation monitor."
  - Why: The PSAR monitors cesium with a radiation monitor; the plugging temperature indicator and oxygen and hydrogen sensors monitor oxygen and hydrogen, and nitrogen monitoring detects sodium-salt reactions. Supporting text: "Cesium concentration is monitored using a radiation monitor."
- **Card** (PSAR design basis; flashcard): What type of reactor is Kemmerer Unit 1, and what is its thermal power?
  - Answer: An 840 MWt pool-type sodium fast reactor (SFR).
