  - Quote: "Advantage of B4C, it has a high absorption cross section, its readily available which keeps cost low. Its relatively easy to fabricate, and it has low levels of radioactivity at the end of its life."
  - Why: The answer restates the quoted text.
- **Quiz** (Reactivity): Withdrawing control rods adds positive reactivity mainly because:
  - Answer: B. The effective core size increases, so there is less leakage out of the core or into the rods
  - Source: LP-CONTROL-RODS, slide 1.8 Control Rods affect on neutron population
  - Quote: "When control rods are withdrawn, the effective core size increases. Resulting in less leakage (out of the core or into the control rods). This results in positive reactivity being added and Keff raises."
  - Why: The lesson plan describes rod motion as changing effective core size; withdrawal lowers leakage and raises keff.
- **Card** (Reactivity): What does control rod worth depend on?
  - Answer: Rod location and the neutron flux there. Rods near the core center generally have more worth than those near the edge.
  - Source: LP-CONTROL-RODS, slide 1.15 Control Rod Worth
  - Quote: "Rod Worth depends on rod location and the neutron flux at that location. Generally rods located near the center of the core have more worth than those located near the edge."
  - Why: The answer restates the quoted text.
- **Quiz** (Reactivity): How are differential rod worth (DRW) and integral rod worth (IRW) related?
  - Answer: A. DRW is the slope of the IRW curve at a given rod position
  - Source: LP-CONTROL-RODS, slide 1.20 KC P134
  - Quote: "X | DRW is the slope of the IRW curve at a given rod position. | Good Job!!"
  - Quote: "X | IRW is the sum of the DRWs between the initial and final control rod positions. | Good Job!!"
  - Why: DRW is the reactivity change per unit rod movement, the slope of the IRW curve; IRW is the sum of DRWs between two positions.
- **Quiz** (Reactivity): Why does differential rod worth increase as coolant temperature rises?
  - Answer: A. Coolant density decreases, increasing the neutron migration length
  - Source: LP-CONTROL-RODS, slide 1.23 KC P54
  - Quote: "X | coolant density decreases, which increases the neutron migration length. | Good Job!!"
  - Why: The lesson plan's answer key: lower coolant density increases neutron migration length, so rods see more neutrons.
- **Card** (Reactivity): What are rod insertion limits designed to do?
  - Answer: Minimize the consequences of an uncontrolled rod withdrawal, provide an even axial flux distribution, and provide adequate shutdown margin.
  - Source: LP-CONTROL-RODS, slide 1.36 Rod Insertion Limits
  - Quote: "Rod insertion limits are designed to: Minimize the consequences of an uncontrolled rod withdrawal event To provide an even axial flux distribution To provide adequate shutdown margin"
  - Why: The answer restates the quoted text.
- **Card** (Reactivity): What is a key concept of flux shaping with control rods?
  - Answer: Flux follows the control rods; withdrawing rods shifts flux upward.
  - Source: LP-CONTROL-RODS, slide 1.34 Flux Profiles
  - Quote: "A key concept to understand is that flux will follow control rods."
  - Why: The answer restates the quoted text.
- **Card** (Reactivity): What is a reactor reflector?
  - Answer: Material in or near the reactor that reflects neutrons back into the core.
  - Source: LP-CONTROL-RODS, slide 1.29 Homogenous - Reflected
  - Quote: "a Reflector is material that is present in or near the reactor, which reflects neutrons back into core."
  - Why: The answer restates the quoted text.
- **Card** (Reactivity): What happens to the control rods on a reactor scram?
  - Answer: They are de-energized, and all partly or fully withdrawn rods drop into the core by gravity.
  - Source: LP-CONTROL-RODS, slide 1.37 Reactor Trip/Scram
  - Quote: "A reactor scram or trip denergizes control rods and allows all partially or fully withdrawn rods to drop into the reactor core by gravity."
  - Why: The answer restates the quoted text.

## 2026-11-02: LP-POWER-CHANGES (Power Changes)

Approved lesson plan: Power Changes.docx. Quotes are from the slide notes and on-slide text extracted with python-docx (RTF notes chunks converted with textutil); the section is the slide number and heading.

- **Quiz** (Reactor kinetics): A reactor is prompt critical when:
  - Answer: B. Net positive reactivity in the core is greater than or equal to the effective delayed neutron fraction
  - Source: LP-POWER-CHANGES, slide 1.29 KC P549
  - Quote: "X | The net positive reactivity in the core is greater than or equal to the magnitude of the effective delayed neutron fraction. | Good Job!!"
  - Why: The delayed neutron fraction depends on the fissioning isotopes, not fission rate; prompt criticality is net reactivity at or above beta-eff.
- **Quiz** (Reactor kinetics): For positive and negative reactivity additions of equal magnitude, the power increase has the shorter period because:
  - Answer: D. The effective delayed neutron precursor decay constant is larger during a power increase
  - Source: LP-POWER-CHANGES, slide 1.5 KC P7797
  - Quote: "X | Case 1, because the effective delayed neutron precursor decay constant is larger during a power increase. | Good Job!!"
  - Quote: "The effective delayed neutron fraction is unchanged by power changes. It is a function of the balance of fissile isotopes in the core."
  - Why: Beta-eff is not changed by power changes; the effective precursor decay constant is larger on a power increase, shortening the period.
- **Card** (Kinetics): How does core age affect startup rate for a given reactivity insertion?
  - Answer: As the core ages and beta-eff decreases, SUR becomes larger in magnitude.
  - Source: LP-POWER-CHANGES, slide 1.21 KC P3449
  - Quote: "As the core ages, and the effective delayed neutron fraction decreases, SUR will become larger in magnitude for a given reactivity insertion."
  - Why: The answer restates the quoted text.
- **Card** (Kinetics): What stable negative period follows a large negative reactivity insertion such as a scram, and what sets it?
  - Answer: About -80 seconds (-1/3 dpm), set by Br-87, the longest-lived precursor (decay constant 0.0124 per second).
  - Source: LP-POWER-CHANGES, slide 1.24 Step Insertion – Reactor Trip
  - Quote: "The negative 1/3 dpm startup rate (or – 80 second period) can be calculated if you use the decay constant of 0.0124 inverse seconds and any fairly large negative reactivity."
  - Quote: "The 0.0124 decay constant is the decay constant for Bromine 87, which is the longest lived precursor of all the precursors."
  - Why: The answer restates the quoted text.
- **Card** (Kinetics): A subcritical reactor receives +0.15 %Δk/k of positive reactivity and becomes supercritical. What reactivity value is used to find its period?
  - Answer: The net +0.05 %Δk/k in the core.
  - Source: LP-POWER-CHANGES, slide 1.18 KC P6825
  - Quote: "Also note that even though 0.15 %ΔK/K of positive reactivity is added to the reactor, since it was subcritical, it is only supercritical by 0.05 %ΔK/K (net amount of reactivity in the core). This is the value used in the calculation!"
  - Why: The answer restates the quoted text.
- **Card** (Kinetics): When does a prompt drop usually occur?
  - Answer: With a reactor scram, when a very large amount of negative reactivity is added.
  - Source: LP-POWER-CHANGES, slide 1.23 Step Insertion – Prompt Drop
  - Quote: "A prompt drop is often associated with a reactor scram where a very large amount of negative reactivity is added."
  - Why: The answer restates the quoted text.

## 2026-11-02: NUREG-1021 content changes

At the user's confirmation ("Apply all"), the 95 replacements proposed in NUREG-1021-REVIEW.md were applied to 83 quiz questions. Every changed correct answer keeps its fact; only Q122 and Q295 reword the correct answer. Explanations, sources and flags are unchanged. For length fixes, most items follow ES-4.2 D.2: "Model D is useful when it is not possible to create four options of similar length."

### ES-4.2 D.15.f, p. 16 (71 changes)
> "a correct answer that is longer or shorter than the distractors"

- **Q2** (option): "Measure turbine output" -> "Measure the fuel temperature rise as rods are withdrawn toward criticality"
- **Q3** (option): "Coolant pressure only" -> "The pressure ratio across the turbine and the mass flow rate of the working fluid"
- **Q4** (option): "Pump head" -> "Pressure differences maintained by the cover gas system"
- **Q35** (option): "friction as the dominant term" -> "friction losses that convert flow energy into internal energy"
- **Q38** (option): "pump speed exceeds design" -> "discharge pressure rises above the shutoff head, forcing flow back through the impeller"
- **Q41** (option): "good throttling" -> "precise throttling of flow with the disk held at mid-travel"
- **Q44** (option): "viscosity and velocity only" -> "fluid viscosity, flow velocity, and the bulk temperature of the coolant"
- **Q45** (option): "average to maximum heat flux" -> "the average heat flux in the hottest channel to the minimum core heat flux"
- **Q46** (option): "fast flux to thermal flux" -> "peak heat flux on the hottest fuel rod to the average heat flux of the coolest fuel rod"
- **Q66** (option): "From the point where the pump curve meets zero flow" -> "From the point where the pump curve meets zero flow, known as the shutoff head of the pump"
- **Q67** (option): "The pump develops its maximum head at a set speed" -> "The pump develops its maximum head at a set speed because the discharge valve is fully shut"
- **Q80** (option): "The Sodium Cover Gas System" -> "The Sodium Cover Gas System (argon cover gas above the primary sodium pool)"
- **Q90** (option): "It is hydraulically driven by the primary sodium pumps" -> "It is hydraulically driven by the primary sodium pumps and fails as-is on loss of electrical power"
- **Q98** (option): "During normal full-power operation" -> "During any loss of offsite power with the primary pumps coasting down"
- **Q107** (option): "Control rods move radially" -> "Control rods sit at the core edge, so radial expansion changes their worth more than axial expansion"
- **Q108** (option): "No feedback, because fuel temperature is constant" -> "No feedback"
- **Q114** (option): "A higher melting point than oxide fuel" -> "A higher melting point than oxide fuel, so a larger margin to fuel melting"
- **Q115** (option): "To moderate neutrons before they reach the core" -> "To keep the steam generator outside containment so its tubes can be inspected at power"
- **Q116** (option): "Its primary system runs at high pressure" -> "Its primary system runs at high pressure, which raises the sodium boiling point"
- **Q117** (option): "To reduce pumping power" -> "To keep the pipes cooler by placing them in the cover gas region"
- **Q125** (option): "Each pin carries a unique radioactive tracer detected in the sodium" -> "Each pin carries a unique radioactive tracer that delayed neutron detectors find in the sodium"
- **Q127** (option): "Pressurizer level instruments" -> "Thermocouples on the steam outlet and flow meters on the feedwater line"
- **Q128** (option): "To support the piping weight" -> "To support the piping weight and allow for thermal expansion of the lines"
- **Q129** (option): "Steam generator tube leaks" -> "Sodium-water reaction detection in full-scale steam generator tubes"
- **Q130** (option): "A control rod ejection" -> "Sodium boiling caused by a stuck-open bypass valve in the primary loop"
- **Q134** (option): "The operators inserted the control rods" -> "The control rods inserted automatically on low primary flow, bringing power to decay heat"
- **Q136** (option): "Loss of all primary flow" -> "A complete stagnation of primary flow followed by a delayed start of natural circulation"
- **Q142** (option): "Sodium voiding in the center of the core" -> "Core sodium voiding"
- **Q144** (option): "To cool the sodium faster" -> "To cool the remaining sodium faster and allow the tubes to be inspected"
- **Q145** (option): "Sodium boiling in the upper plenum" -> "Sodium boiling in the upper plenum, which voids the center of the core"
- **Q148** (option): "Hydrogen recombiners" -> "Hydrogen recombiners that keep the containment atmosphere below flammability limits"
- **Q150** (option): "A loss of flow with the reactor kept at power" -> "A loss of flow with the reactor kept at 5% power for about 30 hours on pony motors"
- **Q151** (option): "To vent the cover gas" -> "To raise the sodium temperature so the pony motors could be restarted"
- **Q167** (option): "Provide HVAC for personnel comfort, freeze protection and equipment operability" -> "Provide Nuclear Island HVAC"
- **Q186** (option): "Provide a controlled sodium environment for temporary storage of new and irradiated core assemblies" -> "Store new and irradiated core assemblies in sodium"
- **Q194** (option): "Process cover gas waste streams and hold them up so radioactive isotopes such as argon-41 decay" -> "Process and hold up gaseous radwaste"
- **Q198** (option): "Suppress and control fire with water, clean agents and chemical means" -> "Suppress and control fire with water, clean agents and chemical means, and detect fires with smoke and heat detectors"
- **Q217** (option): "Manual start of the RAC blowers by operators" -> "Manual start of the RAC blowers by operators from the main control room after the reactor trip"
- **Q218** (option): "Its primary sodium pumps run at full speed on backup power" -> "Its primary sodium pumps run at reduced speed on backup power to force sodium through the intermediate heat exchangers"
- **Q222** (option): "To keep the cesium trap in service" -> "To keep the fuel assemblies aligned with the IVTM so damaged assemblies can be removed after the accident"
- **Q223** (option): "It inserts control rods with its own drive motors" -> "It inserts the control rods with its own drive motors, independent of the RPS and the trip breakers"
- **Q225** (option): "Steam generator tube leak detection" -> "Steam generator tube leak detection from hydrogen meters in the sodium outlet"
- **Q229** (option): "Reactivity control and reactor scram" -> "Reactivity control, criticality monitoring, and a path for emergency sodium makeup"
- **Q230** (option): "Sodium purification, cover gas supply, and leak detection" -> "Sodium purification, cover gas supply, leak detection, and transfer of assemblies back to the reactor"
- **Q232** (option): "It stores emergency makeup sodium" -> "It stores emergency makeup sodium that drains to the reactor vessel if the level falls"
- **Q236** (option): "The coils" -> "The copper windings of the stator coils"
- **Q238** (option): "Gas keeps the detector from overheating" -> "Gas keeps the detector from overheating when it is exposed to high radiation fields"
- **Q239** (option): "Neutrons directly ionize the gas" -> "Neutrons directly ionize the gas because they carry a charge as they enter"
- **Q240** (option): "Gamma rays are blocked by the U-235 coating" -> "Gamma rays are absorbed by the U-235 coating before they can reach the argon fill gas"
- **Q242** (option): text removed in ECI review.
- **Q247** (option): "High" -> "To the maximum of the indicated range"
- **Q248** (option): "They are burned out by fast neutrons" -> "They are burned out quickly by the high fast neutron flux in the core"
- **Q249** (option): "From the change in core inlet temperature" -> "From the change in core inlet temperature and the primary sodium flow rate over the cycle"
- **Q266** (option): "It removes impurities from the sodium" -> "It removes impurities from the sodium, like a cold trap, while it measures them"
- **Q274** (option): "Guides the arc away from the breaker operator" -> "Guides the arc away from the breaker operator and vents the hot gases out of the case"
- **Q282** (option): "Full closed" -> "Full closed, normally the spring-return position of the valve"
- **Q283** (option): "Plates transfer less heat than tubes" -> "Plates transfer less heat than tubes for the same surface area and flow rate"
- **Q289** (option): "A delayed neutron, because it is born later" -> "A delayed neutron, because it is born with more kinetic energy than a prompt neutron"
- **Q310** (option): "A process with no heat transfer into or out of the system" -> "A process with no heat transfer into or out of the system, such as flow through a well-insulated turbine"
- **Q319** (option): "To regulate reactor temperature" -> "To regulate reactor temperature by removing heat from the primary sodium"
- **Q340** (option): "Discharge pressure minus saturation pressure" -> "Discharge pressure minus the saturation pressure of the fluid being pumped"
- **Q350** (option): "Turn the handwheel in the open direction to confirm it moves" -> "Turn the handwheel a short distance in the open direction; checking toward open avoids disturbing an isolation"
- **Q359** (option): "Senses valve position for the control room only" -> "Senses valve stem position and sends it to the control room for indication"
- **Q360** (option): "It uses a compensating chamber to subtract gamma current" -> "It uses a compensating chamber to subtract the gamma-induced current from the total detector current"
- **Q363** (option): "Reactivity increase from higher coolant temperature, always positive" -> "Reactivity change per degree of fuel temperature, which is negative because of Doppler broadening of U-238 resonances"
- **Q364** (option): "Reduced neutron leakage" -> "Reduced neutron leakage from the core as the sodium density falls"
- **Q366** (option): "Reactivity change per degree of fuel temperature; positive at end of life" -> "Reactivity change per degree of fuel temperature; positive at end of life because Pu-239 builds up in the fuel"
- **Q371** (option): "So that control rods can be withdrawn faster" -> "So that control rods can be withdrawn faster during a startup without a period trip"
- **Q372** (option): "The worth of the most reactive control rod" -> "The worth of the most reactive control rod during a rod withdrawal accident"
- **Q374** (option): "The coolant density increases" -> "The coolant density increases as the rods leave the core, so more neutrons are moderated"
- **Q376** (option): "Control rod absorber burns out" -> "Control rod absorber burns out faster at higher temperature"

### ES-4.2 D.15.h, p. 16 (8 changes)
> "words such as "never" or "always" that suggest an incorrect option"

- **Q149** (option): "Offsite consequences are always zero for SFRs" -> "CDF and LRF cannot be calculated for a pool-type reactor with unpressurized coolant"
- **Q231** (option): "None; it has no safety classification" -> "Controlling reactivity"
- **Q356** (option): "It always overshoots setpoint" -> "It overshoots setpoint on large step changes in the process variable"
- **Q56** (option): "None, because heat production stops when fission stops" -> "About 20% immediately, falling to about 5% within one hour"
- **Q284** (option): "Its hottest cold-fluid temperature is always below the coldest hot-fluid temperature" -> "Its hottest cold-fluid temperature stays below the coldest hot-fluid temperature"
- **Q335** (option): "Elevation head always exceeds velocity and pressure heads combined" -> "Elevation head exceeds velocity and pressure heads combined"
- **Q367** (option): "Removes them entirely" -> "Shifts them to higher energy with no change in capture"
- **Q122** (option): "It is done only at power" -> "With the reactor at power"

### ES-4.2 D.4, p. 11 (9 changes)
> "Do not present a collection of true/false (T/F) statements as a multiple-choice item."

- **Q295** (stem): "Which statement about a subcritical reactor is correct?" -> "In a subcritical reactor, how does the steady-state subcritical neutron level relate to the neutron source strength?"
- **Q295** (option): "Doubling count rate reduces the margin to criticality by about one quarter" -> "It is inversely proportional to the source strength"
- **Q295** (option): "The subcritical neutron level is directly proportional to the neutron source strength" -> "It is directly proportional to the source strength"
- **Q295** (option): "A given rod withdrawal gives the same count rate increase at keff 0.88 or 0.92" -> "It is proportional to the square of the source strength"
- **Q295** (option): "Equal reactivity additions reach equilibrium count rate faster as keff approaches 1" -> "It does not depend on the source strength"
- **Q312** (stem): "Which statement about entropy is correct?" -> "What does a change in entropy indicate?"
- **Q312** (option): "Entropy always decreases, so order naturally increases" -> "The amount of energy that disappears in the process"
- **Q312** (option): "Entropy shows that energy disappears in every process" -> "The rate at which the process proceeds toward equilibrium"
- **Q312** (option): "Entropy means all processes lead to chaos" -> "The work the process does on its surroundings during a cycle"

### ES-4.2 D.7, p. 13 (2 changes)

- **Q248** (stem): "Why do gaseous fission product poisons NOT pose a significant negative reactivity factor in a sodium fast reactor?" -> "Why do gaseous fission product poisons have little negative reactivity effect in a sodium fast reactor?"

- **Q31** (option): "3.7 x 10^10 per second" -> "1.67 x 10^-24 MeV per amu"

## 2026-11-02: Q295 explanation

At the user's confirmation, Q295's explanation was replaced to match its rewritten stem. Source: Approved lesson plan, Power Changes (Power Changes.docx), knowledge-check feedback.
> "If source strength (So) is doubled (for a given keff), total neutron population (Nt) would also double (directly proportional)."

- **Q295** (explanation): "Near criticality, equilibrium takes longer and the same reactivity addition gives a much larger count rate change; doubling count rate halves the margin." -> "If source strength (So) is doubled (for a given keff), total neutron population (Nt) would also double (directly proportional)."

## 2026-11-04: DOE-1017-V2 (Material Science, Vol 2)

Added 8 quiz questions and 10 flashcards. Every quote was matched against work/text/DOE-HDBK-1017-93_VOL2.txt.

- **C389** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What operational limits reduce the severity of thermal shock?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Thermal Stress, MS-03 p. 5 (PDF page 23)
  - Quote: "Operational limits to reduce the severity of thermal shock include: Heatup and cooldown rate limits Temperature limits for placing systems into operation Specific temperatures for specific pressures for system operation"
- **C390** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is pressurized thermal shock (PTS)?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Pressurized Thermal Shock, MS-03 p. 6 (PDF page 24)
  - Quote: "Shock experienced by a thick-walled vessel due to the combined stresses from a rapid temperature and/or pressure change."
- **C391** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): During system heatup, which vessel wall location is limiting, and why?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Pressurized Thermal Shock, MS-03 p. 7 (PDF page 25)
  - Quote: "For this reason the 3/4 T location is limiting during system heatup."
  - Figure: images/doe-1017-v2-ms-03-fig2.png
- **C392** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): During system cooldown, which vessel wall location is limiting?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Pressurized Thermal Shock, MS-03 p. 7 (PDF page 25)
  - Quote: "Thus, the 1/4 T location is limiting during system cooldown."
  - Figure: images/doe-1017-v2-ms-03-fig3.png
- **C393** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What three conditions does brittle fracture require?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Brittle Fracture Mechanism, MS-04 p. 6 (PDF page 40)
  - Quote: "Brittle fracture requires three conditions: Flaw such as a crack Stress sufficient to develop a small deformation at the crack tip Temperature at or below NDT"
- **C394** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is the nil-ductility transition (NDT) temperature?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Brittle Fracture Mechanism, MS-04 p. 6 (PDF page 40)
  - Quote: "Nil-Ductility Transition (NDT) temperature is the temperature above which a material is ductile and below which it is brittle."
  - Figure: images/doe-1017-v2-ms-04-fig2.png
- **C395** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which components limit heatup and cooldown rates?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Heatup and Cooldown Rate Limits, MS-04 p. 13 (PDF page 47)
  - Quote: "Large components such as flanges, reactor vessel head, and the vessel itself are the limiting components."
- **C396** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What causes thermal fatigue?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Plant Material Problems, MS-05 p. 31 (PDF page 91)
  - Quote: "Thermal fatigue results from thermal stresses produced by cyclic changes in temperature."
- **C397** (Control Rods): What are the advantages of boron as a control material?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Control Materials, MS-05 p. 17 (PDF page 77)
  - Quote: "Very high thermal-absorption cross-section and low cost."
- **C398** (Core Thermal Limits): What operational limit lessens fuel pellet-cladding interaction (PCI)?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Nuclear Reactor Core Problems, MS-05 p. 25 (PDF page 85)
  - Quote: "Plant procedures limit the maximum permissible rate at which power may be increased to lessen the effect of PCI."
- **Q379** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): How do smaller grain size and irradiation affect the NDT temperature?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Brittle Fracture Mechanism, MS-04 p. 6 (PDF page 40)
  - Quote: "NDT decreases due to smaller grain size and increases due to irradiation"
- **Q380** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What does irradiation do to the minimum pressurization-temperature (MPT) curve?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Minimum Pressurization-Temperature Curves, MS-04 p. 10 (PDF page 44)
  - Quote: "MPT curve will shift to the right due to irradiation."
- **Q381** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is the first normal action if MPT curves are exceeded during critical operation?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Minimum Pressurization-Temperature Curves, MS-04 p. 10 (PDF page 44)
  - Quote: "Normal actions if MPT curves are exceeded during critical operation are: Scram reactor Cool down and depressurize Conduct engineering evaluation prior to further plant operation"
- **Q382** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Heatup and cooldown rate limits are based on the impact on the plant's future:
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Heatup and Cooldown Rate Limits, MS-04 p. 13 (PDF page 47)
  - Quote: "Heatup and cooldown rate limits are based upon impact on the future fatigue life of the plant."
- **Q383** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Why is thermal stress a major concern?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Thermal Stress, MS-03 p. 5 (PDF page 23)
  - Quote: "Thermal stress is a major concern due to the magnitude of the stresses involved with rapid heating (or cooling)."
- **Q384** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Why does pressure in a closed system raise the severity of thermal shock?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Pressurized Thermal Shock, MS-03 p. 8 (PDF page 26)
  - Quote: "Pressure in closed system raises the severity of thermal shock due to the additive effect of thermal and pressure tensile stresses on the inside reactor vessel wall."
- **Q385** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): In the figure, what happens to tensile strength and yield strength as temperature goes down?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Brittle Fracture Mechanism, MS-04 p. 3 (PDF page 37)
  - Quote: "Figure 2 illustrates that as the temperature goes down, the tensile strength (Curve A) and the yield strength (Curve B) increase."
  - Figure: images/doe-1017-v2-ms-04-fig2.png
- **Q386** (Core Thermal Limits): What can fuel pellet-cladding interaction (PCI) lead to?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Nuclear Reactor Core Problems, MS-05 p. 25 (PDF page 85)
  - Quote: "PCI may lead to cladding failure and subsequent release of fission products into the reactor coolant."

### Figures

- **doe-1017-v2-ms-03-fig2.png** (24 KB, in flashcards): Figure 2. Heatup Stress Profile. Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), MS-03 p. 7. PDF page 25. Alt text: Reactor vessel wall stress profile during heatup. Pressure stress and temperature-induced stress are plotted between the inner and outer wall, with tensile stress to the right and compressive stress to the left, and the 1/4T and 3/4T locations marked.
- **doe-1017-v2-ms-03-fig3.png** (25 KB, in flashcards): Figure 3. Cooldown Stress Profile. Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), MS-03 p. 7. PDF page 25. Alt text: Reactor vessel wall stress profile during cooldown, with the same layout as the heatup profile. Pressure stress and temperature-induced stress are plotted between the inner and outer wall at the 1/4T and 3/4T locations.
- **doe-1017-v2-ms-04-fig2.png** (64 KB, in flashcards and quiz): Figure 2. Stress-Temperature Diagram for Crack Initiation and Arrest. Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), MS-04 p. 3. PDF page 37. Alt text: Graph of stress against temperature. Tensile strength and yield strength curves rise as temperature falls and meet at the NDT with no flaw, near 10 degrees F. The NDT with a small flaw is near 60 degrees F, and the crack arrest curve rises to the FTE and FTP points near 70 degrees F.

## 2026-11-04: DOE-1013-V1 (Instrumentation and Control, Vol 1)

Added 7 quiz questions and 10 flashcards. Every quote was matched against work/text/DOE-HDBK-1013-92-VOL1.txt.

- **C399** (Sensors and Detectors): How does the resistance of an RTD change with temperature?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Resistance Temperature Detectors, IC-01 p. 4 (PDF page 22)
  - Quote: "The resistance of an RTD varies directly with temperature: - As temperature increases, resistance increases."
- **C400** (Sensors and Detectors): In a thermocouple, what does the voltmeter measure?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Thermocouples, IC-01 p. 7 (PDF page 25)
  - Quote: "The difference between the two voltages is proportional to the difference in temperature and can be measured on a voltmeter."
  - Figure: images/doe-1013-v1-ic-01-fig6.png
- **C401** (Sensors and Detectors): When is a temperature bridge circuit considered balanced?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Temperature Detection Circuitry, IC-01 p. 16 (PDF page 34)
  - Quote: "The bridge circuit is considered balanced when the sensing ammeter reads zero current."
- **C402** (Sensors and Detectors): Why does a bourdon tube move as pressure rises?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detectors, IC-02 p. 3 (PDF page 45)
  - Quote: "As pressure increases, the tube tends to restore to its original round cross-section. This change in cross-section causes the tube to straighten."
  - Figure: images/doe-1013-v1-ic-02-fig2.png
- **C403** (Sensors and Detectors): How does a strain gauge sense pressure?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detection Circuitry, IC-02 p. 13 (PDF page 55)
  - Quote: "A strain gauge measures the pressure applied to a fine wire."
- **C404** (Sensors and Detectors): In a closed tank with a wet reference leg, how does transmitter output relate to tank level?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Level Detectors, IC-03 p. 9 (PDF page 73)
  - Quote: "As a result, the differential pressure and the transmitter output are inversely proportional to the tank level."
  - Figure: images/doe-1013-v1-ic-03-fig11.png
- **C405** (Sensors and Detectors): By what three means is level density compensation accomplished?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Density Compensation, IC-03 p. 14 (PDF page 78)
  - Quote: "Density compensation is accomplished by using either: - Electronic circuitry - Pressure detector input - Instrument calibration"
- **C406** (Sensors and Detectors): What are three major reasons for remote level indication?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Level Detection Circuitry, IC-03 p. 17 (PDF page 81)
  - Quote: "There are three major reasons for utilizing remote level indication: - Level measurements may be taken at locations far from the main facility. - The level to be controlled may be a long distance from the point of control. - The level being measured may be in an unsafe/radioactive area."
- **C407** (Sensors and Detectors): What does the extractor do in a differential pressure flow circuit?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Flow Circuitry, IC-04 p. 19 (PDF page 109)
  - Quote: "The extractor is used to electronically calculate the square root of the differential pressure and to provide an output proportional to system flow."
- **C408** (Sensors and Detectors): What does a basic synchro system consist of?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Synchro Equipment, IC-05 p. 4 (PDF page 122)
  - Quote: "A basic synchro system consists of a transmitter (synchro generator) and receiver (synchro motor)."
- **Q387** (Sensors and Detectors): In the wet reference leg system shown, what happens to differential pressure as tank level goes down?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Level Detectors, IC-03 p. 9 (PDF page 73)
  - Quote: "As the tank level goes down, the pressure applied to the low pressure side goes down also, and the differential pressure increases."
  - Figure: images/doe-1013-v1-ic-03-fig11.png
- **Q388** (Sensors and Detectors): In a wet reference leg system, what is the differential pressure when liquid level is at its maximum?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Level Detectors, IC-03 p. 9 (PDF page 73)
  - Quote: "The ∆P transmitter is exposed to equal pressure on the high and low pressure sides when the liquid level is at its maximum; therefore, the differential pressure is zero."
- **Q389** (Sensors and Detectors): Heating a thermocouple's measuring junction produces a voltage that is:
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Thermocouples, IC-01 p. 7 (PDF page 25)
  - Quote: "Heating the measuring junction of the thermocouple produces a voltage that is greater than the voltage across the reference junction."
  - Figure: images/doe-1013-v1-ic-01-fig6.png
- **Q390** (Sensors and Detectors): What greatly affects indicated steam flow?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Steam Flow Detection, IC-04 p. 16 (PDF page 106)
  - Quote: "Changes in temperature and pressure greatly affect indicated steam flow."
- **Q391** (Sensors and Detectors): Head flow meters operate by:
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Head Flow Meters, IC-04 p. 7 (PDF page 97)
  - Quote: "Head flow meters operate on the principle of placing a restriction in the line to cause a pressure drop."
- **Q392** (Sensors and Detectors): In a reed switch position indicator, what happens as the magnet approaches the switch?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Switches, IC-05 p. 6 (PDF page 124)
  - Quote: "As the magnet approaches the reed switch, the switch shuts."
- **Q393** (Sensors and Detectors): What does an LVDT use as the movable core of a transformer?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Variable Output Devices, IC-05 p. 10 (PDF page 128)
  - Quote: "An LVDT uses the extension shaft or control rod as a movable core of a transformer."

### Figures

- **doe-1013-v1-ic-01-fig6.png** (27 KB, in flashcards and quiz): Figure 6. Simple Thermocouple Circuit. Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), IC-01 p. 6. PDF page 24. Alt text: Two dissimilar metal wires joined at a hot measuring junction above a heat source and at a cold reference junction, with a voltmeter connected in the circuit.
- **doe-1013-v1-ic-02-fig2.png** (37 KB, in flashcards): Figure 2. Bourdon Tube. Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), IC-02 p. 2. PDF page 44. Alt text: Bourdon tube gauge. Inlet pressure enters a curved tube linked through a mechanical linkage and pinion to a pointer on a dial. Cross sections show the tube flattened with no internal pressure and rounder with internal pressure.
- **doe-1013-v1-ic-03-fig11.png** (19 KB, in flashcards and quiz): Figure 11. Closed Tank, Wet Reference Leg. Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), IC-03 p. 9. PDF page 73. Alt text: Closed tank with a differential pressure transmitter. The high pressure side connects to a liquid-filled wet reference leg with a fill connection, tied into the tank at the maximum detectable level. The low pressure side connects to the tank at the minimum detectable level.

## 2026-11-04: DOE-1013-V2 (Instrumentation and Control, Vol 2)

Added 10 quiz questions and 11 flashcards. Every quote was matched against work/text/DOE-HDBK-1013-92-VOL2.txt.

- **C409** (Sensors and Detectors): What is specific ionization?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Radiation Detection Terminology, IC-06 p. 1 (PDF page 25)
  - Quote: "Specific ionization is that number of ion pairs produced per centimeter of travel through matter."
- **C410** (Sensors and Detectors): What is gas amplification?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Gas-Filled Detector, IC-06 p. 13 (PDF page 37)
  - Quote: "This multiplication of electrons is called gas amplification."
  - Figure: images/doe-1013-v2-ic-06-fig8.png
- **C411** (Sensors and Detectors): Why is a quenching gas added to a proportional counter?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Proportional Counter, IC-06 p. 22 (PDF page 46)
  - Quote: "A quenching gas is added to give up electrons to the chamber gas so that inaccuracies are NOT introduced due to ionizations caused by the positive ion."
- **C412** (Sensors and Detectors): How is gamma sensitivity reduced in an ionization chamber?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Ionization Chamber, IC-06 p. 34 (PDF page 58)
  - Quote: "Gamma sensitivity reduction is accomplished by either reducing the amount of chamber gas or increasing the boron coated surface area."
- **C413** (Sensors and Detectors): How does a compensated ion chamber cancel gamma current?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Compensated Ion Chamber, IC-06 p. 39 (PDF page 63)
  - Quote: "The voltages to each chamber are set so that the current from the gammas in the boron-coated chamber cancels the current from the gammas in the uncoated chamber."
  - Figure: images/doe-1013-v2-ic-06-fig19.png
- **C414** (Sensors and Detectors): What does a multichannel analyzer do in a gamma spectrometer?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Gamma Spectroscopy, IC-06 p. 50 (PDF page 74)
  - Quote: "A multichannel analyzer separates the pulses based on pulse height."
- **C415** (Sensors and Detectors): What does decades per minute measure?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Circuitry and Circuit Elements, IC-06 p. 62 (PDF page 86)
  - Quote: "Decades per minute is the rate at which neutron flux is changing by a power of 10 in each minute."
- **C416** (Controllers and Positioners): What separates an open-loop from a closed-loop control system?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Principles of Control Systems, IC-07 p. 2 (PDF page 110)
  - Quote: "An open-loop control system is one in which the control action is independent of the output."
- **C417** (Controllers and Positioners): What is the proportional band?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Proportional Control Systems, IC-07 p. 27 (PDF page 135)
  - Quote: "The proportional band is the change in input required to produce a full range of change in the output due to the proportional control action."
- **C418** (Controllers and Positioners): What is an inherent disadvantage of proportional plus reset controllers subject to large error signals?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Proportional Plus Reset Control Systems, IC-07 p. 36 (PDF page 144)
  - Quote: "Reset windup is an inherent disadvantage of proportional plus reset controllers that are subject to large error signals."
- **C419** (Controllers and Positioners): What does each action in a PID controller do?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), PID Control Systems, IC-07 p. 46 (PDF page 154)
  - Quote: "The proportional action responds to the error amplitude. The integral action eliminates the offset error. The derivative action provides additional stability to the process."
- **Q394** (Sensors and Detectors): On the gas ionization curve shown, which region collects all ion pairs with no gas amplification?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Detector Voltage, IC-06 p. 18 (PDF page 42)
  - Quote: "The voltage is sufficient to ensure all ion pairs produced by the incident radiation are collected. No gas amplification takes place."
  - Figure: images/doe-1013-v2-ic-06-fig8.png
- **Q395** (Sensors and Detectors): In a compensated ion chamber, what interacts in the uncoated chamber?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Compensated Ion Chamber, IC-06 p. 39 (PDF page 63)
  - Quote: "Only gammas interact in the uncoated chamber."
  - Figure: images/doe-1013-v2-ic-06-fig19.png
- **Q396** (Sensors and Detectors): Why is a quenching gas used in a Geiger-Müller detector?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Geiger-Müller Detector, IC-06 p. 44 (PDF page 68)
  - Quote: "A quenching gas is used in order to prevent a secondary pulse due to ionization by the positive ions."
- **Q397** (Sensors and Detectors): In a self-powered neutron detector, what does the central wire do?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Miscellaneous Detectors, IC-06 p. 54 (PDF page 78)
  - Quote: "The central wire, made of a neutron-absorbing material, absorbs a neutron and undergoes beta decay."
- **Q398** (Sensors and Detectors): In a scintillation counter, what happens when an excited crystal center de-excites?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Scintillation Counter, IC-06 p. 48 (PDF page 72)
  - Quote: "When the center de-excites, the crystal emits a photon in the visible light range."
- **Q399** (Sensors and Detectors): What does the discriminator do in a source range channel?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Source Range Nuclear Instrumentation, IC-06 p. 64 (PDF page 88)
  - Quote: "The discriminator excludes passage of pulses that are less than a predetermined level."
- **Q400** (Controllers and Positioners): In the closed-loop system shown, the level signal to the controller is an example of:
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Principles of Control Systems, IC-07 p. 3 (PDF page 111)
  - Quote: "Feedback is information in a closed-loop control system about the condition of a process variable."
  - Figure: images/doe-1013-v2-ic-07-fig2.png
- **Q401** (Controllers and Positioners): Why is the integral control mode not normally used by itself?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Reset (Integral) Control Systems, IC-07 p. 32 (PDF page 140)
  - Quote: "The integral control mode is not normally used by itself because of its slow response to an error signal."
- **Q402** (Controllers and Positioners): What is true of proportional plus rate control?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Proportional Plus Rate Control Systems, IC-07 p. 42 (PDF page 150)
  - Quote: "Proportional plus rate control does not eliminate offset error."
- **Q403** (Controllers and Positioners): Deviation is the difference between a process variable's:
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Two Position Control Systems, IC-07 p. 20 (PDF page 128)
  - Quote: "Deviation is the difference between the setpoint of a process variable and its actual value."

### Figures

- **doe-1013-v2-ic-06-fig8.png** (19 KB, in flashcards and quiz): Figure 8. Gas Ionization Curve. Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), IC-06 p. 20. PDF page 44. Alt text: Graph of number of electrons collected, on a log scale, against detector voltage from 0 to about 1800 volts, showing the recombination region rising, the flat ionization region, and the rising proportional region.
- **doe-1013-v2-ic-06-fig19.png** (16 KB, in flashcards and quiz): Figure 19. Compensated Ion Chamber. Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), IC-06 p. 35. PDF page 59. Alt text: Two circuit drawings of a compensated ion chamber. A boron-lined chamber A and an unlined chamber B are connected to an electrometer with opposing voltage supplies, so the electrometer current equals neutron current minus gamma current.
- **doe-1013-v2-ic-07-fig2.png** (25 KB, in quiz): Figure 2. Closed-Loop Control System. Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), IC-07 p. 3. PDF page 111. Alt text: Water storage tank with a level transmitter sending a level signal to a level controller, which sends a control signal to a level control valve on the tank supply line. Demand by system leaves the bottom of the tank.

## 2026-11-04: DOE-1017-V1 (Material Science, Vol 1)

Added 6 quiz questions and 7 flashcards. Every quote was matched against work/text/DOE-HDBK-1017-93_VOL1.txt.

- **C420** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is stress?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Stress, MS-02 p. 6 (PDF page 58)
  - Quote: "Stress is the internal resistance of a material to the distorting effects of an external force or load."
- **C421** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is strain?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Strain, MS-02 p. 10 (PDF page 62)
  - Quote: "Strain is the proportional dimensional change, or the intensity or degree of distortion, in a material under stress."
- **C422** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is plastic deformation?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Strain, MS-02 p. 10 (PDF page 62)
  - Quote: "Plastic deformation is the dimensional change that does not disappear when the initiating stress is removed."
- **C423** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): State Hooke's Law.
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Young's Modulus, MS-02 p. 14 (PDF page 66)
  - Quote: "Hooke's Law states that in the elastic range of a material strain is proportional to stress."
- **C424** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is yield strength?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Physical Properties, MS-02 p. 28 (PDF page 80)
  - Quote: "Yield strength is the stress at which a predetermined amount of permanent deformation occurs."
  - Figure: images/doe-1017-v1-ms-02-fig5.png
- **C425** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is ultimate tensile strength (UTS)?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Physical Properties, MS-02 p. 21 (PDF page 73)
  - Quote: "Ultimate tensile strength (UTS) is the maximum resistance to fracture."
  - Figure: images/doe-1017-v1-ms-02-fig5.png
- **C426** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is creep?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Grain Structure and Boundary, MS-01 p. 9 (PDF page 27)
  - Quote: "Creep is the permanent deformation that increases with time under constant load or stress."
- **Q404** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which conditions decrease ductility?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Physical Properties, MS-02 p. 28 (PDF page 80)
  - Quote: "Ductility decreases with lower temperatures, cold working, and irradiation."
- **Q405** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): How does heat treatment affect steel?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Working of Metals, MS-02 p. 31 (PDF page 83)
  - Quote: "Hardness and tensile strength increase in heat-treated steel; toughness and ductility decrease."
- **Q406** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Small grain size in a metal:
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Grain Structure and Boundary, MS-01 p. 11 (PDF page 29)
  - Quote: "Small grain size increases tensile strength and ductility."
- **Q407** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Compressive stress is the reverse of:
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Stress, MS-02 p. 4 (PDF page 56)
  - Quote: "Compressive stress is the reverse of tensile stress."
- **Q408** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): In steel, hydrogen embrittlement results from hydrogen combining with carbon to form:
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Hydrogen Embrittlement, MS-02 p. 39 (PDF page 91)
  - Quote: "Hydrogen embrittlement is the result of hydrogen that diffuses along the grain boundaries and combines with the carbon to form methane gas."
- **Q409** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): How are welding stresses minimized?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Working of Metals, MS-02 p. 31 (PDF page 83)
  - Quote: "Stresses are minimized by using heat sink welding and annealing"

### Figures

- **doe-1017-v1-ms-02-fig5.png** (27 KB, in flashcards): Figure 5. Typical Brittle Material Stress-Strain Curve. Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), MS-02 p. 22. PDF page 74. Alt text: Stress-strain curve with stress on the vertical axis and elongation in percent on the horizontal axis. Numbered points mark the proportional limit, yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and fracture point within about 1 percent elongation.

## 2026-11-04: DOE-1010 (Classical Physics)

Added 6 quiz questions and 8 flashcards. Every quote was matched against work/text/DOE-HDBK-1010-92.txt.

- **C427** (Basic Energy Concepts): What is energy?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Energy and Work, CP-05 p. 5 (PDF page 135)
  - Quote: "Energy is the ability to do work."
- **C428** (Basic Energy Concepts): What is kinetic energy?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Energy and Work, CP-05 p. 5 (PDF page 135)
  - Quote: "Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because of its motion."
- **C429** (Basic Energy Concepts): What is potential energy?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Energy and Work, CP-05 p. 5 (PDF page 135)
  - Quote: "Potential energy is the energy of an object due to its position."
- **C430** (Basic Energy Concepts): How is the work done by a force defined?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Energy and Work, CP-05 p. 5 (PDF page 135)
  - Quote: "The work done by a force on an object is the product of the force and the distance the object moves in the direction of the force."
- **C431** (Basic Energy Concepts): State the law of conservation of energy.
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Law of Conservation of Energy, CP-05 p. 6 (PDF page 136)
  - Quote: "Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only altered in form."
- **C432** (Basic Energy Concepts): What is power?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Power, CP-05 p. 11 (PDF page 141)
  - Quote: "Power is the amount of energy used per unit time."
- **C433** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): What are derived units?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Fundamental Dimensions, CP-01 p. 8 (PDF page 26)
  - Quote: "Derived units are made up of a combination of units to describe various physical quantities."
- **C434** (Basic Energy Concepts): State the conservation of momentum.
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Momentum Principles, CP-03 p. 10 (PDF page 92)
  - Quote: "The conservation of momentum states that if no net external force acts upon a system, the momentum of the system remains constant."
- **Q410** (Basic Energy Concepts): Under Newton's first law, an object moves in a straight line with constant velocity when:
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Newton's Laws of Motion, CP-03 p. 1 (PDF page 83)
  - Quote: "An object remains at rest (if originally at rest) or moves in a straight line with constant velocity if the net force on it is zero."
- **Q411** (Basic Energy Concepts): Under Newton's third law, the forces of action and reaction between interacting bodies are:
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Newton's Laws of Motion, CP-03 p. 4 (PDF page 86)
  - Quote: "The forces of action and reaction between interacting bodies are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction."
- **Q412** (Basic Energy Concepts): An object is in equilibrium when:
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Force Equilibrium, CP-04 p. 12 (PDF page 112)
  - Quote: "If the vector sum of all the forces acting on an object is equal to zero, then the object is in equilibrium."
- **Q413** (Basic Energy Concepts): What does a free-body diagram do?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Free-Body Diagrams, CP-04 p. 10 (PDF page 110)
  - Quote: "A free-body diagram isolates a body and illustrates all the forces that act on the body"
  - Figure: images/doe-1010-cp-04-fig3.png
- **Q414** (Basic Energy Concepts): Weight is the force exerted on an object due to:
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Force and Weight, CP-04 p. 4 (PDF page 104)
  - Quote: "Weight is the force exerted on an object due to gravity."
- **Q415** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): A tensile force tends to:
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Types of Force, CP-04 p. 21 (PDF page 121)
  - Quote: "A tensile force is an applied force that tends to pull an object apart."

### Figures

- **doe-1010-cp-04-fig3.png** (9 KB, in quiz): Figure 3. Free-Body Diagram. Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), CP-04 p. 8. PDF page 108. Alt text: Free-body diagram of a car with four force arrows from its center: normal force N upward, weight W downward, applied force F app to the right, and kinetic friction F k to the left.

## 2026-11-04: DOE-1011-V1 (Electrical Science, Vol 1)

Added 5 quiz questions and 7 flashcards. Every quote was matched against work/text/DOE-HDBK-1011-92_VOL1.txt.

- **C435** (Sensors and Detectors): What do thermocouples convert, and into what?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1011/1-92), DC Sources, ES-02 p. 11 (PDF page 107)
  - Quote: "Thermocouples convert energy from temperature into a DC voltage."
- **C436** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What is a short circuit?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1011/1-92), DC Circuit Terminology, ES-02 p. 22 (PDF page 118)
  - Quote: "A short circuit is a circuit with a path that has little or no resistance to current flow."
- **C437** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What is an open circuit?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1011/1-92), DC Circuit Terminology, ES-02 p. 22 (PDF page 118)
  - Quote: "An open circuit is one that does not have a complete path for current flow."
- **C438** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What does a shorted DC circuit do to circuit current?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1011/1-92), DC Circuit Faults, ES-02 p. 69 (PDF page 165)
  - Quote: "A shorted DC circuit will result in a sudden and very large increase in circuit current."
- **C439** (Motors and Generators): What causes hysteresis losses?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1011/1-92), Magnetic Circuits, ES-01 p. 44 (PDF page 68)
  - Quote: "Hysteresis losses are caused by reversing current direction thousands of times in a coil."
- **C440** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): State Kirchhoff's voltage law.
  - Source: DOE-1011-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1011/1-92), Kirchhoff's Laws, ES-02 p. 48 (PDF page 144)
  - Quote: "Kirchhoff’s voltage law states that the sum of the voltage drops around a closed loop is equal to the sum of the voltage sources of that loop."
- **C441** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): State Kirchhoff's current law.
  - Source: DOE-1011-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1011/1-92), Kirchhoff's Laws, ES-02 p. 48 (PDF page 144)
  - Quote: "Kirchhoff’s current law states that the current arriving at any junction point in a circuit is equal to the current leaving that junction."
- **Q416** (Motors and Generators): Which method of producing electricity uses coils of wire and a magnetic field in relative rotation?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1011/1-92), Methods of Producing Voltage, ES-01 p. 26 (PDF page 50)
  - Quote: "Rotating coils of wire through a stationary magnetic field or by rotating a magnetic field through a stationary coil of wire produces a potential."
- **Q417** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): Electron current flow is current flow from:
  - Source: DOE-1011-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1011/1-92), Electrical Terminology, ES-01 p. 12 (PDF page 36)
  - Quote: "Electron Current Flow - current flow from negative to positive potentials"
- **Q418** (Motors and Generators): What does a rectifier do?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1011/1-92), DC Sources, ES-02 p. 11 (PDF page 107)
  - Quote: "A rectifier converts AC to DC."
- **Q419** (Motors and Generators): How much of the sine wave does a full-wave rectifier convert?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1011/1-92), DC Sources, ES-02 p. 11 (PDF page 107)
  - Quote: "Full-wave rectifiers convert the AC to a pulsating DC and convert all of the sine wave."
- **Q420** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): An open in a series DC circuit results in:
  - Source: DOE-1011-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1011/1-92), DC Circuit Faults, ES-02 p. 69 (PDF page 165)
  - Quote: "An open series DC circuit will result in no power being consumed by any of the loads."

## 2026-11-04: DOE-1011-V2 (Electrical Science, Vol 2)

Added 6 quiz questions and 7 flashcards. Every quote was matched against work/text/DOE-HDBK-1011-92_VOL2.txt.

- **C442** (Motors and Generators): What three conditions are necessary to induce a voltage into a conductor?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1011/2-92), DC Generator Theory, ES-05 p. 12 (PDF page 90)
  - Quote: "The three conditions necessary to induce a voltage into a conductor are: - Magnetic field - Conductor - Relative motion between the two"
- **C443** (Motors and Generators): How is the terminal voltage of a DC generator adjusted?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1011/2-92), DC Generator Theory, ES-05 p. 12 (PDF page 90)
  - Quote: "The terminal voltage of a DC generator is adjusted by varying the field strength."
- **C444** (Motors and Generators): What is counter-electromotive force (CEMF)?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1011/2-92), DC Equipment Terminology, ES-05 p. 2 (PDF page 80)
  - Quote: "Counter-electromotive force (CEMF) is defined as the induced voltage that acts to counter the applied voltage in a DC motor or a DC generator."
- **C445** (Motors and Generators): Why do large DC motors need starting resistors?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1011/2-92), DC Motor Operation, ES-06 p. 14 (PDF page 118)
  - Quote: "Starting resistors are necessary for large DC motors to prevent damage due to high currents while starting the motor."
- **C446** (Motors and Generators): What two conditions produce a force on a conductor?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1011/2-92), DC Motor Theory, ES-06 p. 7 (PDF page 111)
  - Quote: "There are two conditions necessary to produce a force on a conductor: - The conductor must be carrying current. - The conductor must be within a magnetic field."
- **C447** (Motors and Generators): What is the purpose of a battery?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1011/2-92), Battery Theory, ES-04 p. 4 (PDF page 52)
  - Quote: "The purpose of a battery is to store chemical energy and to convert this chemical energy into electrical energy when the need arises."
- **C448** (Motors and Generators): What is specific gravity?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1011/2-92), Battery Terminology, ES-04 p. 1 (PDF page 49)
  - Quote: "Specific gravity is defined as the ratio comparing the weight of any liquid to the weight of an equal volume of water."
  - Figure: images/doe-1011-v2-es-04-fig6.png
- **Q421** (Motors and Generators): In what form does a capacitor store energy?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1011/2-92), Capacitance, ES-03 p. 18 (PDF page 38)
  - Quote: "A capacitor will store energy in the form of an electric field caused by the attraction"
- **Q422** (Motors and Generators): In what form does an inductor carrying DC current store energy?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1011/2-92), Inductance, ES-03 p. 8 (PDF page 28)
  - Quote: "When an inductor has a DC current flowing through it, the inductor will store energy in the form of a magnetic field."
- **Q423** (Motors and Generators): What happens to the voltage of a shunt-wound DC generator as load current increases?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1011/2-92), DC Generator Construction, ES-05 p. 18 (PDF page 96)
  - Quote: "The voltage of a shunt-wound DC generator decreases with an increase in load current."
- **Q424** (Motors and Generators): How does the torque of a shunt-wound DC motor change as speed increases?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1011/2-92), Types of DC Motors, ES-06 p. 11 (PDF page 115)
  - Quote: "A shunt-wound DC motor has a decreasing torque as speed increases."
- **Q425** (Motors and Generators): What is the adverse effect of battery gassing if the gases collect?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1011/2-92), Battery Hazards, ES-04 p. 19 (PDF page 67)
  - Quote: "The adverse effect of gassing is that if gassing occurs and the gases are allowed to collect, an explosive mixture of hydrogen and oxygen can be readily produced."
- **Q426** (Motors and Generators): The output voltage of cells connected in series equals:
  - Source: DOE-1011-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1011/2-92), Battery Operations, ES-04 p. 13 (PDF page 61)
  - Quote: "The output voltage of a battery connected in series is equal to the sum of the cell voltages."

## 2026-11-04: DOE-1011-V3 (Electrical Science, Vol 3)

Added 6 quiz questions and 7 flashcards. Every quote was matched against work/text/DOE-HDBK-1011-92_VOL3.txt.

- **C449** (Motors and Generators): What is the armature of an AC generator?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1011/3-92), AC Generator Components, ES-10 p. 4 (PDF page 104)
  - Quote: "The armature is the part of an AC generator in which output voltage is produced."
- **C450** (Motors and Generators): What is a prime mover?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1011/3-92), AC Generator Components, ES-10 p. 1 (PDF page 101)
  - Quote: "The prime mover is the component that is used to drive the AC generator."
- **C451** (Motors and Generators): What do slip rings do in an AC generator?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1011/3-92), AC Generator Components, ES-10 p. 4 (PDF page 104)
  - Quote: "Slip rings are electrical connections that are used to transfer power to and from the rotor of an AC generator."
- **C452** (Motors and Generators): What three requirements must be met to parallel AC generators?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1011/3-92), AC Generator Operation, ES-10 p. 14 (PDF page 114)
  - Quote: "There are three requirements that must be met to parallel AC generators: 1) Their terminal voltages must be equal. A mismatch may cause high currents and generator or distribution system damage. 2) Their frequencies must be equal."
- **C453** (Motors and Generators): What is impedance?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1011/3-92), Impedance, ES-08 p. 18 (PDF page 56)
  - Quote: "Impedance (Z) is the total opposition to current flow in an AC circuit."
- **C454** (Motors and Generators): In the power triangle shown, what does the angle θ represent?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1011/3-92), Power Triangle, ES-09 p. 16 (PDF page 82)
  - Quote: "θ is the angle between voltage and current."
  - Figure: images/doe-1011-v3-es-09-fig1.png
- **C455** (Controllers and Positioners): What is the purpose of a voltage regulator?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1011/3-92), Voltage Regulators, ES-11 p. 4 (PDF page 126)
  - Quote: "Purpose - to maintain the output voltage of a generator at a desired value"
- **Q427** (Motors and Generators): In a purely inductive circuit, current:
  - Source: DOE-1011-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1011/3-92), Inductance, ES-08 p. 4 (PDF page 42)
  - Quote: "Current (I) lags applied voltage (E) in a purely inductive circuit by 90° phase angle."
- **Q428** (Motors and Generators): An unbalanced three-phase circuit is indicated by:
  - Source: DOE-1011-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1011/3-92), Three-Phase Circuits, ES-09 p. 25 (PDF page 91)
  - Quote: "Unbalanced three-phase circuits are indicated by abnormally high currents in one or more of the phases."
- **Q429** (Motors and Generators): When paralleling AC generators, what can a frequency mismatch cause?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1011/3-92), AC Generator Operation, ES-10 p. 14 (PDF page 114)
  - Quote: "A mismatch in frequencies can cause one generator to "motor,""
- **Q430** (Motors and Generators): How is the frequency of an AC generator calculated?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1011/3-92), AC Generator Theory, ES-10 p. 8 (PDF page 108)
  - Quote: "The frequency of the generated voltage in an AC generator can be calculated by multiplying the number of poles by the speed of the generator and dividing by a factor of 120."
- **Q431** (Motors and Generators): The current rating of an AC generator is based on the machine's:
  - Source: DOE-1011-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1011/3-92), AC Generator Operation, ES-10 p. 14 (PDF page 114)
  - Quote: "The current rating of an AC generator is based on the insulation rating of the machine."
- **Q432** (Controllers and Positioners): In a voltage regulator, which circuit compares reference voltage to output voltage?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1011/3-92), Voltage Regulators, ES-11 p. 4 (PDF page 126)
  - Quote: "Comparison circuit - compares reference voltage to output voltage and provides an error signal to the amplification circuit"

## 2026-11-04: DOE-1011-V4 (Electrical Science, Vol 4)

Added 7 quiz questions and 9 flashcards. Every quote was matched against work/text/DOE-HDBK-1011-92_VOL4.txt.

- **C456** (Motors and Generators): What is slip in an AC motor?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), AC Motor Theory, ES-12 p. 8 (PDF page 28)
  - Quote: "Slip is the percentage difference between the speed of the rotor and the speed of the rotating magnetic field."
- **C457** (Motors and Generators): Why is a synchronous motor not self-starting?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), AC Motor Types, ES-12 p. 15 (PDF page 35)
  - Quote: "A synchronous motor is not a self-starting motor because torque is only developed when running at synchronous speed."
- **C458** (Motors and Generators): What is starting torque in an induction motor?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), AC Motor Theory, ES-12 p. 7 (PDF page 27)
  - Quote: "Starting torque is the value of torque at 100% slip and is normally 150 to 200% of full-load torque."
  - Figure: images/doe-1011-v4-es-12-fig4.png
- **C459** (Motors and Generators): What is a transformer turns ratio?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Transformer Theory, ES-13 p. 2 (PDF page 46)
  - Quote: "The turns ratio is defined as the ratio of turns of wire in the primary winding to the number of turns of wire in the secondary winding."
- **C460** (Sensors and Detectors): What does a megger measure?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Test Equipment, ES-14 p. 30 (PDF page 102)
  - Quote: "Meggers measure insulation resistance."
- **C461** (Sensors and Detectors): How is a ground detector connected?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Other Electrical Measuring Devices, ES-14 p. 27 (PDF page 99)
  - Quote: "Measures conductor insulation Connected out of circuit to ground"
  - Figure: images/doe-1011-v4-es-14-fig16.png
- **C462** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What is the purpose of a circuit breaker?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Circuit Breakers, ES-15 p. 14 (PDF page 126)
  - Quote: "The purpose of a circuit breaker is to provide a means for connecting and disconnecting circuits of relatively high capacities without causing damage to them."
- **C463** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What are the three most commonly-used automatic trip features for a circuit breaker?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Circuit Breakers, ES-15 p. 14 (PDF page 126)
  - Quote: "The three most commonly-used automatic trip features for a circuit breaker are overcurrent, underfrequency, and undervoltage."
- **C464** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What does a motor controller do?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Motor Controllers, ES-15 p. 20 (PDF page 132)
  - Quote: "Motor controller - controls and protects the operation of a motor"
- **Q433** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What does a low voltage protection (LVP) controller do on low voltage?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Motor Controllers, ES-15 p. 20 (PDF page 132)
  - Quote: "LVP - de-energizes motor on low voltage and keeps it from automatically restarting"
- **Q434** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What does a low voltage release (LVR) controller do on low voltage?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Motor Controllers, ES-15 p. 20 (PDF page 132)
  - Quote: "LVR - de-energizes motor on low voltage and restarts when the voltage is restored to normal"
- **Q435** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What does neutral grounding help prevent?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), System Components and Protection Devices, ES-15 p. 6 (PDF page 118)
  - Quote: "Neutral grounding - helps prevent accidents to personnel and damage to property by fire"
- **Q436** (Motors and Generators): On the curve shown, torque reaches its maximum value at about what percent slip?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), AC Motor Theory, ES-12 p. 7 (PDF page 27)
  - Quote: "the torque will reach a maximum value at about 25% slip."
  - Figure: images/doe-1011-v4-es-12-fig4.png
- **Q437** (Motors and Generators): What happens if an induction motor's load is increased beyond the point of maximum torque?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), AC Motor Theory, ES-12 p. 7 (PDF page 27)
  - Quote: "If load is increased beyond this point, the motor will stall and come to a rapid stop."
- **Q438** (Motors and Generators): At the same load, increasing field excitation on a synchronous motor makes it operate at:
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), AC Motor Types, ES-12 p. 15 (PDF page 35)
  - Quote: "Keeping the same load, when the field excitation is increased on a synchronous motor, the motor operates at a leading power factor."
- **Q439** (Sensors and Detectors): How is an ohm meter connected to measure resistance?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Ohm Meters, ES-14 p. 19 (PDF page 91)
  - Quote: "Measures circuit resistance Connected to a component removed from the circuit"

## 2026-11-04: DOE-1015-V1 (Chemistry, Vol 1)

Added 5 quiz questions and 6 flashcards. Every quote was matched against work/text/DOE-HDBK-1015-93_VOL1.txt.

- **C465** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): What is corrosion?
  - Source: DOE-1015-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1015/1-93), Corrosion Theory, CH-02 p. 2 (PDF page 104)
  - Quote: "Corrosion is the deterioration of a material due to interaction with its environment."
- **C466** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): What is crud?
  - Source: DOE-1015-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1015/1-93), Crud and Galvanic Corrosion, CH-02 p. 25 (PDF page 127)
  - Quote: "Crud is corrosion products in the form of finely divided, insoluble oxide particles suspended in the reactor coolant or loosely adhered to metal surfaces or activated corrosion and wear products."
- **C467** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): What is scale?
  - Source: DOE-1015-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1015/1-93), Crud and Galvanic Corrosion, CH-02 p. 25 (PDF page 127)
  - Quote: "Scale is the deposition on the surfaces of the piping from the formation of insoluble compounds from normally soluble salts."
- **C468** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): What is galvanic corrosion?
  - Source: DOE-1015-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1015/1-93), Crud and Galvanic Corrosion, CH-02 p. 23 (PDF page 125)
  - Quote: "Galvanic corrosion is the corrosion that results when two dissimilar metals with different potentials are placed in electrical contact in an electrolyte."
  - Figure: images/doe-1015-v1-ch-02-fig10.png
- **C469** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): State Le Chatelier's principle.
  - Source: DOE-1015-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1015/1-93), Chemical Equations, CH-01 p. 45 (PDF page 67)
  - Quote: "Le Chatelier's principle states that if a stress is applied to an equilibrium, the system will adjust to minimize the effect of the stress."
- **C470** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is stress corrosion cracking (SCC)?
  - Source: DOE-1015-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1015/1-93), Specialized Corrosion, CH-02 p. 31 (PDF page 133)
  - Quote: "Stress corrosion cracking (SCC) is a type of intergranular attack corrosion that occurs at the grain boundaries under tensile stress."
- **Q440** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): Which two conditions does pitting corrosion require?
  - Source: DOE-1015-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1015/1-93), Specialized Corrosion, CH-02 p. 36 (PDF page 138)
  - Quote: "Pitting corrosion requires two conditions to occur, low flow and areas of both high and low oxygen concentration."
- **Q441** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): Crevice corrosion is a type of:
  - Source: DOE-1015-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1015/1-93), Specialized Corrosion, CH-02 p. 28 (PDF page 130)
  - Quote: "Crevice corrosion is a type of pitting corrosion that occurs specifically within the low flow region of a crevice."
- **Q442** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): How does an extremely high water velocity affect general corrosion?
  - Source: DOE-1015-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1015/1-93), General Corrosion, CH-02 p. 20 (PDF page 122)
  - Quote: "An extremely high water velocity, 30 to 40 ft per second, tends to remove the oxide film allowing the corrosion rate to increase."
- **Q443** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): Conductivity is a measure of a substance's ability to:
  - Source: DOE-1015-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1015/1-93), Corrosion Theory, CH-02 p. 2 (PDF page 104)
  - Quote: "Conductivity is a measure of the ability of a substance to allow electron flow."
- **Q444** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): pH is defined as:
  - Source: DOE-1015-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1015/1-93), Acids, Bases, Salts, and pH, CH-01 p. 53 (PDF page 75)
  - Quote: "pH - the negative logarithm of the hydrogen concentration [H+] in moles/liter"

### Figures

- **doe-1015-v1-ch-02-fig10.png** (59 KB, in flashcards): Figure 10. Galvanic Corrosion at Iron-Copper Pipe Junction. Source: DOE-1015-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1015/1-93), CH-02 p. 24. PDF page 126. ## 2026-11-04: DOE-1015-V2 (Chemistry, Vol 2)

Added 5 quiz questions and 6 flashcards. Every quote was matched against work/text/DOE-HDBK-1015-93_VOL2.txt.

- **C471** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): What are the three general reasons to treat water for impurities?
  - Source: DOE-1015-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1015/2-93), Purpose of Water Treatment, CH-04 p. 2 (PDF page 58)
  - Quote: "There are three general reasons to treat water for its impurities: 1. To minimize corrosion, which is enhanced by impurities 2. To minimize radiation levels in the reactor facility 3. To minimize fouling of heat transfer surfaces"
- **C472** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): What does ion exchange do?
  - Source: DOE-1015-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1015/2-93), Water Treatment Processes, CH-04 p. 3 (PDF page 59)
  - Quote: "Ion exchange is a process used extensively in nuclear facilities to control the purity and pH of water by removing undesirable ions and replacing them with acceptable ones."
  - Figure: images/doe-1015-v2-ch-04-fig3.png
- **C473** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): What does demineralize mean?
  - Source: DOE-1015-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1015/2-93), Water Treatment Processes, CH-04 p. 13 (PDF page 69)
  - Quote: "Demineralize is defined as the process whereby impurities present in the incoming fluid (water) are removed by exchanging impure ions with H+ and OH- ions resulting in the formation of pure water."
- **C474** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): What is a mixed-bed demineralizer?
  - Source: DOE-1015-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1015/2-93), Water Treatment Processes, CH-04 p. 13 (PDF page 69)
  - Quote: "Mixed-bed demineralizer is a vessel containing resin that is a uniform mixture of cation and anion resins"
- **C475** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): How may resin performance be monitored?
  - Source: DOE-1015-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1015/2-93), Water Treatment Processes, CH-04 p. 11 (PDF page 67)
  - Quote: "Resin performance may be monitored using a history curve that plots DF with respect to time."
  - Figure: images/doe-1015-v2-ch-04-fig4.png
- **C476** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): How is the radiation-driven decomposition of reactor water suppressed?
  - Source: DOE-1015-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1015/2-93), Effects of Radiation on Water Chemistry, CH-03 p. 11 (PDF page 29)
  - Quote: "The decomposition is suppressed by adding excess hydrogen."
- **Q445** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): What can injection of air into the reactor coolant lead to?
  - Source: DOE-1015-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1015/2-93), Chemistry Parameters, CH-03 p. 30 (PDF page 48)
  - Quote: "Injection of air will cause the hydrogen inventory to become depleted, which in turn can lead to a pH swing towards the acidic end."
- **Q446** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): What does a crud burst cause?
  - Source: DOE-1015-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1015/2-93), Chemistry Parameters, CH-03 p. 30 (PDF page 48)
  - Quote: "The crud burst causes higher radiation levels and an increase in conductivity."
- **Q447** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): Why is pretreatment of makeup water necessary?
  - Source: DOE-1015-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1015/2-93), Dissolved Gases, Suspended Solids, and pH Control, CH-04 p. 26 (PDF page 82)
  - Quote: "Pretreatment of makeup water is necessary to reduce corrosion, minimize radiation, and limit fouling of heat transfer surfaces."
- **Q448** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): Using the hydrogen and hydroxyl forms of resin produces:
  - Source: DOE-1015-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1015/2-93), Dissolved Gases, Suspended Solids, and pH Control, CH-04 p. 26 (PDF page 82)
  - Quote: "If the hydrogen and hydroxyl forms of resin are used, the result is pure, neutral water."
- **Q449** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): On a resin history curve, what does point X mark?
  - Source: DOE-1015-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1015/2-93), Water Treatment Processes, CH-04 p. 11 (PDF page 67)
  - Quote: "with the resin considered "exhausted" at point X."
  - Figure: images/doe-1015-v2-ch-04-fig4.png

### Figures
