## 2026-11-04: PSAR systems exam detail

Added 51 quiz questions and 49 flashcards. Every quote was matched against the extracted source text.

- **C624** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): What is the initial Natrium fuel, and what is its cladding?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.1.1, p. 7.1-1 (PDF page 1234)
  - Quote: "sodium-bonded uranium - 10 weight percent Zirconium (U-10Zr) that is encapsulated by HT-9 ferritic-martensitic steel cladding"
- **Q513** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): What controls primary sodium flow through each core assembly?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.1.1, p. 7.1-1 (PDF page 1234)
  - Quote: "contain orifice plates that control the primary sodium coolant flow through each core assembly"
- **C625** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): What is the neutron-related purpose of the reflector assemblies?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.1.1, p. 7.1-3 (PDF page 1236)
  - Quote: "Reflect neutrons into the core's fueled region, which reduces core reactivity loss and limits radiation damage to permanent reactor structures"
- **Q514** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): What do the shield assemblies do?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.1.1, p. 7.1-3 (PDF page 1236)
  - Quote: "Absorb radial neutron leakage outside of the reflector assemblies to limit activation of intermediate sodium coolant"
- **C626** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): What is tag gas in the fuel pins used for?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.1.1, p. 7.1-3 (PDF page 1236)
  - Quote: "Tag gas is used to identify assemblies containing failed fuel pins using an online fuel monitoring system"
- **C627** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): What are the core inlet and outlet temperatures at 100% power and flow?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.1, Table 7.1.1-1, p. 7.1-12 (PDF page 1245)
  - Quote: "Inlet Temperature at 100% power and flow 680°F (360°C)" / "Outlet Temperature at 100% power and flow 950°F (510°C)"
- **Q515** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): What is the core outlet temperature at 100% power and flow?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.1, Table 7.1.1-1, p. 7.1-12 (PDF page 1245)
  - Quote: "Outlet Temperature at 100% power and flow 950°F (510°C)"
- **C628** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): Trace the primary coolant flow loop.
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.3.1, p. 7.1-50 (PDF page 1283)
  - Quote: "The primary coolant flows in a loop through the reactor core, hot pool, IHXs, cold pool, and PSPs."
- **Q516** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): How does the primary coolant flow path during natural circulation compare with normal operation?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.3.1, p. 7.1-50 (PDF page 1283)
  - Quote: "The same flow path is applicable during normal operations and during natural circulation conditions when the PSPs are unavailable."
- **C629** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): What type of pumps are the Primary Sodium Pumps, and where are they?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.3.2.1, p. 7.1-60 (PDF page 1293)
  - Quote: "The PSPs are two identical vertically-oriented centrifugal pumps located on opposite sides of the RV."
- **C630** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): Why does PSP coastdown matter after a scram, PSP trip, or loss of offsite power?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.3.2.1, p. 7.1-60 (PDF page 1293)
  - Quote: "The PSPs provide sufficient coastdown momentum during reactor scram, PSP trips, and loss of offsite power to establish natural circulation flow sufficient to assure that fuel design limits are not exceeded."
- **Q517** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): Which combination trips the PSP circuit breakers in safety-related function DL3-HR2?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.3.1.1, p. 7.1-56 (PDF page 1289)
  - Quote: "The PSP circuit breakers trip on a combination of a" / "low neutron flux signal, existence of a scram" / "signal, and cold pool temperature at the high high"
- **Q518** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): What do the PSPs normally do during a reactor scram?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.3.2.3, p. 7.1-61 (PDF page 1294)
  - Quote: "During reactor scrams, the PSPs are ramped down using a predefined ramp down curve to minimum flow."
- **C631** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): After PSP coastdown on a loss of offsite power, what happens to primary flow?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.3.1.2, p. 7.1-59 (PDF page 1292)
  - Quote: "the pumps transition to a minimum flow if power is" / "restored via the standby diesel generators." / "If power is not restored, flow reduces to natural"
- **Q519** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): During a power runback, the power-to-flow ratio is kept:
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.3.1.2, p. 7.1-58 (PDF page 1291)
  - Quote: "The power-to-flow ratio is kept less than or equal to one during the power runback."
- **C632** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): How is primary sodium raised to the hot zero power temperature during startup?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.3.2.3, p. 7.1-61 (PDF page 1294)
  - Quote: "During startup of the reactor, the PSPs raise the primary sodium temperature to the hot zero power temperature."
- **C633** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): What is the nominal PSP flow at the full power operating point?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.3.2.3, Table 7.1.3-3, p. 7.1-67 (PDF page 1300)
  - Quote: "Flow @ Full Power Operating Point 40,000 gpm (150 m3/s)"
  - Flag: The source table gives both values, but 40,000 gpm is about 150 m3 per minute, not per second.
- **Q520** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): What is the nominal PSP coastdown halving time?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.3.2.3, Table 7.1.3-3, p. 7.1-67 (PDF page 1300)
  - Quote: "Coastdown Halving Time 3.5 - 5 s"
- **C634** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): What type of heat exchangers are the IHXs?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.3.3.1, p. 7.1-62 (PDF page 1295)
  - Quote: "The IHXs are vertical, counter-flow, single-pass, straight-tube type heat exchangers"
- **Q521** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): In the IHX, primary sodium flows on the:
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.3.3.1, p. 7.1-63 (PDF page 1296)
  - Quote: "Flow in the IHX includes the primary sodium on the shell side and the intermediate sodium on the tube side."
- **C635** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): How would intermediate sodium leaking into primary sodium be detected?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.3.3.3, p. 7.1-63 (PDF page 1296)
  - Quote: "Leakage of intermediate sodium into primary sodium would be detected by IHT expansion tank level decrease (see Section 7.1.4) and PHT hot pool level increase."
- **Q522** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): How is PSP lube oil kept from primary sodium?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.3.1.1, p. 7.1-55 (PDF page 1288)
  - Quote: "The PSP lube oil system is designed such that a double barrier exists between lube oil to primary sodium."
- **C636** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): How is intermediate loop sodium flow rate controlled?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.4.1, p. 7.1-75 (PDF page 1308)
  - Quote: "Intermediate loop sodium flow rate is controlled by controlling ISP speed, which is accomplished with an adjustable speed drive unit that varies frequency and voltage of the input power to the pump motors."
- **Q523** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): What powers the Intermediate Sodium Pumps when normal power is unavailable?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.4.1, p. 7.1-75 (PDF page 1308)
  - Quote: "In the event that normal power is unavailable, the ISPs are powered for low flow operation by the standby diesel generators."
- **C637** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): Which abnormal conditions initiate emergency shutdown of the ISPs?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.4.3, p. 7.1-81 (PDF page 1314)
  - Quote: "Low level in an IHT expansion tank (trips associated ISP)" / "High-High primary sodium level (trips both ISPs)" / "High-High primary sodium temperature (trips both ISPs)"
- **Q524** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): Which condition trips only the associated Intermediate Sodium Pump rather than both?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.4.3, p. 7.1-81 (PDF page 1314)
  - Quote: "Low level in an IHT expansion tank (trips associated ISP)"
- **C638** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): What limits how much intermediate sodium can siphon into the primary system after an IHX leak?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.4.3, p. 7.1-80 (PDF page 1313)
  - Quote: "Introduction of cover gas at the IHT piping high points in the intermediate loop flow path prevents a siphon from forming"
- **Q525** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): Where is the IHT expansion tank located?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.4.1, p. 7.1-75 (PDF page 1308)
  - Quote: "Thermal expansion of intermediate coolant is accommodated by an expansion tank located at the highest point in each intermediate loop."
- **C639** (PSAR: Nuclear Heat Supply Systems): Why is the IHT piping sloped?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.1.4.1, p. 7.1-75 (PDF page 1308)
  - Quote: "The IHT piping is sloped to allow for gravity drainage to drain tanks connected to piping low points."
- **C640** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): What does the Reactor Air Cooling System consist of?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.1.1, p. 7.2-1 (PDF page 1319)
  - Quote: "The RAC consists of four inlet and four outlet stacks, a Collector Cylinder Assembly (CCA), and associated inlet and outlet ducting."
- **Q526** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): Which parameters are monitored to indicate RAC heat removal performance?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.1.5, p. 7.2-7 (PDF page 1325)
  - Quote: "The RAC inlet temperature, outlet temperature, and outlet mass flow rate are monitored to indicate heat removal performance."
- **Q527** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): What sets how much heat the RAC removes?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.1.3, p. 7.2-7 (PDF page 1325)
  - Quote: "RAC heat removal capacity increases or decreases based on the heat removal requirements from the primary coolant and the reactor core."
- **C641** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): Why is the RAC inlet at a minimum elevation of 30 feet?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.1.3, p. 7.2-6 (PDF page 1324)
  - Quote: "The minimum RAC inlet elevation of 30 feet protects the inlet louvers from the external large missile (automobile) hazard"
- **C642** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): In IAC Active Mode, what moves the sodium and the air?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.2.3, p. 7.2-16 (PDF page 1334)
  - Quote: "IAC Active Mode provides normal operation cooling to the intermediate loop with forced circulation of the intermediate sodium provided by operation of the ISPs and forced airflow across the AHXs from operation of the IAC blowers."
- **Q528** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): Which IAC mode uses natural circulation of intermediate sodium with forced airflow from the blowers?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.2.3, p. 7.2-17 (PDF page 1335)
  - Quote: "IAC Blower Mode provides off-normal operation cooling to the intermediate loop with natural circulation of the intermediate sodium and forced airflow across the AHXs from operation of the IAC blowers when the ISPs are unavailable."
- **Q529** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): How many IAC trains are needed in Passive Mode for the limiting decay heat load?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.2.3, p. 7.2-17 (PDF page 1335)
  - Quote: "In Passive Mode, the IAC provides the required heat removal for the limiting decay heat load with" / "two trains in operation."
- **Q530** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): How do the air dampers above and below the AHXs fail on loss of power?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.2.1, p. 7.2-13 (PDF page 1331)
  - Quote: "The dampers fail open on loss of power."
- **C643** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): What position are the AHX air dampers in during Mode-1, and why?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.2.1, p. 7.2-13 (PDF page 1331)
  - Quote: "The air dampers above and below the AHXs are normally closed during Mode-1 operation to limit heat transferred from the intermediate sodium when the IAC is not required."
- **Q531** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): If the reactor vessel leaks sodium into the RV-GV annulus, what happens to the annulus oxygen content?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.3.3, p. 7.2-35 (PDF page 1353)
  - Quote: "If a leak occurs, the diatomic oxygen content is expected to drop as sodium or sodium vapor oxidizes."
- **Q532** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): How does the Sodium Cover Gas System identify which fuel assembly has a breach?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.3.3, p. 7.2-34 (PDF page 1352)
  - Quote: "The tag gas analysis cabinet analyzes the xenon and krypton isotopic ratios present with a mass spectrometer"
- **C644** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): How are sodium vapors and aerosols removed from the primary cover gas exhaust?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.3.1.1, p. 7.2-22 (PDF page 1340)
  - Quote: "the gas passes through the vapor trap which consists of a preheater and vapor condenser, then through an aerosol filter to remove sodium vapors and aerosols."
- **Q533** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): If cesium is present in the primary cover gas exhaust, the gas is routed through:
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.3.1.1, p. 7.2-22 (PDF page 1340)
  - Quote: "If cesium is present the gas is routed through a cesium vapor filter before being exhausted to the Gaseous Radwaste Processing System (RWG)"
- **Q534** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): How is Guard Vessel pressure maintained relative to the Head Access Area and the reactor?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.3.3, p. 7.2-34 (PDF page 1352)
  - Quote: "Maintaining GV pressure above HAA pressure and below reactor pressure."
- **C645** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): Which impurities are monitored in the primary cover gas?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.3.3, p. 7.2-34 (PDF page 1352)
  - Quote: "Impurity monitoring for hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, and methane."
- **C646** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): Which Primary SCG load has the highest delivered pressure?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.3.1.1, p. 7.2-22 (PDF page 1340)
  - Quote: "The highest delivered pressure from the Primary SCG is to the SCRAM cylinders, which sets the minimum delivered pressure by NGA."
- **C647** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): How are the IHT loops filled with sodium from the drain tanks?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.3.3, p. 7.2-35 (PDF page 1353)
  - Quote: "Providing gas pressure to the drain tanks for pneumatic loop fill."
- **C648** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): How does the intermediate SPS (SPS-I) differ from the primary SPS (SPS-P)?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.4.1, p. 7.2-41 (PDF page 1359)
  - Quote: "The SPS-I contains similar equipment and functions as the SPS-P with the exception that the SPS-I does not contain a cesium trap or associated radiological monitoring."
- **Q535** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): What draws primary sodium from the Reactor Vessel into the Primary SPS loop?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.4.1, p. 7.2-41 (PDF page 1359)
  - Quote: "using a submersible electromagnetic (EM) pump within the RV"
- **C649** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): What reduces tritium levels in the primary coolant?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.4.3, p. 7.2-50 (PDF page 1368)
  - Quote: "Tritium levels in the primary coolant are reduced, along with hydrogen, using the primary cold traps."
- **Q536** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): What problem can oxides in sodium cause on cold surfaces?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.4.3, p. 7.2-50 (PDF page 1368)
  - Quote: "Oxides can precipitate from the sodium on cold surfaces and cause plugging of small orifices."
- **C650** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): What is the key process indicator for sodium purity?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.4.3.1, p. 7.2-51 (PDF page 1369)
  - Quote: "The key process indicator for sodium purity is the saturation temperature which correlates directly with impurity concentration."
- **Q537** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): What is the dominant radionuclide background for the SPS-P cesium monitors?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.4.3.3, p. 7.2-51 (PDF page 1369)
  - Quote: "The radiation monitors are designed to detect cesium against the normal background of Na-24 gamma rays, the dominant radionuclide in the SPS-P system."
- **C651** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): What material fills the cesium traps?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.4.3, p. 7.2-50 (PDF page 1368)
  - Quote: "Cesium is removed from the primary coolant using cesium traps filled with reticulated vitreous carbon."
- **Q538** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): How are SPS safety-related functions carried out?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.4.5, p. 7.2-53 (PDF page 1371)
  - Quote: "All SPS SR functions are passive or are executed on a loss of power such as pumps securing, and valves failing shut."
- **Q539** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): How many scram valves must actuate to vent the scram cylinder and release a control rod assembly?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.5.3, p. 7.2-65 (PDF page 1383)
  - Quote: "Actuation of two out of the three scram valves is sufficient to vent the scram cylinder gas pressure and release the CRA"
- **C652** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): What does driveline scram follow provide?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.5.1, p. 7.2-59 (PDF page 1377)
  - Quote: "Driveline scram follow provides assurance that the CRA is fully inserted and provides CRA insertion position indication."
- **Q540** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): How is CRDM motor rotation converted to linear driveline motion?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.5.1, p. 7.2-58 (PDF page 1376)
  - Quote: "through a ball screw drive assembly within the CRDM housing"
- **C653** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): What prevents control rod driveline motion when no demand signal is present?
  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.2.5.1, p. 7.2-58 (PDF page 1376)
  - Quote: "An electro-mechanical brake prevents driveline motion unless a demand signal is present."
- **Q541** (PSAR: Reactor Auxiliary Systems): How is coupled control rod assembly position indicated to the RMC?

  - Source: PSAR Rev 1, ML25276A288, Sec. 7.3.2.1.1, p. 7.3-17 (PDF page 1406)

Fundamentals and PSAR spread questions evenly across their own topics. Mixed is half Fundamentals and half PSAR, with each half spread across its topics. Requested as: "I want three options. Fundamentals only with a distribution across topics, PSAR only with distribution across topics, and a mix of Fundamentals and PSAR with distribution across topics."

They no longer depend on an item's position, so removing an item can't renumber the others. Question and card content did not change.

## 2026-11-05: Lesson topics (knowledge checks and key facts)

Added 35 quiz questions and 26 flashcards from the lesson topics. Every quote passed scripts/verify-quotes.py. Calculation questions use new numbers with the method the quote supports.

- **Q582** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): Why is weight not one of the three fundamental dimensions?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Fundamental Dimensions, CP-01 p. 1
  - Quote: "Weight (a derived unit, not a fundamental unit) is a measurement that describes the force of gravity on the "mass" of an object."
- **Q583** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): Which units are the standard units of the English system?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Fundamental Dimensions, CP-01 p. 3
  - Quote: "The foot-pound-second (FPS) system is the usual unit system used in the U.S. when dealing with physics."
- **Q584** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): Which of these is a derived measurement?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Fundamental Dimensions, CP-01 p. 7
  - Quote: "Density is a measure of the mass of an object per unit volume"
- **Q585** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): Using 1 in. = 0.0254 m, what is 100.00 in. in meters?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Unit Conversions, CP-01 p. 10
  - Quote: "1 in. = 0.0254 m"
- **Q586** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): Using 2.205 lbm = 1 kg, what is 10 kg in lbm?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Unit Conversions, CP-01 p. 10
  - Quote: "2.205 lbm = 1 kg"
- **Q587** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): Using 3600 sec = 1 hr, how many seconds are in 3 hours?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Unit Conversions, CP-01 p. 10
  - Quote: "3600 sec = 1 hr"
- **C687** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): What are the three fundamental dimensions?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Fundamental Dimensions, CP-01 p. 1
  - Quote: "Length, mass, and time are the three fundamental dimensions on which the measurement of all physical quantities is dependent."
- **C688** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): How does the handbook define mass?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Fundamental Dimensions, CP-01 p. 1
  - Quote: "Mass is the amount of material present in an object."
- **C689** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): What two related systems make up the SI system?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Fundamental Dimensions, CP-01 p. 3
  - Quote: "The SI system is made up of two related systems, the meter-kilogram-second (MKS) system and the centimeter-gram-second (CGS) system."
- **C690** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): What must be done when the conversion table has no direct relationship between two units?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Unit Conversions, CP-01 p. 12
  - Quote: "If an equivalent relationship between the given units and the desired units cannot be found in the conversion tables, multiple conversion factors must be used."
- **C691** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): What are conversion factors based on?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Unit Conversions, CP-01 p. 9
  - Quote: "Conversion factors are based on relationships of equivalents from different measurement systems."
- **Q588** (Basic Energy Concepts): Which of these is a vector quantity?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Scalar and Vector Quantities, CP-02 p. 2
  - Quote: "Displacement, velocity, acceleration, and force are examples of vector quantities."
- **Q589** (Basic Energy Concepts): A vector is described in degrees. How is its line segment positioned?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Vector Identification, CP-02 p. 5
  - Quote: "the line segment can be rotated counterclockwise from the x-axis to the proper orientation"
- **Q590** (Basic Energy Concepts): A resultant of 100 lbf acts at 53°. Using cos 53° = 0.6018, what is the x component?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Vectors: Resultants and Components, CP-02 p. 12
  - Quote: "Trigonometry may also be used to determine vector components."
- **Q591** (Basic Energy Concepts): In the graphic method, where is the resultant drawn?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Graphic Method of Vector Addition, CP-02 p. 17
  - Quote: "from the point of origin of the axes to the head of the final vector."
- **Q592** (Basic Energy Concepts): Using component addition, what is the sum of F1 = (3,5) and F2 = (-1,2)?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Component Addition Method, CP-02 p. 20
  - Quote: "Mathematically combine all x-axis components."
- **Q593** (Basic Energy Concepts): A person walks 6 miles, turns 90°, and walks 8 more miles. What is the net displacement?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Analytical Method of Vector Addition, CP-02 p. 23
  - Quote: "The Pythagorean Theorem states that in any right triangle, the square of the length of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the lengths of the other two sides."
- **C692** (Basic Energy Concepts): Name four examples of vector quantities.
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Scalar and Vector Quantities, CP-02 p. 2
  - Quote: "Displacement, velocity, acceleration, and force are examples of vector quantities."
- **C693** (Basic Energy Concepts): What does the length of a drawn vector represent, and what does the arrow represent?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Scalar and Vector Quantities, CP-02 p. 2
  - Quote: "The length of the line represents the magnitude of the vector, and the arrow represents the direction of the vector."
- **C694** (Basic Energy Concepts): What are the components of a vector?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Vectors: Resultants and Components, CP-02 p. 10
  - Quote: "Components of a vector are vectors, which when added, yield the vector."
- **C695** (Basic Energy Concepts): Which vector addition method is required for a high degree of accuracy?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Graphic Method of Vector Addition, CP-02 p. 16
  - Quote: "If a high degree of accuracy is required, an analytical method using geometric and trigonometric functions is required."
- **C696** (Basic Energy Concepts): State the Pythagorean Theorem.
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Analytical Method of Vector Addition, CP-02 p. 23
  - Quote: "The Pythagorean Theorem states that in any right triangle, the square of the length of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the lengths of the other two sides."
- **Q594** (Basic Energy Concepts): Under Newton's second law, the acceleration of a body is:
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Newton's Laws of Motion, CP-03 p. 1
  - Quote: "the acceleration of a body is proportional to the net (i.e., sum or resultant) force acting on it and in the direction of that net force."
- **Q595** (Basic Energy Concepts): The distance between two masses is doubled. What happens to the gravitational force between them?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Newton's Laws of Motion, CP-03 p. 2
  - Quote: "For any two masses, the force is directly proportional to the product of the two masses and is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them."
- **Q596** (Basic Energy Concepts): What is the momentum of a 10 lbm object moving at 5 ft/sec?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Momentum Principles, CP-03 p. 5
  - Quote: "It is the result of the product of the body's mass and the velocity at which it is moving."
- **Q597** (Basic Energy Concepts): Which statement is true of an inelastic collision?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Momentum Principles, CP-03 p. 8
  - Quote: "In an inelastic collision, momentum is conserved, but system kinetic energy is not conserved."
- **Q598** (Basic Energy Concepts): A 1000 lbm car moving at 20 ft/sec couples with a 3000 lbm car moving at 4 ft/sec in the same direction. What is their final velocity?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Momentum Principles, CP-03 p. 8
  - Quote: "the sum of a system's initial momentum is equal to the sum of a system's final momentum."
- **C697** (Basic Energy Concepts): How is force related to the rate of change of momentum?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Momentum Principles, CP-03 p. 6
  - Quote: "The rate at which momentum changes with time is equal to the net force applied to an object."
- **C698** (Basic Energy Concepts): Why is momentum a vector quantity?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Momentum Principles, CP-03 p. 5
  - Quote: "Momentum is a vector quantity since it results from the velocity of the object."
- **C699** (Basic Energy Concepts): What is conserved in an elastic collision?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Momentum Principles, CP-03 p. 8
  - Quote: "In an elastic collision, both momentum and kinetic energy (i.e., energy due to an objects velocity) are conserved."
- **C700** (Basic Energy Concepts): State Newton's second law.
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Newton's Laws of Motion, CP-03 p. 1
  - Quote: "the acceleration of a body is proportional to the net (i.e., sum or resultant) force acting on it and in the direction of that net force."
- **C701** (Basic Energy Concepts): State the universal law of gravitation for two masses.
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Newton's Laws of Motion, CP-03 p. 2
  - Quote: "For any two masses, the force is directly proportional to the product of the two masses and is inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them."
- **Q599** (Basic Energy Concepts): What three things characterize a force?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Force and Weight, CP-04 p. 2
  - Quote: "Force is characterized by its point of application, its magnitude, and its direction."
- **Q600** (Basic Energy Concepts): A body moves from the earth to the moon. What happens to its mass and weight?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Force and Weight, CP-04 p. 3
  - Quote: "The mass of a body is the same wherever the body is, whether on the moon or on the earth."
- **Q601** (Basic Energy Concepts): Which forces are left off a free-body diagram?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Free-Body Diagrams, CP-04 p. 6
  - Quote: "Do not show the forces that the object exerts on anything else, since these forces do not affect the object itself."
- **Q602** (Basic Energy Concepts): What is an equilibrant?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Force Equilibrium, CP-04 p. 15
  - Quote: "If the sum of all the forces is not equal to zero, any force or system of forces capable of balancing the system is defined as an equilibrant."
- **Q603** (Basic Energy Concepts): How does the handbook define net force?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Force Equilibrium, CP-04 p. 11
  - Quote: "The force which results from all the forces acting on a body is defined as the net force."
- **Q604** (Basic Energy Concepts): What kind of load can a cable support?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Types of Force, CP-04 p. 17
  - Quote: "ropes, cables, etc., that are attached to bodies can only support tensile loads"
- **Q605** (Basic Energy Concepts): A block that was held by static friction starts to slide. What happens to the friction force?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Types of Force, CP-04 p. 18
  - Quote: "As soon as the block has been set in motion, the magnitude of F drops from FM to a lower value"
- **Q606** (Basic Energy Concepts): Which of these does NOT change the coefficients of friction?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Types of Force, CP-04 p. 19
  - Quote: "do not depend upon the area of the surfaces in contact."
- **Q607** (Basic Energy Concepts): How does centrifugal force differ from centripetal force?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Types of Force, CP-04 p. 20
  - Quote: "This is actually a fictitious force, but is an apparent force that is used to describe the forces present due to an object's rotation."
- **C702** (Basic Energy Concepts): What is inertia?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Force Equilibrium, CP-04 p. 12
  - Quote: "Inertia is the tendency of a body to resist a change in its state of motion."
- **C703** (Basic Energy Concepts): What is a normal force?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Free-Body Diagrams, CP-04 p. 5
  - Quote: "A normal force is defined as any perpendicular force with which any two surfaces are pressed against each other."
- **C704** (Basic Energy Concepts): How does the handbook define force?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Force and Weight, CP-04 p. 2
  - Quote: "Force is defined as a vector quantity that tends to produce an acceleration of a body in the direction of its application."
- **C705** (Basic Energy Concepts): What direction do frictional forces act?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Types of Force, CP-04 p. 19
  - Quote: "frictional forces are always opposite in direction to the motion (or impending motion) of the object."
- **C706** (Basic Energy Concepts): Are fluid forces usually tensile or compressive?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Types of Force, CP-04 p. 17
  - Quote: "fluid forces are almost always compressive forces."
- **Q608** (Basic Energy Concepts): What is thermal energy in motion commonly called?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Energy and Work, CP-05 p. 3
  - Quote: "referred to as transient energy or, more commonly in the case of thermal energy, heat."
- **Q609** (Basic Energy Concepts): A body's energy is stored because of its position. What type of energy is this?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Energy and Work, CP-05 p. 1
  - Quote: "Potential energy is defined as the energy stored in an object because of its position."
- **Q610** (Basic Energy Concepts): Which expression gives kinetic energy in English units?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Energy and Work, CP-05 p. 2
  - Quote: "Kinetic energy is defined as the energy stored in an object because of its motion."
- **Q611** (Basic Energy Concepts): What is the potential energy of a 20 lbm object held 10 feet above the ground?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Energy and Work, CP-05 p. 1
  - Quote: "Potential energy is defined as the energy stored in an object because of its position."
- **Q612** (Basic Energy Concepts): A constant force of 300 lbf is applied to a box, but the box does not move. How much work is done?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Energy and Work, CP-05 p. 4
  - Quote: "if no movement is achieved, no work has been accomplished."
- **Q613** (Basic Energy Concepts): A horizontal force of 100 lbf moves a box 6 feet horizontally. How much work is done?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Energy and Work, CP-05 p. 4
  - Quote: "Work is done by a force acting on a moving object if the object has some component of motion in the direction of the force."
- **Q614** (Basic Energy Concepts): How is the First Law of Thermodynamics simply stated?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Law of Conservation of Energy, CP-05 p. 6
  - Quote: "energy cannot be created or destroyed, only altered in form."
- **Q615** (Basic Energy Concepts): With force in lbf and velocity in ft/s, which expression gives power in horsepower?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Power, CP-05 p. 9
  - Quote: "One horsepower is equivalent to 550 ft-lbf/s and 745.7 watts."
- **Q616** (Basic Energy Concepts): A steady force of 100 lbf moves an object at a constant 11 ft/s. What is the power in horsepower?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Power, CP-05 p. 9
  - Quote: "One horsepower is equivalent to 550 ft-lbf/s and 745.7 watts."
- **C707** (Basic Energy Concepts): What are the two categories of thermal and mechanical energy?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Energy and Work, CP-05 p. 1
  - Quote: "Stored energy is the energy contained within a substance or object."
- **C708** (Basic Energy Concepts): What is internal energy?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Energy and Work, CP-05 p. 3
  - Quote: "Internal energy is the energy stored in a substance because of the motion and position of the particles of the substance."
- **C709** (Basic Energy Concepts): What is transient mechanical energy commonly called?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Energy and Work, CP-05 p. 3
  - Quote: "Transient mechanical energy is commonly referred to as work."
- **C710** (Basic Energy Concepts): How many ft-lbf/s and watts equal one horsepower?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Power, CP-05 p. 9
  - Quote: "One horsepower is equivalent to 550 ft-lbf/s and 745.7 watts."
- **C711** (Basic Energy Concepts): What is thermal power?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Power, CP-05 p. 8
  - Quote: "Thermal power is the measure of thermal energy used per unit time."
- **C712** (Basic Energy Concepts): What is mechanical power?
  - Source: DOE-1010 (DOE-HDBK-1010-92), Power, CP-05 p. 9
  - Quote: "Mechanical power is the rate at which work is done."
