  - Quote: "The three most commonly-used automatic trip features for a circuit breaker are overcurrent (as discussed previously), underfrequency, and undervoltage."
- **Q812** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What are the basic functions of a motor controller?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Motor Controllers, ES-15 p. 15
  - Quote: "The basic functions of a motor controller are to control and protect the operation of a motor."
- **Q813** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): Which set lists the overload devices commonly used in motor-control equipment?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Motor Controllers, ES-15 p. 17
  - Quote: "The following types of overload devices are commonly used in motor-control equipment."
- **Q814** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What does an LVRE controller do?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Motor Controllers, ES-15 p. 19
  - Quote: "The LVRE controller maintains the motor across the line at all times."
- **Q815** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What is ampacity?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Wiring Schemes and Grounding, ES-15 p. 22
  - Quote: "Ampacity - the current in amperes that a conductor can carry continuously under the conditions of use without exceeding its temperature rating."
- **Q816** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What is a neutral?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Wiring Schemes and Grounding, ES-15 p. 22
  - Quote: "Neutral - a current-carrying conductor normally tied to ground so that the electrical potential is zero."
- **Q817** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What is a bond?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Wiring Schemes and Grounding, ES-15 p. 22
  - Quote: "Bond - the permanent joining of metallic parts or circuits assuring electrical continuity and capacity to safely conduct any current likely to be imposed."
- **Q818** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What are the two methods of connecting single-phase loads to a three-phase source?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Wiring Schemes and Grounding, ES-15 p. 23
  - Quote: "is referred to as a phase-to-ground scheme."
- **Q819** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What is the only approved method of wiring single-phase power?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Wiring Schemes and Grounding, ES-15 p. 23
  - Quote: "The only approved method of wiring single-phase power is the scheme commonly referred to as the 3-wire, single-phase Edison system."
- **Q820** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What is the 3-wire, three-phase Delta system normally used for?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Wiring Schemes and Grounding, ES-15 p. 24
  - Quote: "normally used for transmission of power in the intermediate voltage class from approximately 15,000 volts to 600 volts."
- **Q821** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): Which system is recognized as the safest possible multi-purpose distribution system for low voltage?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Wiring Schemes and Grounding, ES-15 p. 27
  - Quote: "This system is recognized as the safest possible multi-purpose distribution system for low voltage"
- **Q822** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What does the 4-wire, three-phase Delta system combine?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Wiring Schemes and Grounding, ES-15 p. 25
  - Quote: "with the convenience of the Edison system for single-phase loads."
- **C788** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What is the difference between an LVP and an LVR controller?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Motor Controllers, ES-15 p. 19
  - Quote: "The LVRE controller maintains the motor across the line at all times."
- **C789** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What must be done before operating a disconnect?
  - Source: LP-BREAKERS-RELAYS-AND-DISCONNECTS-PART-1 (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects Part 1.docx), slide 1.24 Knowledge Check
  - Quote: "Never operate a disconnect under load."
- **C790** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): How is a breaker in the TRIP FREE position reset?
  - Source: LP-BREAKERS-RELAYS-AND-DISCONNECTS-PART-2 (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects Part 2.docx), slide 1.41 Resetting a Breaker
  - Quote: "To reset a breaker in the TRIP FREE position, it must be positioned to the OPEN position first."
- **C791** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What protects a circuit from an overcurrent condition only?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), System Components and Protection Devices, ES-15 p. 5
  - Quote: "A fuse is a device that protects a circuit from an overcurrent condition only."
- **C792** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What is a leg in a power distribution system?
  - Source: DOE-1011-V4 (DOE-HDBK-1011/4-92), Wiring Schemes and Grounding, ES-15 p. 22
  - Quote: "Leg - a current-carrying conductor intended to deliver power to or from a load normally at an electrical potential other than ground."

## 2026-11-05: Lesson topics, batch 4 (ES-11 to ES-15)

- Added five Electrical Science lessons in topics/, completing the handbook. ES-12, ES-14 and ES-15 use Word files; ES-11 and ES-13 are handbook only. All are Draft.
- ES-15 shows both definitions of the 600 volt class boundary, because the handbook and Breakers Part 2 differ. No check or flashcard tests that boundary.
- A lesson can now cite more than one Word file.

## 2026-11-05: Lesson topics (knowledge checks and key facts)

Added 148 quiz questions and 29 flashcards from the lesson topics. Every quote passed scripts/verify-quotes.py. Calculation questions use new numbers with the method the quote supports.

- **Q823** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): How are density and specific volume related?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Thermodynamic Properties, HT-01 p. 3
  - Quote: "The density ( ρ ) of a substance is the reciprocal of its specific volume (ν)."
- **Q824** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): A quantity of matter is divided into two equal parts. What happens to its intensive properties?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Thermodynamic Properties, HT-01 p. 4
  - Quote: "An intensive property is independent of the amount of mass. The value of an extensive property varies directly with the mass."
- **Q825** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): Which of these is an extensive property?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Thermodynamic Properties, HT-01 p. 4
  - Quote: "Mass and total volume are examples of extensive properties."
- **Q826** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): What is absolute zero on the Fahrenheit scale, as used in the handbook?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Temperature and Pressure Measurements, HT-01 p. 12
  - Quote: "Absolute zero = -460 °F or -273 °C"
- **Q827** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): What is the Rankine equivalent of 80 °C?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Temperature and Pressure Measurements, HT-01 p. 8
  - Quote: "What is the Rankine equivalent of 80°C?"
- **Q828** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): What does a pressure gauge open to the atmosphere normally read?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Temperature and Pressure Measurements, HT-01 p. 9
  - Quote: "almost all pressure gauges register zero when open to the atmosphere."
- **Q829** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): Using the handbook's conversions, 14.7 psia equals how many inches of water?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Temperature and Pressure Measurements, HT-01 p. 11
  - Quote: "14.7 psia = 408 inches of water"
- **Q830** (Basic Energy Concepts): Which equation defines specific enthalpy?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Energy, Work, and Heat, HT-01 p. 18
  - Quote: "Specific enthalpy (h) is defined as h = u + Pν"
- **Q831** (Basic Energy Concepts): What is P-V energy also called?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Energy, Work, and Heat, HT-01 p. 17
  - Quote: "This form of energy is called P-V energy because it arises from the pressure (P) and the volume (V) of a fluid."
- **Q832** (Basic Energy Concepts): What is sensible heat?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Energy, Work, and Heat, HT-01 p. 20
  - Quote: "The heat added to or removed from a substance to produce a change in its temperature is called sensible heat."
- **Q833** (Basic Energy Concepts): What happens to temperature while latent heat is added?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Energy, Work, and Heat, HT-01 p. 21
  - Quote: "When latent heat is added, no temperature change occurs."
- **Q834** (Basic Energy Concepts): What does a positive value for work mean in the handbook's sign convention?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Energy, Work, and Heat, HT-01 p. 19
  - Quote: "A positive value for work indicates that work is done by the system on its surroundings; a negative value indicates that work is done on the system by its surroundings."
- **Q835** (Basic Energy Concepts): One Btu equals about how many foot-pounds-force?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Energy, Work, and Heat, HT-01 p. 24
  - Quote: "1 Btu = 778.3 ft-lbf"
- **Q836** (Thermodynamic Processes): Which type of system allows both mass and energy to cross its boundary?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Thermodynamic Systems and Processes, HT-01 p. 27
  - Quote: "An open system is one that may have a transfer of both mass and energy with its surroundings."
- **Q837** (Thermodynamic Processes): What can cross the boundary of a closed system?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Thermodynamic Systems and Processes, HT-01 p. 27
  - Quote: "A closed system has no transfer of mass with its surroundings, but may have a transfer of energy (either heat or work) with its surroundings."
- **Q838** (Thermodynamic Processes): What describes steady state?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Thermodynamic Systems and Processes, HT-01 p. 27
  - Quote: "Steady state is that circumstance in which there is no accumulation of mass or energy within the control volume, and the properties at any point within the system are independent of time."
- **Q839** (Thermodynamic Processes): A process is both reversible and adiabatic. What kind of process is it?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Thermodynamic Systems and Processes, HT-01 p. 29
  - Quote: "An isentropic process is one in which the entropy of the fluid remains constant."
- **Q840** (Thermodynamic Processes): Which is one of the most common causes of irreversibility?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Thermodynamic Systems and Processes, HT-01 p. 29
  - Quote: "Four of the most common causes of irreversibility are friction, unrestrained expansion of a fluid, heat transfer through a finite temperature difference, and mixing of two different substances."
- **Q841** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): A mixture has 0.2 lbm of vapor and 0.8 lbm of liquid at saturation. What is its moisture content?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Change of Phase, HT-01 p. 35
  - Quote: "The moisture content of a substance is the opposite of its quality."
- **Q842** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): What is the change of phase directly from solid to vapor called?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Change of Phase, HT-01 p. 37
  - Quote: "Sublimation is a special term used for cases in which the transition between the solid phase and the vapor phase occurs directly, without passing through the liquid phase."
- **Q843** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): What defines the triple point?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Change of Phase, HT-01 p. 37
  - Quote: "the triple point, defined as the state in which all three phases may be present in equilibrium."
- **Q844** (Steam): On a T-s diagram, what does the area under the curve of a process represent?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Property Diagrams and Steam Tables, HT-01 p. 46
  - Quote: "the heat transferred to or from a system equals the area under the T-s curve of the process."
- **Q845** (Steam): At 14.7 psia, what is the saturation temperature of water?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Change of Phase, HT-01 p. 33
  - Quote: "for water at 14.7 psia, the saturation temperature is 212°F."
- **Q846** (Steam): How many properties must usually be known to determine a substance's other properties?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Property Diagrams and Steam Tables, HT-01 p. 49
  - Quote: "Usually, two properties (for example, v, p, T, h, s) of the substance must be known in order to determine the other needed properties."
- **Q847** (Thermodynamic Processes): In open system analysis, which two terms are combined into enthalpy?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), First Law of Thermodynamics, HT-01 p. 59
  - Quote: "enthalpy, has been defined as h = u + Pν."
- **Q848** (Thermodynamic Processes): Which approach is usually used today to analyze thermodynamic systems?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), First Law of Thermodynamics, HT-01 p. 57
  - Quote: "The control volume approach is usually used today in analyzing thermodynamic systems."
- **Q849** (Thermodynamic Processes): Why can Q̇ = ṁcp∆T not be used across a phase change?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), First Law of Thermodynamics, HT-01 p. 63
  - Quote: "It is important to note that the later equation can only be used when no phase change occurs since ∆T = 0 during a phase change."
- **Q850** (Thermodynamic Cycles): In a steam plant cycle, what is the heat-rejection mechanism?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), First Law of Thermodynamics, HT-01 p. 62
  - Quote: "The condensation process is the heat-rejection mechanism for the cycle."
- **Q851** (Thermodynamic Cycles): What does the second law deny?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Second Law of Thermodynamics, HT-01 p. 70
  - Quote: "the second law denies the possibility of completely converting into work all of the heat supplied to a system operating in a cycle"
- **Q852** (Thermodynamic Cycles): What information does the second law give that the first law does not?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Second Law of Thermodynamics, HT-01 p. 70
  - Quote: "However, no information about the direction of the process can be obtained by the application of the first law."
- **Q853** (Thermodynamic Cycles): For a cyclic system, how can entropy change?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Second Law of Thermodynamics, HT-01 p. 71
  - Quote: "entropy must increase or stay the same for a cyclic system; it can never decrease."
- **Q854** (Thermodynamic Cycles): A system receives heat at 800 °R and rejects it at 520 °R. What is its Carnot efficiency?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Second Law of Thermodynamics, HT-01 p. 75
  - Quote: "1 - 520/800"
- **Q855** (Thermodynamic Cycles): How is an ideal expansion shown on a T-s or h-s diagram?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Second Law of Thermodynamics, HT-01 p. 77
  - Quote: "These isentropic processes will be represented by vertical lines on either T-s or h-s diagrams"
- **Q856** (Thermodynamic Cycles): How is pump efficiency defined?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Second Law of Thermodynamics, HT-01 p. 81
  - Quote: "A pump requires more work because of unavoidable losses due to friction and fluid turbulence."
- **Q857** (Thermodynamic Cycles): Why does an actual turbine do less work than an ideal turbine?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Second Law of Thermodynamics, HT-01 p. 80
  - Quote: "An actual turbine does less work because of friction losses in the blades, leakage past the blades and, to a lesser extent, mechanical friction."
- **Q858** (Thermodynamic Cycles): What is the main feature of the Rankine cycle?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Second Law of Thermodynamics, HT-01 p. 88
  - Quote: "The main feature of the Rankine cycle, shown in Figure 31, is that it confines the isentropic compression process to the liquid phase only"
- **Q859** (Thermodynamic Cycles): What is the effect of excessive condenser subcooling?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Second Law of Thermodynamics, HT-01 p. 92
  - Quote: "excessive condenser subcooling will decrease cycle efficiency."
- **Q860** (Thermodynamic Cycles): Which of these contributes to component inefficiency in turbines, pumps, and compressors?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Second Law of Thermodynamics, HT-01 p. 95
  - Quote: "Turbines, pumps, and compressors all behave non-ideally due to heat losses, friction and windage losses."
- **Q861** (Thermodynamic Processes): At constant temperature, how does the pressure of a gas vary with its volume?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Compression Processes, HT-01 p. 97
  - Quote: "the pressure of a gas expanding at constant temperature varies inversely to the volume"
- **Q862** (Thermodynamic Processes): In the ideal gas equation, pressure and temperature must be expressed as what?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Compression Processes, HT-01 p. 98
  - Quote: "where the pressure and temperature are absolute values."
- **Q863** (Thermodynamic Processes): What is the effect of a temperature rise on a liquid-filled closed container?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Compression Processes, HT-01 p. 101
  - Quote: "this results in a tremendous increase in pressure for a relatively minor temperature change."
- **Q864** (Thermodynamic Processes): A gas confined in a fixed volume has a 5% rise in absolute temperature. What happens to its absolute pressure?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Compression Processes, HT-01 p. 101
  - Quote: "A 5% increase in absolute temperature will result in a 5% increase in the absolute pressure."
- **Q865** (Thermodynamic Processes): What does a pressure increase do to an incompressible fluid's density?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Compression Processes, HT-01 p. 100
  - Quote: "An increase in the pressure of an incompressible fluid will not have a significant effect on the density."
- **Q866** (Thermodynamic Processes): Which equation gives the work done in a constant pressure process?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Compression Processes, HT-01 p. 100
  - Quote: "W1-2 = P(∆V)"
- **C793** (Thermodynamic Units and Properties): How do intensive and extensive properties differ?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Thermodynamic Properties, HT-01 p. 4
  - Quote: "An intensive property is independent of the amount of mass. The value of an extensive property varies directly with the mass."
- **C794** (Thermodynamic Processes): How do isolated, closed, and open systems differ?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Thermodynamic Systems and Processes, HT-01 p. 27
  - Quote: "An open system is one that may have a transfer of both mass and energy with its surroundings."
- **C795** (Basic Energy Concepts): What does entropy quantify?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Energy, Work, and Heat, HT-01 p. 22
  - Quote: "Entropy quantifies the energy of a substance that is no longer available to perform useful work."
- **C796** (Thermodynamic Cycles): What is the Carnot efficiency equation?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Second Law of Thermodynamics, HT-01 p. 74
  - Quote: "the Carnot efficiency serves as an unattainable upper limit for any real system’s efficiency."
- **C797** (Thermodynamic Cycles): How does a real expansion look on a T-s diagram compared with an ideal one?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Second Law of Thermodynamics, HT-01 p. 77
  - Quote: "the dashed lines representing the real process will slant slightly towards the right since the entropy will increase from the start to the end of the process."
- **C798** (Steam): What is the thumb rule for pressure in a water-solid system?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1012/1-92), Compression Processes, HT-01 p. 101
  - Quote: "pressure in a water-solid system will increase about 100 psi for every 1 °F increase in temperature."
- **Q867** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): What is the difference between heat and temperature?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Heat Transfer Terminology, HT-02 p. 1
  - Quote: "Heat is energy in transit."
- **Q868** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): Can a system contain or store heat or work?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Heat Transfer Terminology, HT-02 p. 2
  - Quote: "Heat can be transferred into or out of a system and work can be done on or by a system, but a system cannot contain or store either heat or work."
- **Q869** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): Which mode of heat transfer involves the mixing and motion of macroscopic portions of a fluid?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Heat Transfer Terminology, HT-02 p. 2
  - Quote: "Convection involves the transfer of heat by the mixing and motion of macroscopic portions of a fluid."
- **Q870** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): What is heat flux?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Heat Transfer Terminology, HT-02 p. 3
  - Quote: "The heat flux can be determined by dividing the heat transfer rate by the area through which the heat is being transferred."
- **Q871** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): What does the overall heat transfer coefficient combine?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Heat Transfer Terminology, HT-02 p. 4
  - Quote: "The overall heat transfer coefficient combines the heat transfer coefficient of the two heat exchanger fluids and the thermal conductivity of the heat exchanger tubes."
- **Q872** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): What is another name for the convective heat transfer coefficient?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Heat Transfer Terminology, HT-02 p. 4
  - Quote: "The convective heat transfer coefficient is sometimes referred to as a film coefficient"
- **Q873** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): In the equivalent resistance method, what plays the part of voltage?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Conduction Heat Transfer, HT-02 p. 9
  - Quote: "It is possible to compare heat transfer to current flow in electrical circuits."
- **Q874** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): Why is a log mean area used for conduction through a pipe wall?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Conduction Heat Transfer, HT-02 p. 12
  - Quote: "it is necessary to define a log mean cross-sectional area (Alm)."
- **Q875** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): Why is the convective heat transfer coefficient higher for turbulent flow than for laminar flow?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Convection Heat Transfer, HT-02 p. 19
  - Quote: "This is due to turbulent flow having a thinner stagnant fluid film layer on the heat transfer surface."
- **Q876** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): What causes natural convection?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Convection Heat Transfer, HT-02 p. 18
  - Quote: "The term natural convection is used if this motion and mixing is caused by density variations resulting from temperature differences within the fluid."
- **Q877** (Thermal Hydraulics): How does wire wrap on a fuel pin affect the laminar boundary layer?
  - Source: LP-THERMAL-HYDRAULICS (Thermal Hydraulics.docx), slide 1.7 Wire Wrapped Fuel Pins
  - Quote: "The addition of the wire tends to break up the laminar boundary layer by making the surface rough instead of smooth."
- **Q878** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): Heat passes from one fluid through a tube wall to a second fluid. What are the three processes, in order?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Convection Heat Transfer, HT-02 p. 20
  - Quote: "Many of the heat transfer processes encountered in nuclear facilities involve a combination of both conduction and convection."
- **Q879** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): What is the maximum value of emissivity?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Radiant Heat Transfer, HT-02 p. 27
  - Quote: "Emissivity is a dimensionless number and has a maximum value of 1.0."
- **Q880** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): What does the radiation configuration factor take into account?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Radiant Heat Transfer, HT-02 p. 28
  - Quote: "which takes into account the emissivity of both bodies and their relative geometry."
- **Q881** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): In a parallel flow heat exchanger, how does the cold fluid outlet temperature compare with the hot fluid?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Heat Exchangers, HT-02 p. 32
  - Quote: "the temperature of the cold fluid exiting the heat exchanger never exceeds the lowest temperature of the hot fluid."
- **Q882** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): What is the primary advantage of a regenerative heat exchanger?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Heat Exchangers, HT-02 p. 35
  - Quote: "The primary advantage of a regenerative heat exchanger application is conservation of system energy"
- **Q883** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): How does a non-regenerative heat exchanger differ from a regenerative one?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Heat Exchangers, HT-02 p. 34
  - Quote: "One fluid cools or heats the other with no interconnection between the two fluids."
- **Q884** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): A counterflow exchanger has temperature differences of 280 °F at one end and 190 °F at the other. What is the LMTD?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Heat Transfer Terminology, HT-02 p. 3
  - Quote: "A precise temperature change between two fluids across the heat exchanger is best represented by the log mean temperature difference"
- **Q885** (Steam): What is the heat flux associated with DNB called?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Boiling Heat Transfer, HT-02 p. 42
  - Quote: "The heat flux associated with DNB is commonly called the critical heat flux (CHF)."
- **Q886** (Steam): In film boiling, what covers the heat transfer surface?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Boiling Heat Transfer, HT-02 p. 41
  - Quote: "The condition after the stable steam blanket has formed is referred to as film boiling."
- **Q887** (Steam): What happens to bubbles in nucleate boiling?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Boiling Heat Transfer, HT-02 p. 40
  - Quote: "In nucleate boiling, steam bubbles form at the heat transfer surface and then break away and are carried into the main stream of the fluid."
- **Q888** (Thermal Hydraulics): If reactor power stays constant and flow rate rises, what happens to the temperature difference across the core?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Heat Generation, HT-02 p. 45
  - Quote: "If flow rate is constant, temperature will vary directly with power. If power is constant, temperature will vary inversely with flow rate."
- **Q889** (Thermal Hydraulics): Which of these affect the fission rate and therefore the heat generation rate?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Heat Generation, HT-02 p. 45
  - Quote: "The density of the fuel, the neutron flux, and the type of fuel all affect the fission rate and, therefore, the heat generation rate."
- **Q890** (Core Thermal Limits): How is average linear power density found?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Heat Generation, HT-02 p. 47
  - Quote: "dividing the total thermal output of the core by the total length of all the fuel components in the core."
- **Q891** (Core Thermal Limits): What does a hot channel factor of 1.0 imply?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Heat Generation, HT-02 p. 46
  - Quote: "This peaking factor is referred to as the hot channel factor."
- **Q892** (Core Thermal Limits): What is the average volumetric thermal source strength?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Heat Generation, HT-02 p. 50
  - Quote: "The heat generation rate divided by the volume of fuel will give the average volumetric thermal source strength."
- **Q893** (Thermal Hydraulics): Why are fuel temperatures higher in the upper axial region of the core?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Heat Generation, HT-02 p. 49
  - Quote: "the fuel cladding and, thus, the fuel temperatures are higher in the upper axial region of the core."
- **Q894** (Thermal Hydraulics): What gap material is expected in the fuel pins of this sodium reactor?
  - Source: LP-THERMAL-HYDRAULICS (Thermal Hydraulics.docx), slide 1.10 Radial Fuel Temperature Profile
  - Quote: "we expect the gap material to be liquid sodium, which has fabulous heat transfer."
- **Q895** (Thermal Hydraulics): If coolant flow is raised, what happens to the coolant temperature rise through the core?
  - Source: LP-THERMAL-HYDRAULICS (Thermal Hydraulics.docx), slide 1.20 Axial Temperature Profiles Changes
  - Quote: "As the flow is raised, the coolant spends less time in the core, and so heats up less."
- **Q896** (Thermal Hydraulics): About what fraction of sodium flow is typically bypass flow?
  - Source: LP-THERMAL-HYDRAULICS (Thermal Hydraulics.docx), slide 1.16 Bypass Flow
  - Quote: "a small fraction of the flow, usually about 5% to 10% of the total, is used to cool other components."
- **Q898** (Thermal Hydraulics): What is decay heat?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Decay Heat, HT-02 p. 52
  - Quote: "This release of energy by the decay of fission products is called decay heat."
- **Q899** (Thermal Hydraulics): What does the amount of decay heat depend on?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Decay Heat, HT-02 p. 52
  - Quote: "This release of energy by the decay of fission products is called decay heat."
- **Q900** (Thermal Hydraulics): What are the two categories of methods for removing decay heat?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Decay Heat, HT-02 p. 56
  - Quote: "The other category includes methods which operate in an open system, drawing in cool fluid from some source and discharging warmer fluid to some storage area or the environment."
- **C799** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): What are the three modes of heat transfer?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Heat Transfer Terminology, HT-02 p. 2
  - Quote: "Radiation, or radiant heat transfer, involves the transfer of heat by electromagnetic radiation that arises due to the temperature of a body."
- **C800** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): What is the equation for convection heat transfer?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Convection Heat Transfer, HT-02 p. 19
  - Quote: "The basic relationship for heat transfer by convection has the same form as that for heat transfer by conduction"
- **C801** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): What is a black body?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Radiant Heat Transfer, HT-02 p. 26
  - Quote: "A body that emits the maximum amount of heat for its absolute temperature is called a black body."
- **C802** (Heat Transfer and Heat Exchangers): What are the advantages of a counter-flow heat exchanger?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Heat Exchangers, HT-02 p. 33
  - Quote: "the outlet temperature of the cold fluid can approach the highest temperature of the hot fluid (the inlet temperature)."
- **C803** (Steam): What is DNB?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Boiling Heat Transfer, HT-02 p. 42
  - Quote: "The point of transition from nucleate boiling to film boiling is called the point of departure from nucleate boiling, commonly written as DNB."
- **C804** (Thermal Hydraulics): How do temperature, flow, and power relate in the core?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Heat Generation, HT-02 p. 45
  - Quote: "If flow rate is constant, temperature will vary directly with power. If power is constant, temperature will vary inversely with flow rate."
- **C805** (Thermal Hydraulics): About how much does decay heat fall after shutdown, per the handbook?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1012/2-92), Decay Heat, HT-02 p. 52
  - Quote: "Decay heat may decrease to about 2% of the pre-shutdown power level within the first hour after shutdown and to 1% within the first day."
- **C806** (Core Thermal Limits): What is FCCI?
  - Source: LP-CORE-THERMAL-LIMITS-WORD (Core Thermal Limits word.docx), slide 1.2 Differences
  - Quote: removed in ECI review. The card now cites ML19149A371.
- **Q901** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): What happens to a fluid's density and specific volume as temperature rises?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Continuity Equation, HT-03 p. 2
  - Quote: "As the temperature of the fluid increases, the density decreases and the specific volume increases."
- **Q902** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): How much fluid does a floating body displace?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Continuity Equation, HT-03 p. 3
  - Quote: "A floating body displaces its own weight of the fluid in which it floats."
- **Q903** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): A fluid column's pressure at the bottom is NOT affected by which of these?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Continuity Equation, HT-03 p. 5
  - Quote: "is independent of the cross-sectional area of the column."
- **Q904** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): How is mass flow rate related to volumetric flow rate?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Continuity Equation, HT-03 p. 9
  - Quote: "The mass flow rate (ṁ) of a system is a measure of the mass of fluid passing a point in the system per unit time."
- **Q905** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): Water at 62.44 lbm/ft³ flows at 1.22 ft³/sec. What is the mass flow rate?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Continuity Equation, HT-03 p. 10
  - Quote: "The water in the pipe of the previous example had a density of 62.44 lbm/ft3."
- **Q906** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): What happens to flow velocity when a pipe's diameter decreases at steady state?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Continuity Equation, HT-03 p. 12
  - Quote: "a decrease in pipe diameter will cause an increase in flow velocity."
- **Q907** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): What is the shape of the velocity profile for laminar flow in a pipe?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Laminar and Turbulent Flow, HT-03 p. 18
  - Quote: "the velocity distribution at a cross section will be parabolic in shape with the maximum velocity at the center being about twice the average velocity in the pipe."
- **Q908** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): What is the fluid velocity at the pipe wall?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Laminar and Turbulent Flow, HT-03 p. 18
  - Quote: "The velocity of the fluid in contact with the pipe wall is essentially zero"
- **Q909** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): For most fluids, what happens to viscosity as temperature rises?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Laminar and Turbulent Flow, HT-03 p. 19
  - Quote: "For most fluids, as the temperature of the fluid increases, the viscosity of the fluid decreases."
- **Q910** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): What describes an ideal fluid?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Laminar and Turbulent Flow, HT-03 p. 19
  - Quote: "An ideal fluid is one that is incompressible and has no viscosity."
- **Q911** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): A flow has a Reynolds number of 5000. What is the flow regime?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Laminar and Turbulent Flow, HT-03 p. 20
  - Quote: "if the Reynolds number is less than 2000, the flow is laminar. If it is greater than 3500, the flow is turbulent."
- **Q912** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): Which head represents the kinetic energy of a fluid?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Bernoulli's Equation, HT-03 p. 23
  - Quote: "The velocity head represents the kinetic energy of the fluid."
- **Q913** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): An ideal fluid flows through a horizontal pipe that gradually expands. What happens to its pressure?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Bernoulli's Equation, HT-03 p. 23
  - Quote: "a decrease in flow velocity in a horizontal pipe will result in an increase in pressure."
- **Q914** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): What two restrictions apply to the simplified Bernoulli equation?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Bernoulli's Equation, HT-03 p. 25
  - Quote: "The second restriction on Bernoulli’s equation is that no work is allowed to be done on or by the fluid."
- **Q915** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): How is volumetric flow rate through a venturi related to differential pressure?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Bernoulli's Equation, HT-03 p. 29
  - Quote: "the flow velocity at the throat of the venturi and the volumetric flow rate are directly proportional to the square root of the differential pressure."
- **Q916** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): If fluid velocity doubles in a pipe, what happens to frictional head loss?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Head Loss, HT-03 p. 31
  - Quote: "The head loss for fluid flow is directly proportional to the length of pipe, the square of the fluid velocity, and a term accounting for fluid friction called the friction factor."
- **Q917** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): Why is the term minor losses a misnomer?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Head Loss, HT-03 p. 34
  - Quote: "This is a misnomer because in many cases these losses are more important than the losses due to pipe friction"
- **Q918** (Thermal Hydraulics): Where must the heat source be relative to the heat sink for natural circulation?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Natural Circulation, HT-03 p. 38
  - Quote: "The heat source must be at a lower elevation than the heat sink."
- **Q919** (Thermal Hydraulics): What is forced circulation?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Natural Circulation, HT-03 p. 37
  - Quote: "Circulation of fluid in systems by pumps is referred to as forced circulation."
- **Q920** (Thermal Hydraulics): Why must natural circulation in the sodium system be inferred from temperature instruments?
  - Source: LP-THERMAL-HYDRAULICS (Thermal Hydraulics.docx), slide 1.35 Indications of Natural Circulation
  - Quote: "the flow rates involved in natural circulation are typically below the sensitivity range of the flow instruments designed for forced flow"
- **Q921** (Thermal Hydraulics): Which core exit temperature behavior indicates natural circulation flow?
  - Source: LP-THERMAL-HYDRAULICS (Thermal Hydraulics.docx), slide 1.36 Indications of Natural Circulation
  - Quote: "A core exit temperature that rises initially and then stabilizes is a good indication of natural circulation flow."
- **Q922** (Thermal Hydraulics): When enhancing natural circulation by removing more heat at the sink, what must be avoided?
  - Source: LP-THERMAL-HYDRAULICS (Thermal Hydraulics.docx), slide 1.38 Enhancing Natural Circulation
  - Quote: "Generally, removing more heat at the heat sink will enhance natural circulation flow, however care must be taken to avoid freezing the sodium, which would block natural circulation flow."
- **Q923** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): How does two-phase flow friction compare with single-phase friction for the same conduit and mass flow?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Two-Phase Fluid Flow, HT-03 p. 41
  - Quote: "Two-phase flow friction is greater than single-phase friction for the same conduit dimensions and mass flow rate."
- **Q924** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): Which two-phase flow pattern has a liquid film on the wall and droplets in a vapor core?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Two-Phase Fluid Flow, HT-03 p. 42
  - Quote: "Annular flow: the liquid is now distributed between a liquid film flowing up the wall and a dispersion of droplets flowing in the vapor core of the flow."
- **Q925** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): Which problem can sustained flow oscillations cause?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Two-Phase Fluid Flow, HT-03 p. 42
  - Quote: "sustained flow oscillations can cause undesirable forced mechanical vibration of components."
- **Q926** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): What is water hammer?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Two-Phase Fluid Flow, HT-03 p. 43
  - Quote: "Water hammer is a liquid shock wave resulting from the sudden starting or stopping of flow."
- **Q927** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): What causes pipe whip?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Two-Phase Fluid Flow, HT-03 p. 43
  - Quote: "If a pipe were to rupture, the reaction force created by the high velocity fluid jet could cause the piping to displace and cause extensive damage to components, instrumentation, and equipment in the area of the rupture."
- **Q928** (Steam): Why is steam hammer less severe than water hammer?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Two-Phase Fluid Flow, HT-03 p. 45
  - Quote: "Steam hammer is a gaseous shock wave resulting from the sudden starting or stopping of flow."
- **Q929** (Pumps): How can cavitation be avoided?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Centrifugal Pumps, HT-03 p. 49
  - Quote: "By maintaining the available NPSH at a level greater than the NPSH required by the pump manufacturer, cavitation can be avoided."
- **Q930** (Pumps): What does the volute of a centrifugal pump do?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Centrifugal Pumps, HT-03 p. 47
  - Quote: "The volute is a region of continuously increasing cross-sectional area designed to convert the kinetic energy of the fluid into fluid pressure."
- **Q931** (Pumps): A pump at 1800 rpm uses 45 kW. What power does it need at 3600 rpm?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Centrifugal Pumps, HT-03 p. 49
  - Quote: "the flow rate or capacity is directly proportional to the pump speed; the discharge head is directly proportional to the square of the pump speed; and the power required by the pump motor is directly proportional to the cube of the pump speed."
- **Q932** (Pumps): How does system head loss vary with volumetric flow rate?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Centrifugal Pumps, HT-03 p. 52
  - Quote: "the system head loss must be directly proportional to the square of the volumetric flow rate."
- **Q933** (Pumps): Two identical centrifugal pumps run in parallel. How does system flow compare with one pump?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Centrifugal Pumps, HT-03 p. 54
  - Quote: "the volumetric flow rate is actually less than twice the flow rate achieved by using a single pump."
- **Q934** (Pumps): For two identical centrifugal pumps in series, how is the combined curve found?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Centrifugal Pumps, HT-03 p. 54
  - Quote: "the head produced by both pumps is the sum of the individual heads."
- **C807** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): What are the Reynolds number limits for flow regimes?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Laminar and Turbulent Flow, HT-03 p. 20
  - Quote: "if the Reynolds number is less than 2000, the flow is laminar. If it is greater than 3500, the flow is turbulent."
- **C808** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): What is the term head with respect to fluid flow?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Bernoulli's Equation, HT-03 p. 23
  - Quote: "The term head is used by engineers in reference to pressure."
- **C809** (Pumps): What are the pump laws?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Centrifugal Pumps, HT-03 p. 49
  - Quote: "the flow rate or capacity is directly proportional to the pump speed; the discharge head is directly proportional to the square of the pump speed; and the power required by the pump motor is directly proportional to the cube of the pump speed."
- **C810** (Steam): What is two-phase flow?
  - Source: DOE-1012-V3 (DOE-HDBK-1012/3-92), Two-Phase Fluid Flow, HT-03 p. 41
  - Quote: "At certain important locations in fluid flow systems the simultaneous flow of liquid water and steam occurs, known as two-phase flow."
- **C811** (Thermal Hydraulics): What are the indications of natural circulation in the sodium system?
  - Source: LP-THERMAL-HYDRAULICS (Thermal Hydraulics.docx), slide 1.36 Indications of Natural Circulation
  - Quote: "A core exit temperature that rises initially and then stabilizes is a good indication of natural circulation flow."
- **Q935** (Sensors and Detectors): What happens to RTD resistance when temperature decreases?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Resistance Temperature Detectors (RTDs), IC-01 p. 4
  - Quote: "The resistance of an RTD varies directly with temperature"
- **Q936** (Sensors and Detectors): What are RTD elements normally made of?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Resistance Temperature Detectors (RTDs), IC-01 p. 2
  - Quote: "RTD elements are normally constructed of platinum, copper, or nickel."
- **Q937** (Sensors and Detectors): Why is Inconel normally used for the RTD sheath?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Resistance Temperature Detectors (RTDs), IC-01 p. 3
  - Quote: "Inconel, a nickel-iron-chromium alloy, is normally used in manufacturing the RTD sheath because of its inherent corrosion resistance."
- **Q938** (Sensors and Detectors): What does the insulator in an RTD do?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Resistance Temperature Detectors (RTDs), IC-01 p. 3
  - Quote: "The insulator prevents a short circuit between the wire and the metal sheath."
- **Q939** (Sensors and Detectors): What is a thermocouple constructed of?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Thermocouples, IC-01 p. 5
  - Quote: "A thermocouple is constructed of two dissimilar metal wires joined at one end."
- **Q940** (Sensors and Detectors): What is the most important factor when selecting thermocouple materials?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Thermocouples, IC-01 p. 5
  - Quote: "The most important factor to be considered when selecting a pair of materials is the "thermoelectric difference" between the two materials."
- **Q941** (Sensors and Detectors): Why does magnesium oxide surround thermocouple wires?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Thermocouples, IC-01 p. 6
  - Quote: "Magnesium oxide surrounds the thermocouple wires to prevent vibration that could damage the fine wires and to enhance heat transfer between the measuring junction and the medium surrounding the thermocouple."
- **Q942** (Sensors and Detectors): What are the three basic functions of temperature detectors?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Functional Uses of Temperature Detectors, IC-01 p. 8
  - Quote: "temperature detectors are used to provide three basic functions: indication, alarm, and control."
- **Q943** (Sensors and Detectors): If an installed spare is not available, what can measure temperature on accessible equipment?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Functional Uses of Temperature Detectors, IC-01 p. 8
  - Quote: "a contact pyrometer (portable thermocouple) may be used to obtain temperature readings on those pieces of equipment or systems that are accessible."
- **Q944** (Sensors and Detectors): Which two environmental concerns can affect temperature detection instrumentation?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Functional Uses of Temperature Detectors, IC-01 p. 9
  - Quote: "High humidity causes moisture to collect on the equipment."
- **Q945** (Sensors and Detectors): What condition shows that a bridge circuit is balanced?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Temperature Detection Circuitry, IC-01 p. 12
  - Quote: "When this condition exists, there is no current flow through the ammeter, and the bridge is said to be balanced."
- **Q946** (Sensors and Detectors): In a bridge circuit, what is the purpose of R1 and R2?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Temperature Detection Circuitry, IC-01 p. 11
  - Quote: "Resistors R1 and R2 are the ratio arms of the bridge."
- **Q947** (Sensors and Detectors): What does the adjustable resistor R3 do?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Temperature Detection Circuitry, IC-01 p. 11
  - Quote: "R3 is a variable resistor known as the standard arm that is adjusted to match the unknown resistor."
- **Q948** (Sensors and Detectors): What instrument does an unbalanced bridge circuit use to indicate temperature?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Temperature Detection Circuitry, IC-01 p. 12
  - Quote: "The unbalanced bridge circuit (Figure 9) uses a millivoltmeter that is calibrated in units of temperature that correspond to the RTD resistance."
- **Q949** (Sensors and Detectors): In a balanced bridge circuit, what is moved to balance the arms?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Temperature Detection Circuitry, IC-01 p. 13
  - Quote: "A slidewire resistor is used to balance the arms of the bridge."
- **Q950** (Sensors and Detectors): An RTD becomes shorted. What does the temperature meter indicate?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Temperature Detection Circuitry, IC-01 p. 14
  - Quote: "If it becomes shorted, resistance will be zero, and the meter will indicate a very low temperature."
- **Q951** (Sensors and Detectors): In a temperature detection circuit, what does the balancing motor do?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Temperature Detection Circuitry, IC-01 p. 14
  - Quote: "The bi-directional motor positions the slider on the slidewire to balance the circuit resistance."
- **Q952** (Sensors and Detectors): What does the bridge network do in a temperature detection circuit?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Temperature Detection Circuitry, IC-01 p. 14
  - Quote: "The bridge network converts this resistance to a DC voltage signal."
- **Q953** (Sensors and Detectors): Why are three and four wire RTD circuits used?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Temperature Detection Circuitry, IC-01 p. 15
  - Quote: "To compensate for this change, three and four wire RTD circuits are used."
- **C812** (Sensors and Detectors): How does an RTD respond to a temperature rise?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Resistance Temperature Detectors (RTDs), IC-01 p. 4
  - Quote: "The resistance of an RTD varies directly with temperature"
- **C813** (Sensors and Detectors): What is a dual-element RTD?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Functional Uses of Temperature Detectors, IC-01 p. 8
  - Quote: "The dual-element RTD has two sensing elements of which only one is normally connected."
- **C814** (Sensors and Detectors): What is a contact pyrometer?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Functional Uses of Temperature Detectors, IC-01 p. 8
  - Quote: "a contact pyrometer (portable thermocouple) may be used to obtain temperature readings on those pieces of equipment or systems that are accessible."
- **C815** (Sensors and Detectors): What are the three methods of bridge compensation for ambient temperature?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Temperature Detection Circuitry, IC-01 p. 15
  - Quote: "To compensate for this change, three and four wire RTD circuits are used."
- **C816** (Sensors and Detectors): How does an open RTD fail compared with a shorted RTD?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Temperature Detection Circuitry, IC-01 p. 14
  - Quote: "If the RTD becomes open in either the unbalanced and balanced bridge circuits, the resistance will be infinite, and the meter will indicate a very high temperature."
- **Q954** (Sensors and Detectors): In a bellows-type detector, where is system pressure applied?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detectors, IC-02 p. 2
  - Quote: "System pressure is applied to the internal volume of the bellows."
- **Q955** (Sensors and Detectors): How does a bellows produce an output as pressure changes?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detectors, IC-02 p. 2
  - Quote: "As the bellows and linkage assembly moves, either an electrical signal is generated or a direct pressure indication is provided."
- **Q956** (Sensors and Detectors): In what range is the metallic bellows most accurate?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detectors, IC-02 p. 1
  - Quote: "The metallic bellows is most accurate when measuring pressures from 0.5 to 75 psig."
- **Q957** (Sensors and Detectors): What happens to a bourdon tube as internal pressure increases?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detectors, IC-02 p. 2
  - Quote: "This change in cross-section causes the tube to straighten slightly."
- **Q958** (Sensors and Detectors): What are the three functions of pressure measuring instrumentation?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detector Functional Uses, IC-02 p. 4
  - Quote: "all pressure detectors are used to provide up to three basic functions: indication, alarm, and control."
- **Q959** (Sensors and Detectors): Which is NOT one of the three environmental concerns for pressure instruments?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detector Functional Uses, IC-02 p. 4
  - Quote: "Pressure instruments are sensitive to variations in the atmospheric pressure surrounding the detector."
- **Q960** (Sensors and Detectors): A pressure detector fails and no spare is installed. What may be used?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detector Functional Uses, IC-02 p. 4
  - Quote: "the pressure may be read at an independent local mechanical gauge, if available, or a precision pressure gauge may be installed in the system at a convenient point."
- **Q961** (Sensors and Detectors): How does a strain gauge detect pressure?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detection Circuitry, IC-02 p. 6
  - Quote: "The pressure change causes a resistance change due to the distortion of the wire."
- **Q962** (Sensors and Detectors): What happens to a strain gauge wire's resistance when it is stretched by elastic deformation?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detection Circuitry, IC-02 p. 7
  - Quote: "As the wire grid is distorted by elastic deformation, its length is increased, and its cross-sectional area decreases."
- **Q963** (Sensors and Detectors): How is the strain gauge's change in resistance turned into a signal?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detection Circuitry, IC-02 p. 7
  - Quote: "This change in resistance is used as the variable resistance in a bridge circuit that provides an electrical signal for indication of pressure."
- **Q964** (Sensors and Detectors): What are the three parts of an inductance-type pressure transducer?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detection Circuitry, IC-02 p. 9
  - Quote: "The inductance-type transducer consists of three parts: a coil, a movable magnetic core, and a pressure sensing element."
- **Q965** (Sensors and Detectors): In a differential transformer, what is the output with the core at mid-position?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detection Circuitry, IC-02 p. 10
  - Quote: "When the core is in the mid-position, there is no secondary output."
- **Q966** (Sensors and Detectors): In a capacitive pressure transducer, what happens as pressure increases?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detection Circuitry, IC-02 p. 11
  - Quote: "As pressure increases, the flexible conductive plates will move farther apart, changing the capacitance of the transducer."
- **Q967** (Sensors and Detectors): In a pressure detection device, what does the transducer do?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detection Circuitry, IC-02 p. 12
  - Quote: "The transducer converts the mechanical signal to an electrical signal that is proportional to system pressure."
- **Q968** (Sensors and Detectors): What does the sensing element of a pressure detection device do?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detection Circuitry, IC-02 p. 12
  - Quote: "The sensing element senses the pressure of the monitored system and converts the pressure to a mechanical signal."
- **Q969** (Sensors and Detectors): A sensing element in a pressure detector ruptures. How does the detector fail?
  - Source: LP-PRESSURE-DETECTORS (Pressure Detectors.docx), slide 1.16 Pressure Detector Failures
  - Quote: "Sensing Element Leak or Rupture | Fails Low"
- **Q970** (Sensors and Detectors): A pressure detector is overpressurized. How does it fail?
  - Source: LP-PRESSURE-DETECTORS (Pressure Detectors.docx), slide 1.16 Pressure Detector Failures
  - Quote: "Overpressurization | Fails high"
- **C817** (Sensors and Detectors): What is a bourdon tube?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detectors, IC-02 p. 2
  - Quote: "the movement of the tip of the tube can then be used to position a pointer or to develop an equivalent electrical signal"
- **C818** (Sensors and Detectors): What are the three environmental concerns for pressure instruments?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detector Functional Uses, IC-02 p. 4
  - Quote: "Pressure instruments are sensitive to variations in the atmospheric pressure surrounding the detector."
- **C819** (Sensors and Detectors): What must oppose a metallic bellows in practice?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detectors, IC-02 p. 2
  - Quote: "in practice, the bellows must always be opposed by a spring"
- **C820** (Sensors and Detectors): What does a strain gauge measure?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detection Circuitry, IC-02 p. 6
  - Quote: "A strain gauge measures the external force (pressure) applied to a fine wire."
- **C821** (Sensors and Detectors): What three kinds of change can a pressure transducer produce?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Pressure Detection Circuitry, IC-02 p. 6
  - Quote: "Transducers can produce a change in resistance, inductance, or capacitance."

## 2026-11-05: Lesson topics (knowledge checks and key facts)

Added 117 quiz questions and 28 flashcards from the lesson topics. Every quote passed scripts/verify-quotes.py. Calculation questions use new numbers with the method the quote supports.

- **Q971** (Sensors and Detectors): What operating principle does a gauge glass use?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Level Detectors, IC-03 p. 2
  - Quote: "the liquid seeks its own level due to the pressure of the liquid in the vessel."
- **Q972** (Sensors and Detectors): A pressure gauge at the bottom of a tank reads hydrostatic head. Which group of level measurement is this?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Level Detectors, IC-03 p. 1
  - Quote: "Liquid level measuring devices are classified into two groups: (a) direct method, and (b) inferred method."
- **Q973** (Sensors and Detectors): In a refraction gauge glass, what color shows the portion containing water?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Level Detectors, IC-03 p. 4
  - Quote: "The portion of the gauge containing water appears green; the portion of the gauge from that level upward appears red."
- **Q974** (Sensors and Detectors): What limits the level range of a ball float?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Level Detectors, IC-03 p. 5
  - Quote: "The actual level range is determined by the length of the connecting arm."
- **Q975** (Sensors and Detectors): What limits the level range of a chain float?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Level Detectors, IC-03 p. 5
  - Quote: "The range of level measured will be limited only by the size of the vessel."
- **Q976** (Sensors and Detectors): Why was the magnetic bond method developed?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Level Detectors, IC-03 p. 6
  - Quote: "The magnetic bond method was developed to overcome the problems of cages and stuffing boxes."
- **Q977** (Sensors and Detectors): In a conductivity probe system, what happens when liquid touches an electrode?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Level Detectors, IC-03 p. 6
  - Quote: "When the liquid makes contact with any of the electrodes, an electric current will flow between the electrode and ground."
- **Q978** (Sensors and Detectors): Why must a dry reference leg be kept dry?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Level Detectors, IC-03 p. 8
  - Quote: "The reference leg must be maintained dry so that there is no liquid head pressure on the low pressure side of the transmitter."
- **Q979** (Sensors and Detectors): With a dry reference leg on a pressurized tank, why does gas pressure not affect the level reading?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Level Detectors, IC-03 p. 8
  - Quote: "The gas or vapor pressure is equally applied to the low and high pressure sides."
- **Q980** (Sensors and Detectors): Why is density compensation needed in level detection?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Density Compensation, IC-03 p. 12
  - Quote: "some means of density compensation must be incorporated in order to have an accurate indication of tank level."
- **Q981** (Sensors and Detectors): Which is one way density compensation is accomplished?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Density Compensation, IC-03 p. 13
  - Quote: "Density compensation may also be accomplished through electronic circuitry."
- **Q982** (Sensors and Detectors): Which is one of the three reasons for using remote level indicators?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Level Detection Circuitry, IC-03 p. 15
  - Quote: "The level being measured may be in an unsafe/radioactive area."
- **Q983** (Sensors and Detectors): In a D/P level instrument, what converts diaphragm motion into an electrical signal?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Level Detection Circuitry, IC-03 p. 15
  - Quote: "The transducer changes this mechanical motion into an electrical signal."
- **Q984** (Sensors and Detectors): What are the three environmental concerns for level detection instrumentation?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Level Detection Circuitry, IC-03 p. 16
  - Quote: "It primarily affects level sensing instruments which utilize a wet reference leg."
- **C822** (Sensors and Detectors): What are the two groups of level measuring devices?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Level Detectors, IC-03 p. 1
  - Quote: "Liquid level measuring devices are classified into two groups: (a) direct method, and (b) inferred method."
- **C823** (Sensors and Detectors): How is differential pressure related to level with a wet reference leg?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Level Detectors, IC-03 p. 9
  - Quote: "the differential pressure and the transmitter output are inversely proportional to the tank level."
- **C824** (Sensors and Detectors): How is differential pressure related to level with a dry reference leg?
  - Source: LP-LEVEL-DETECTORS (Level Detectors.docx), slide 1.8 The most important slide of this section!!
  - Quote: "when differential pressure rises, indicated level rises for level detectors in a dry reference leg."
- **C825** (Sensors and Detectors): What are the three methods of density compensation in level detection?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Density Compensation, IC-03 p. 13
  - Quote: "Density compensation may also be accomplished through electronic circuitry."
- **C826** (Sensors and Detectors): What are the three reasons for remote level indication?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Level Detection Circuitry, IC-03 p. 15
  - Quote: "Remote indication is necessary to provide transmittal of vital level information to a central location"
- **Q985** (Sensors and Detectors): What are the two elements of a head flow meter?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Head Flow Meters, IC-04 p. 1
  - Quote: "Head flow meters operate on the principle of placing a restriction in the line to cause a differential pressure head."
- **Q986** (Sensors and Detectors): What does a head flow meter actually measure?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Head Flow Meters, IC-04 p. 2
  - Quote: "The head flow meter actually measures volume flow rate rather than mass flow rate."
- **Q987** (Sensors and Detectors): What are the two distinct disadvantages of orifice plates?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Head Flow Meters, IC-04 p. 3
  - Quote: "they cause a high permanent pressure drop (outlet pressure will be 60% to 80% of inlet pressure), and they are subject to erosion"
- **Q988** (Sensors and Detectors): Which orifice plate is the most common?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Head Flow Meters, IC-04 p. 3
  - Quote: "The concentric orifice plate is the most common of the three types."
- **Q989** (Sensors and Detectors): Which is the most accurate flow-sensing element when properly calibrated?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Head Flow Meters, IC-04 p. 4
  - Quote: "The venturi tube, illustrated in Figure 3, is the most accurate flow-sensing element when properly calibrated."
- **Q990** (Sensors and Detectors): About what is the pressure loss of a dall flow tube?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Head Flow Meters, IC-04 p. 5
  - Quote: "This type of flow tube has a pressure loss of about 5%."
- **Q991** (Sensors and Detectors): What does a pitot tube actually measure?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Head Flow Meters, IC-04 p. 6
  - Quote: "The pitot tube actually measures fluid velocity instead of fluid flow rate."
- **Q992** (Sensors and Detectors): What happens to the float in a rotameter as flow rises?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Other Flow Meters, IC-04 p. 8
  - Quote: "The rotameter consists of a metal float and a conical glass tube, constructed such that the diameter increases with height."
- **Q993** (Sensors and Detectors): How does a nutating disk meter find total flow?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Other Flow Meters, IC-04 p. 9
  - Quote: "As the fluid flows through the chamber, the disk wobbles, or executes a nutating motion."
- **Q994** (Sensors and Detectors): What must a fluid have for an electromagnetic flowmeter to work?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Other Flow Meters, IC-04 p. 10
  - Quote: "However, the fluid should have some degree of electrical conductivity."
- **Q995** (Sensors and Detectors): Why does a steam flow instrument need density compensation?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Steam Flow Detection, IC-04 p. 13
  - Quote: "Since steam is considered to be a gas, changes in pressure and temperature greatly affect its density."
- **Q996** (Sensors and Detectors): In a flow detection circuit, what does the extractor do?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Flow Circuitry, IC-04 p. 18
  - Quote: "The extractor is used to electronically calculate the square root of the differential pressure and provide an output proportional to system flow."
- **Q997** (Sensors and Detectors): What are the three factors that can affect flow sensing instrumentation?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Flow Circuitry, IC-04 p. 19
  - Quote: "The density of the fluid, ambient temperature, and humidity are the three factors which can affect the accuracy and reliability of flow sensing instrumentation."
- **Q998** (Sensors and Detectors): All flow indication is lost. How can flow be approximated?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Flow Circuitry, IC-04 p. 18
  - Quote: "If all means of flow indication are lost, flow can be approximated using pump differential pressure."
- **Q999** (Sensors and Detectors): A D/P flow instrument has a leak on the high pressure connection. How does indicated flow compare with actual?
  - Source: LP-FLOW-DETECTORS (Flow Detectors.docx), slide 1.14 Failure Modes Chart
  - Quote: "Indicated flow would be less than actual because of a lowering Differential Pressure sensed by the instrument."
- **Q1000** (Sensors and Detectors): A D/P flow instrument has a leak on the low pressure connection. How does indicated flow compare with actual?
  - Source: LP-FLOW-DETECTORS (Flow Detectors.docx), slide 1.14 Failure Modes Chart
  - Quote: "Indicated flow would be more than actual because of higher Differential Pressure sensed by the instrument."
- **Q1001** (Sensors and Detectors): What indication results from vapor in the liquid passing through a head flow meter?
  - Source: LP-FLOW-DETECTORS (Flow Detectors.docx), slide 1.14 Failure Modes Chart
  - Quote: "What will be seen is very erratic indication from the detector."
- **C827** (Sensors and Detectors): How is flow related to differential pressure in a head flow meter?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Flow Circuitry, IC-04 p. 18
  - Quote: "flow rate is proportional to the square root of the differential pressure."
- **C828** (Sensors and Detectors): What are the three kinds of orifice plates?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Head Flow Meters, IC-04 p. 3
  - Quote: "Three kinds of orifice plates are used: concentric, eccentric, and segmental"
- **C829** (Sensors and Detectors): What are the major disadvantages of a venturi tube?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Head Flow Meters, IC-04 p. 4
  - Quote: "The major disadvantages of this type of flow detection are the high initial costs for installation and difficulty in installation and inspection."
- **C830** (Sensors and Detectors): What does an extractor do in a flow detection circuit?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Flow Circuitry, IC-04 p. 18
  - Quote: "The extractor is used to electronically calculate the square root of the differential pressure and provide an output proportional to system flow."
- **C831** (Sensors and Detectors): How is pump differential pressure related to pump flow?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Flow Circuitry, IC-04 p. 18
  - Quote: "Pump differential pressure is proportional to the square of pump flow."
- **Q1002** (Sensors and Detectors): What are the two advantages of an electrical synchro over mechanical indicators?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Synchro Equipment, IC-05 p. 1
  - Quote: "An electrical synchro has two distinct advantages over mechanical indicators: (1) greater accuracy, and (2) simpler routing of remote indication."
- **Q1003** (Sensors and Detectors): What does the damping device in a synchro receiver prevent?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Synchro Equipment, IC-05 p. 2
  - Quote: "it incorporates a damping device to prevent hunting."
- **Q1004** (Sensors and Detectors): How many stator windings does a synchro transmitter have?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Synchro Equipment, IC-05 p. 1
  - Quote: "The transmitter, or synchro generator, consists of a rotor with a single winding and a stator with three windings placed 120 degrees apart."
- **Q1005** (Sensors and Detectors): What kind of failure is normal for limit switches?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Switches, IC-05 p. 6
  - Quote: "Limit switch failures are normally mechanical in nature."
- **Q1006** (Sensors and Detectors): Why are reed switches more reliable than limit switches?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Switches, IC-05 p. 6
  - Quote: "Reed switches, illustrated in Figure 4, are more reliable than limit switches, due to their simplified construction."
- **Q1007** (Sensors and Detectors): A reed switch is stuck shut. What does the indication show?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Switches, IC-05 p. 7
  - Quote: "If a reed switch is stuck shut, the open (closed) indication will be continuously illuminated."
- **Q1008** (Sensors and Detectors): What does an electrical short or open do to a potentiometer valve position indicator?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Variable Output Devices, IC-05 p. 8
  - Quote: "An electrical short or open will cause the indication to fail at one extreme or the other."
- **Q1009** (Sensors and Detectors): How does an LVDT differ from a potentiometer position indicator?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Variable Output Devices, IC-05 p. 9
  - Quote: "Unlike the potentiometer position indicator, no physical connection to the extension is required."
- **Q1010** (Sensors and Detectors): What does the indicating and control circuitry of a position indicator provide?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Position Indication Circuitry, IC-05 p. 13
  - Quote: "The indicating and control circuitry provides for remote indication of valve or rod position and/or various control functions."
- **Q1011** (Sensors and Detectors): What form do position control functions usually take?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Position Indication Circuitry, IC-05 p. 11
  - Quote: "Control functions are usually in the form of interlocks."
- **Q1012** (Sensors and Detectors): Which two environmental concerns can affect position indication equipment?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Position Indication Circuitry, IC-05 p. 13
  - Quote: "The accuracy and reliability of position indication instrumentation can be affected by ambient temperature and humidity."
- **C832** (Sensors and Detectors): What is hunting in a synchro?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Synchro Equipment, IC-05 p. 2
  - Quote: "Hunting refers to the overshoot and undershoot that occur as the receiving device tries to match the sending device."
- **C833** (Sensors and Detectors): How does a limit switch indicate position?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Switches, IC-05 p. 5
  - Quote: "The limit switch gives ON/OFF output that corresponds to valve position."
- **C834** (Sensors and Detectors): How can reed switches show incremental position?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Switches, IC-05 p. 6
  - Quote: "By using a large number of magnetic reed switches, incremental position can be measured."
- **C835** (Sensors and Detectors): What happens if potentiometer resistance increases or decreases?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Variable Output Devices, IC-05 p. 8
  - Quote: "If an increase or decrease in the potentiometer resistance occurs, erratic indicated valve position occurs."
- **C836** (Sensors and Detectors): What do control rod interlocks do?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1013/1-92), Position Indication Circuitry, IC-05 p. 11
  - Quote: "Control rod interlocks are normally used to prevent outward motion of certain rods unless certain conditions are met."
- **Q1013** (Sensors and Detectors): What is specific ionization?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Radiation Detection Terminology, IC-06 p. 1
  - Quote: "Specific ionization is that number of ion pairs produced per centimeter of travel through matter."
- **Q1014** (Sensors and Detectors): How are stopping power and specific ionization related?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Radiation Detection Terminology, IC-06 p. 2
  - Quote: "Stopping power, or LET, is proportional to the specific ionization."
- **Q1015** (Sensors and Detectors): Which factor has the greatest effect on specific ionization?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Radiation Detection Terminology, IC-06 p. 1
  - Quote: "A particle’s charge has the greatest effect on specific ionization."
- **Q1016** (Sensors and Detectors): Which is the least penetrating radiation?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Radiation Types, IC-06 p. 4
  - Quote: "Alpha particles are the least penetrating radiation."
- **Q1017** (Sensors and Detectors): Why is the specific ionization of a beta particle low?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Radiation Types, IC-06 p. 5
  - Quote: "The specific ionization of a beta particle is low due to its small mass, small charge, and relatively high speed of travel."
- **Q1018** (Sensors and Detectors): What minimum energy must a gamma have for pair production?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Radiation Types, IC-06 p. 7
  - Quote: "the original gamma must have at least 1.02 MeV energy."
- **Q1019** (Sensors and Detectors): Which gamma attenuation method is most predominant with low energy gammas?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Radiation Types, IC-06 p. 6
  - Quote: "The photoelectric effect is most predominant with low energy gammas"
- **Q1020** (Sensors and Detectors): Why is a neutron fairly difficult to stop?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Radiation Types, IC-06 p. 8
  - Quote: "Neutrons have no electrical charge and have nearly the same mass as a proton"
- **Q1021** (Sensors and Detectors): Which of these is a neutron reaction with a nucleus?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Radiation Types, IC-06 p. 8
  - Quote: "Neutrons may collide with nuclei causing one of the following reactions: inelastic scattering, elastic scattering, radiative capture, or fission."
- **Q1022** (Sensors and Detectors): What is gas amplification?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Gas-Filled Detector, IC-06 p. 12
  - Quote: "This multiplication of electrons is termed gas amplification."
- **Q1023** (Sensors and Detectors): In a gas-filled detector, what attracts the electrons?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Gas-Filled Detector, IC-06 p. 11
  - Quote: "The positive anode attracts the electrons, or negative particles. The detector wall, or cathode, attracts the positive charges."
- **Q1024** (Sensors and Detectors): In which region is pulse height independent of the type of radiation?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Detector Voltage, IC-06 p. 16
  - Quote: "The pulse height in the Geiger-Müller region (Region V) is independent of the type of radiation causing the initial ionizations."
- **Q1025** (Sensors and Detectors): Why is the alpha curve above the beta curve at lower voltages?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Detector Voltage, IC-06 p. 14
  - Quote: "An alpha particle will create more ion pairs than a beta since the alpha has a much greater mass."
- **Q1026** (Sensors and Detectors): Why is the gas amplification region called proportional?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Detector Voltage, IC-06 p. 16
  - Quote: "This region is called the proportional region since the gas amplification factor (A) is proportional to applied voltage."
- **Q1027** (Sensors and Detectors): Why is a quenching gas added to a proportional counter?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Proportional Counter, IC-06 p. 21
  - Quote: "These pulses must be eliminated or "quenched.""
- **Q1028** (Sensors and Detectors): What is the major advantage of a proportional counter over an ionization chamber?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Proportional Counter, IC-06 p. 21
  - Quote: "The high amplification factor of the proportional counter is the major advantage over the ionization chamber."
- **Q1029** (Sensors and Detectors): In a proportional counter circuit, what does the scaler do?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Proportional Counter Circuitry, IC-06 p. 25
  - Quote: "This output is fed to a scaler which counts the number of pulses it receives."
- **Q1030** (Sensors and Detectors): Why can't proportional counters be used at high power levels?
  - Source: DOE-1013-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1013/2-92), Proportional Counter Circuitry, IC-06 p. 27
  - Quote: "Proportional counters cannot be used at high power levels because they are pulse-type detectors."
