  - Source: DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 6
  - Quote: "Figure 7 shows the common symbols for relays, contacts, connectors, lines, resistors, and other miscellaneous electrical components."
- **Q1238** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What do the letters TDO mean next to a contact?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 6
  - Quote: "Figure 7 shows the common symbols for relays, contacts, connectors, lines, resistors, and other miscellaneous electrical components."
- **Q1239** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): Which letters mark a diesel driven generator on an electrical drawing?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 7
  - Quote: "The symbols in Figure 8 are used to identify the larger components that may be found in an electrical diagram or schematic."
- **Q1240** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): Which electrical diagram places equipment to approximate its actual physical location?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 9
  - Quote: "The two most commonly used are the wiring diagram and the schematic diagram."
- **Q1241** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): A load circle on a power distribution single line is marked 350. Unless otherwise stated, what are the units?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 12
  - Quote: "Unless otherwise stated, the common units are kilowatts (kW)."
- **Q1242** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What does an electrical single line show?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 12
  - Quote: "This type of diagram depicts the major power sources, breakers, loads, and protective devices, thereby providing a useful overall view of the flow of power in a large electrical power distribution system."
- **Q1243** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): Unless otherwise noted, in what condition are devices shown on an electrical schematic?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 17
  - Quote: "Electrical components, such as relays, are drawn in the de-energized state unless otherwise noted on the diagram."
- **Q1244** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): How do you find the contacts operated by relay M1 on a schematic?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 14
  - Quote: "The number/letter code for each relay is carried by all associated contacts."
- **Q1245** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): A relay coil on a schematic is energized. An "a" contact with its code is drawn open. What is that contact's state now?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 14
  - Quote: "For electrical schematics that detail individual relays and contacts, the components are always shown in the de-energized condition (also called the shelf- state)."
- **Q1246** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): Two breakers on a drawing are joined by a dashed line. What does that show?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 15
  - Quote: "The dashed line is also used to indicate a mechanical interlock between two circuit components."
- **Q1247** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): Switch 1 and Switch 2 are ganged, and Switch 1 is closed. What is the state of Switch 2?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 15
  - Quote: "In that example, closing Switch 1 also closes Switch 2."
- **Q1248** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): A system single line shows a single-phase air core transformer symbol. What does that prove about the transformer?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 15
  - Quote: "In system single line diagrams, transformers are often represented by the symbol for a single- phase air core transformer; however, that does not necessarily mean that the transformer has an air core or that it is single phase."
- **Q1249** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): Which mark beside a transformer winding shows a delta connection?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 15
  - Quote: "In system single line diagrams, transformers are often represented by the symbol for a single- phase air core transformer; however, that does not necessarily mean that the transformer has an air core or that it is single phase."
- **C889** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What does pole mean for a switch?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 3
  - Quote: "The term "pole," as used to describe the switches in Figure 3, refers to the number of points at which current can enter a switch."
- **C890** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What does throw mean for a switch?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 3
  - Quote: "The term "throw" used in Figure 3 refers to the number of circuits that each pole of a switch can complete or control."
- **C891** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What do chevrons on a breaker symbol show?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 6
  - Quote: "The chevrons represent the point at which the breaker disconnects from the circuit when removed."
- **C892** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): How do you match a relay to its contacts on a schematic?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 14
  - Quote: "The number/letter code for each relay is carried by all associated contacts."
- **C893** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What are ganged switches?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 15
  - Quote: "Such switches are called ganged switches and are symbolized by connecting them with a dashed line as shown in Figure 15 (A)."
- **C894** (Breakers, Relays, and Disconnects): What are the common units for loads on a power distribution single line?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1016/1-93), Electrical Diagrams and Schematics, PR-03 p. 12
  - Quote: "Unless otherwise stated, the common units are kilowatts (kW)."
- **Q1250** (Controllers and Positioners): What is the purpose of an electronic schematic diagram?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Electronic Diagrams, Prints, and Schematics, PR-04 p. 17
  - Quote: "An electronic schematic diagram presents the detailed information about the circuit, each of its components, and how they are wired into the circuit."
- **Q1251** (Controllers and Positioners): Which symbol represents an amplifier on an electronic schematic?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Electronic Diagrams, Prints, and Schematics, PR-04 p. 2
  - Quote: "Figure 1 and Figure 2 illustrate the most common electronic symbols used on electronic schematics."
- **Q1252** (Controllers and Positioners): On an electronic schematic, how is a light emitting diode told apart from a plain diode?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Electronic Diagrams, Prints, and Schematics, PR-04 p. 2
  - Quote: "Figure 1 and Figure 2 illustrate the most common electronic symbols used on electronic schematics."
- **Q1253** (Controllers and Positioners): Which symbol letter marks an ammeter on an electronic drawing?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Electronic Diagrams, Prints, and Schematics, PR-04 p. 2
  - Quote: "Figure 1 and Figure 2 illustrate the most common electronic symbols used on electronic schematics."
- **Q1254** (Controllers and Positioners): What does a pictorial layout diagram show that an electronic schematic does not?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Electronic Diagrams, Prints, and Schematics, PR-04 p. 5
  - Quote: "These drawings show the actual layout of the components on the circuit board."
- **Q1255** (Controllers and Positioners): What is the first observation when reading a detailed electronic schematic?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Electronic Diagrams, Prints, and Schematics, PR-04 p. 7
  - Quote: "The first observation in dealing with a detailed electronic schematic is the source and polarity of power."
- **Q1256** (Controllers and Positioners): A schematic shows +15 volts with no other marking. What type of power may normally be assumed?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Electronic Diagrams, Prints, and Schematics, PR-04 p. 7
  - Quote: "Unless specified as an Alternating Current (AC) power source, the voltages can normally be assumed to be Direct Current (DC)."
- **Q1257** (Controllers and Positioners): An NPN transistor has a positive supply and ground on the emitter. The input goes negative. What happens?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Electronic Diagrams, Prints, and Schematics, PR-04 p. 9
  - Quote: "If the input goes negative, as in Figure 8, the conduction of the device stops because the input, or in this case the base junction, controls the transistor condition."
- **Q1258** (Controllers and Positioners): Which way does the arrow on a diode symbol point?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Electronic Diagrams, Prints, and Schematics, PR-04 p. 10
  - Quote: "The diode symbol, like the transistor symbol, shows the direction of conduction by the direction of the arrow, which is from positive to negative."
- **Q1259** (Controllers and Positioners): Why is a diode simpler than a transistor?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Electronic Diagrams, Prints, and Schematics, PR-04 p. 10
  - Quote: "However, diodes are simpler than transistors because they have only one junction and conduct in only one direction, as indicated in Figure 10."
- **Q1260** (Controllers and Positioners): How is a line continued from one electronic drawing to another generally shown?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Electronic Diagrams, Prints, and Schematics, PR-04 p. 11
  - Quote: "This may be done in many ways, but generally the line or conductor to be continued will end at a terminal board."
- **Q1261** (Controllers and Positioners): What do arrows on a block diagram show?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Electronic Diagrams, Prints, and Schematics, PR-04 p. 12
  - Quote: "Block diagrams are designed to present flow or functional information about the circuit or system, not detailed component data."
- **Q1262** (Controllers and Positioners): Who decides what each block on a block diagram contains?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Electronic Diagrams, Prints, and Schematics, PR-04 p. 13
  - Quote: "The creator of the block diagram decides the content of each block based on the intended use of the drawing."
- **C895** (Controllers and Positioners): What are the two basic categories of electronic prints?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Electronic Diagrams, Prints, and Schematics, PR-04 p. 1
  - Quote: "Electronic prints fall into two basic categories, electronic schematics and block diagrams."
- **C896** (Controllers and Positioners): In what condition do electronic prints show relays and contacts?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Electronic Diagrams, Prints, and Schematics, PR-04 p. 7
  - Quote: "As with electrical systems, the relays and contacts shown are always in the de-energized condition."
- **C897** (Controllers and Positioners): What is the first thing to look for on a detailed electronic schematic?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Electronic Diagrams, Prints, and Schematics, PR-04 p. 7
  - Quote: "The first observation in dealing with a detailed electronic schematic is the source and polarity of power."
- **C898** (Controllers and Positioners): What voltage type can be assumed on an electronic schematic unless stated otherwise?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Electronic Diagrams, Prints, and Schematics, PR-04 p. 7
  - Quote: "Unless specified as an Alternating Current (AC) power source, the voltages can normally be assumed to be Direct Current (DC)."
- **C899** (Controllers and Positioners): Which way does current flow through a transistor, using conventional current flow?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Electronic Diagrams, Prints, and Schematics, PR-04 p. 9
  - Quote: "Using conventional current flow (i.e. from + to -), current will travel through the transistor from most positive to least positive and in the direction of the arrow on the emitter."
- **C900** (Controllers and Positioners): How does a diode differ from a transistor?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Electronic Diagrams, Prints, and Schematics, PR-04 p. 10
  - Quote: "However, diodes are simpler than transistors because they have only one junction and conduct in only one direction, as indicated in Figure 10."
- **Q1263** (Controllers and Positioners): What does a logic diagram let the user determine?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 1
  - Quote: "The use of logic symbology results in a diagram that allows the user to determine the operation of a given component or system as the various input signals change."
- **Q1264** (Controllers and Positioners): An AND gate has three inputs, and two are on. What is its output?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 4
  - Quote: "AND gate - provides an output (on) when all its inputs are on. When any one of the inputs is off, the gate's output is off."
- **Q1265** (Controllers and Positioners): An OR gate has three inputs, and one is on. What is its output?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 4
  - Quote: "OR gate - provides an output (on) when any one or more of its inputs is on. The gate is off only when all of its inputs are off."
- **Q1266** (Controllers and Positioners): A NAND gate has two inputs, and both are on. What is its output?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 4
  - Quote: "NAND gate - is the opposite (NOT) of an AND gate's output. It provides an output (on) except when all the inputs are on."
- **Q1267** (Controllers and Positioners): When does a NOR gate provide an output?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 4
  - Quote: "NOR gate - is the opposite (NOT) of an OR gate's output. It provides an output only when all inputs are off."
- **Q1268** (Controllers and Positioners): Which logic value means the same as off?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 4
  - Quote: "The states of a gate are also commonly referred to as high or low, 1 or 0, or True or False, where on = high = 1 = True, and off = low = 0 = False."
- **Q1269** (Controllers and Positioners): A COINCIDENCE gate shows the fraction 2/3. Two inputs are on. What is its output?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 6
  - Quote: "The numerator of the fraction indicates the number of inputs that must be on for the gate to be on."
- **Q1270** (Controllers and Positioners): An EXCLUSIVE OR gate has two inputs, and both are on. What is its output?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 6
  - Quote: "EXCLUSIVE OR - provides an output (on) when only one of the inputs is on. Any other combination results in no output (off)."
- **Q1271** (Controllers and Positioners): A Type-One device is set for 4 seconds. The input is on for 2 seconds. What is the output?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 7
  - Quote: "the Type-One Time Delay Device delays the output (on) for the specified period of time, but the output will stop (off) as soon as the input signal is removed, as illustrated by Figure 7."
- **Q1272** (Controllers and Positioners): A Type-Two device is set for 4 seconds. What happens when the input is removed?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 7
  - Quote: "but the output is maintained only for a specified period of time once the input signal (off) has been removed."
- **Q1273** (Controllers and Positioners): What are the two input signals to a memory device called?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 8
  - Quote: "The two input signals to a memory device are called set and reset."
- **Q1274** (Controllers and Positioners): What is a binary counter built from?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 10
  - Quote: "Several types of binary counters exist, all of which are constructed of flip-flops."
- **Q1275** (Controllers and Positioners): What does a shift register do?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 10
  - Quote: "Shift register - Is a storage device constructed of flip-flops that is used in computers to provide temporary storage of a binary word."
- **Q1276** (Controllers and Positioners): How many rows does a truth table need for a gate with three inputs?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Truth Tables and Exercises, PR-05 p. 11
  - Quote: "A truth table has a column for the input of each gate and column for the output of each gate."
- **Q1277** (Controllers and Positioners): In a truth table for an OR gate, which inputs give an output of 0?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Truth Tables and Exercises, PR-05 p. 11
  - Quote: "In truth tables, the on and off status of the inputs and outputs is represented using 0s and 1s."
- **Q1278** (Controllers and Positioners): In a truth table for a NOR gate, which inputs give an output of 1?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Truth Tables and Exercises, PR-05 p. 11
  - Quote: "In truth tables, the on and off status of the inputs and outputs is represented using 0s and 1s."
- **Q1279** (Controllers and Positioners): A logic diagram gives no gate status. How do you read it?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Truth Tables and Exercises, PR-05 p. 13
  - Quote: "It simply requires the reader to choose the initial conditions, determine the response of the circuits, and modify the inputs as needed."
- **C901** (Controllers and Positioners): What are the three basic types of logic gates?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 4
  - Quote: "There are three basic types of logic gates. They are AND, OR, and NOT gates."
- **C902** (Controllers and Positioners): When does an AND gate provide an output?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 4
  - Quote: "AND gate - provides an output (on) when all its inputs are on. When any one of the inputs is off, the gate's output is off."
- **C903** (Controllers and Positioners): When is an OR gate off?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 4
  - Quote: "OR gate - provides an output (on) when any one or more of its inputs is on. The gate is off only when all of its inputs are off."
- **C904** (Controllers and Positioners): When does a NAND gate provide an output?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 4
  - Quote: "NAND gate - is the opposite (NOT) of an AND gate's output. It provides an output (on) except when all the inputs are on."
- **C905** (Controllers and Positioners): What does the fraction in a COINCIDENCE gate symbol mean?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 6
  - Quote: "The numerator of the fraction indicates the number of inputs that must be on for the gate to be on."
- **C906** (Controllers and Positioners): When does an EXCLUSIVE OR gate provide an output?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 6
  - Quote: "EXCLUSIVE OR - provides an output (on) when only one of the inputs is on. Any other combination results in no output (off)."
- **C907** (Controllers and Positioners): What does a Type-Two Time Delay Device do?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Logic Diagrams, PR-05 p. 7
  - Quote: "but the output is maintained only for a specified period of time once the input signal (off) has been removed."
- **C908** (Controllers and Positioners): How many rows does a truth table need?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Truth Tables and Exercises, PR-05 p. 11
  - Quote: "A truth table has a column for the input of each gate and column for the output of each gate."

## 2026-11-05: Lesson topics (knowledge checks and key facts)

Added 86 quiz questions and 28 flashcards from the lesson topics. Every quote passed scripts/verify-quotes.py. Calculation questions use new numbers with the method the quote supports.

- **Q1280** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What type of bond does sodium have?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Bonding, MS-01 p. 2
  - Quote: "Metallic bond - In this type of bond, the atoms do not share or exchange electrons to bond together."
- **Q1281** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): In which bond are electrons wholly transferred from one atom to another?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Bonding, MS-01 p. 1
  - Quote: "Ionic bond - In this type of bond, one or more electrons are wholly transferred from an atom of one element to the atom of the other, and the elements are held together by the force of attraction due to the opposite polarity of the charge."
- **Q1282** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is special about the electrons in a metallic bond?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Bonding, MS-01 p. 2
  - Quote: "Instead, many electrons (roughly one for each atom) are more or less free to move throughout the metal, so that each electron can interact with many of the fixed atoms."
- **Q1283** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What do amorphous materials lack?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Bonding, MS-01 p. 4
  - Quote: "Amorphous materials have no regular arrangement of their molecules."
- **Q1284** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What are the three most common crystal patterns in metals?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Common Lattice Types, MS-01 p. 6
  - Quote: "A crystal structure consists of atoms arranged in a pattern that repeats periodically in a three-dimensional geometric lattice."
- **Q1285** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): A unit cell has eight atoms at the corners of a cube and one atom at the center of each face. What structure is it?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Common Lattice Types, MS-01 p. 7
  - Quote: "In a face-centered cubic (FCC) arrangement of atoms, the unit cell consists of eight atoms at the corners of a cube and one atom at the center of each of the faces of the cube."
- **Q1286** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What crystal structure does zirconium have?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Common Lattice Types, MS-01 p. 8
  - Quote: "Metals containing HCP structures include beryllium, magnesium, zinc, cadmium, cobalt, thallium, and zirconium."
- **Q1287** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What crystal structure does austenite have?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Common Lattice Types, MS-01 p. 8
  - Quote: "Metals containing FCC structures include austenite, aluminum, copper, lead, silver, gold, nickel, platinum, and thorium."
- **Q1288** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is a grain boundary?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Grain Structure and Boundary, MS-01 p. 11
  - Quote: "Grain boundary is the outside area of grain that separates it from other grains."
- **Q1289** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which grain size is preferred for improved high-temperature creep properties?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Grain Structure and Boundary, MS-01 p. 9
  - Quote: "A larger grain size is preferred for improved high-temperature creep properties."
- **Q1290** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is polymorphism?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Polymorphism, MS-01 p. 14
  - Quote: "Polymorphism is the property or ability of a metal to exist in two or more crystalline forms depending upon temperature and composition."
- **Q1291** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is the temperature range of the beta phase of uranium?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Polymorphism, MS-01 p. 14
  - Quote: "Alpha phase prevents pure uranium from being used as fuel because of expansion properties."
- **Q1292** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which uranium phase prevents pure uranium from being used as fuel?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Polymorphism, MS-01 p. 14
  - Quote: "Alpha phase prevents pure uranium from being used as fuel because of expansion properties."
- **Q1293** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is an alloy?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Alloys, MS-01 p. 15
  - Quote: "An alloy is a mixture of two or more materials, at least one of which is a metal."
- **Q1294** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): How do alloys generally compare with pure metals?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Alloys, MS-01 p. 15
  - Quote: "Alloys are usually stronger than pure metals, although they generally offer reduced electrical and thermal conductivity."
- **Q1295** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What are the two desirable properties of type 304 stainless steel?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Alloys, MS-01 p. 17
  - Quote: "The two desirable properties of type 304 stainless steel are corrosion resistance and high toughness."
- **Q1296** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What are the three types of microscopic imperfections?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Imperfections in Metals, MS-01 p. 18
  - Quote: "Microscopic imperfections are generally classified as either point, line, or interfacial imperfections."
- **Q1297** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): How does slip occur in a crystal?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Imperfections in Metals, MS-01 p. 22
  - Quote: "Slip occurs when a crystal is subjected to stress and the dislocations march through the crystal until they reach the edge or are arrested by another dislocation."
- **Q1298** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What causes a vacancy defect?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Imperfections in Metals, MS-01 p. 18
  - Quote: "Vacancy defects result from a missing atom in a lattice position."
- **Q1299** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is the most common bulk defect?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Imperfections in Metals, MS-01 p. 21
  - Quote: "The most common bulk defect arises from foreign particles being included in the prime material."
- **C909** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What are the five types of bonding in materials?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Bonding, MS-01 p. 1
  - Quote: "Ionic bond - In this type of bond, one or more electrons are wholly transferred from an atom of one element to the atom of the other, and the elements are held together by the force of attraction due to the opposite polarity of the charge."
- **C910** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is a crystal structure?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Common Lattice Types, MS-01 p. 6
  - Quote: "A crystal structure consists of atoms arranged in a pattern that repeats periodically in a three-dimensional geometric lattice."
- **C911** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which common lattice type gives high strength and low ductility?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Common Lattice Types, MS-01 p. 8
  - Quote: "Metals containing BCC structures include ferrite, chromium, vanadium, molybdenum, and tungsten."
- **C912** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What are the three phases of uranium metal?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Polymorphism, MS-01 p. 14
  - Quote: "Alpha phase prevents pure uranium from being used as fuel because of expansion properties."
- **C913** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Why is pure uranium not used as a fuel?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Polymorphism, MS-01 p. 13
  - Quote: "As shown, heating and cooling of alpha phase uranium can lead to drastic dimensional changes and gross distortions of the metal."
- **C914** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What are the three possible alloy microstructures?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Alloys, MS-01 p. 15
  - Quote: "An alloy is a mixture of two or more materials, at least one of which is a metal."
- **C915** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What are the four types of bulk defects?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Imperfections in Metals, MS-01 p. 21
  - Quote: "Three-dimensional macroscopic defects are called bulk defects."
- **Q1300** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): In which stress do two parts of a material tend to slide across each other?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Stress, MS-02 p. 4
  - Quote: "Shear stress exists when two parts of a material tend to slide across each other in any typical plane of shear upon application of force parallel to that plane as illustrated in Figure 1(c)."
- **Q1301** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): How is the plane of a shear stress oriented?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Stress, MS-02 p. 4
  - Quote: "The plane of a shear stress lies in the plane of the force system from which it originates."
- **Q1302** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): A force of 1,000 lbf acts on a cross-sectional area of 2 in.². What is the stress?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Stress, MS-02 p. 6
  - Quote: "Stress is the internal resistance of a material to the distorting effects of an external force or load."
- **Q1303** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What happens to elastic strain when the stress is removed?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Strain, MS-02 p. 8
  - Quote: "Elastic strain is a transitory dimensional change that exists only while the initiating stress is applied and disappears immediately upon removal of the stress."
- **Q1304** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What are the two common forms of strain?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Strain, MS-02 p. 8
  - Quote: "Strain may take two forms; elastic strain and plastic deformation."
- **Q1305** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which iron lattice deforms more readily under load before breaking?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Strain, MS-02 p. 9
  - Quote: "A face-centered cubic crystal structure will deform more readily under load before breaking than a body-centered cubic structure."
- **Q1306** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is the proportional limit?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Strain, MS-02 p. 8
  - Quote: "The state of stress just before plastic strain begins to appear is known as the proportional limit, or elastic limit, and is defined by the stress level and the corresponding value of elastic strain."
- **Q1307** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): A carbon steel bar 100 in. long with a 1 in.² area carries a 30,000 lb load. E is 3.0 x 10⁷ psi. What is the elongation?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Young's Modulus, MS-02 p. 11
  - Quote: "The elongation of the bar is directly proportional to the tensile force and the length of the bar and inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area and the modulus of elasticity."
- **Q1308** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is Young's Modulus?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Young's Modulus, MS-02 p. 14
  - Quote: "Young's Modulus (Elastic Modulus) is the ratio of stress to strain, or the gradient of the stress-strain graph."
- **Q1309** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): If the length of a bar under a set load is doubled, what happens to its elongation?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Young's Modulus, MS-02 p. 11
  - Quote: "The elongation of the bar is directly proportional to the tensile force and the length of the bar and inversely proportional to the cross-sectional area and the modulus of elasticity."
- **Q1310** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): On a stress-strain curve, what is the highest point?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Physical Properties, MS-02 p. 21
  - Quote: "the ultimate tensile strength appears as the stress coordinate value of the highest point on the curve."
- **Q1311** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): A stress-strain curve has a large plastic region. What type of material does it show?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Stress-Strain Relationship, MS-02 p. 19
  - Quote: "Ductile material will deform (elongate) more than brittle material, shown in the figures within the text."
- **Q1312** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Between which points of the stress-strain curve does Hooke's Law apply?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Stress-Strain Relationship, MS-02 p. 19
  - Quote: "Hooke's Law applies between Points 1 and 2."
- **Q1313** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which part of the stress-strain curve is the plastic region?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Stress-Strain Relationship, MS-02 p. 19
  - Quote: "Plastic region is between Points 2 and 5."
- **Q1314** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is the fracture point?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Stress-Strain Relationship, MS-02 p. 16
  - Quote: "Fracture point is the point where the material fractures due to plastic deformation."
- **Q1315** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): How does an increase in slip affect a metal?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Physical Properties, MS-02 p. 28
  - Quote: "An increase in slip will decrease the strength of a material."
- **Q1316** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Why does decreasing grain size increase the strength of a metal?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Physical Properties, MS-02 p. 21
  - Quote: "Decreasing the grain size through cold or hot working of the metal tends to retard slip and thus increases the strength of the metal."
- **Q1317** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is strength?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Physical Properties, MS-02 p. 20
  - Quote: "Strength is the ability of a material to resist deformation."
- **Q1318** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): For which reactor plant applications is high ductility desirable?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Physical Properties, MS-02 p. 28
  - Quote: "Ductility is desirable in high temperature and high pressure applications."
- **Q1319** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What effect does an increase in temperature have on ductility?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Physical Properties, MS-02 p. 25
  - Quote: "An increase in temperature will increase ductility."
- **Q1320** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which property describes how a material reacts under sudden impacts?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Physical Properties, MS-02 p. 28
  - Quote: "Toughness describes how a material reacts under sudden impacts."
- **Q1321** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What does hardness enable a material to resist?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Physical Properties, MS-02 p. 28
  - Quote: "Hardness is the property of a material that enables it to resist plastic deformation, penetration, indentation, and scratching."
- **Q1322** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is malleability?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Physical Properties, MS-02 p. 28
  - Quote: "Malleability is the ability of a metal to exhibit large deformation or plastic response when being subjected to compressive force."
- **Q1323** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What happens to grain size as a metal is cooled faster?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Working of Metals, MS-02 p. 29
  - Quote: "Generally, the faster a metal is cooled, the smaller the grain sizes will be."
- **Q1324** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What types of stress does welding leave in stainless steel?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Working of Metals, MS-02 p. 30
  - Quote: "This elongation of the material causes residual compressive and tensile stresses in the material."
- **Q1325** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Why is galvanic corrosion a concern in material selection?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Corrosion, MS-02 p. 33
  - Quote: "Material selection is important because different metals come into contact with each other and may form galvanic cells."
- **Q1326** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What two conditions are required for hydrogen embrittlement in steel?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Hydrogen Embrittlement, MS-02 p. 39
  - Quote: "The conditions required for hydrogen embrittlement in steel is the presence of hydrogen dissolved in the water and the carbon in the steel."
- **Q1327** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Is hydrogen embrittlement of steel a permanent condition?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Hydrogen Embrittlement, MS-02 p. 38
  - Quote: "Hydrogen embrittlement is not a permanent condition."
- **Q1328** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Why is zircaloy-4 less susceptible to hydrogen embrittlement than zircaloy-2?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Hydrogen Embrittlement, MS-02 p. 39
  - Quote: "Zircaloy-4 is less susceptible to hydrogen embrittlement than zircaloy-2 because:"
- **C916** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is the formula for stress?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Stress, MS-02 p. 6
  - Quote: "Stress is the internal resistance of a material to the distorting effects of an external force or load."
- **C917** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What are the six categories of stress?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Stress, MS-02 p. 2
  - Quote: "There are many types of stresses, but they can all be generally classified in one of six categories: residual stresses, structural stresses, pressure stresses, flow stresses, thermal stresses, and fatigue stresses."
- **C918** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is elastic strain?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Strain, MS-02 p. 8
  - Quote: "Elastic strain is a transitory dimensional change that exists only while the initiating stress is applied and disappears immediately upon removal of the stress."
- **C919** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is Young's Modulus?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Young's Modulus, MS-02 p. 14
  - Quote: "Young's Modulus (Elastic Modulus) is the ratio of stress to strain, or the gradient of the stress-strain graph."
- **C920** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is ductility?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Physical Properties, MS-02 p. 28
  - Quote: "Ductility is the ability of a material to deform easily upon the application of a tensile force, or the ability of a material to withstand plastic deformation without rupture."
- **C921** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is toughness?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Physical Properties, MS-02 p. 28
  - Quote: "It is defined as the work required to deform one cubic inch of metal until it fractures."
- **C922** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is hydrogen embrittlement of steel?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1017/1-93), Hydrogen Embrittlement, MS-02 p. 37
  - Quote: "Hydrogen embrittlement is the process by which steel loses its ductility and strength due to tiny cracks that result from the internal pressure of hydrogen (H2) or methane gas (CH4), which forms at the grain boundaries."
- **Q1329** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What two stresses result from thermal shock?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Thermal Stress, MS-03 p. 1
  - Quote: "Thermal shock (stress) can lead to excessive thermal gradients on materials, which lead to excessive stresses."
- **Q1330** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What are the two causes of thermal shock?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Thermal Stress, MS-03 p. 1
  - Quote: "Thermal shock is caused by nonuniform heating or cooling of a uniform material, or uniform heating of nonuniform materials."
- **Q1331** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): A carbon steel bar constrained at both ends is heated 100°F. E is 3.0 x 10⁷ psi and α is 5.8 x 10⁻⁶ per °F. What is the thermal stress?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Thermal Stress, MS-03 p. 3
  - Quote: "In the simple case where two ends of a material are strictly constrained, the thermal stress can be calculated using Hooke's Law"
- **Q1332** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which equation gives the thermal stress in a material constrained at both ends?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Thermal Stress, MS-03 p. 3
  - Quote: "In the simple case where two ends of a material are strictly constrained, the thermal stress can be calculated using Hooke's Law"
- **Q1333** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): When the inside wall of a thick vessel is cooled faster than the outside, which side is in tensile stress?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Thermal Stress, MS-03 p. 4
  - Quote: "This sets up a thermal stress, placing the cold side in tensile stress and the hot side in compressive stress, which can cause cracks in the cold side of the wall."
- **Q1334** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which is an operational limit intended to reduce the severity of thermal shock?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Thermal Stress, MS-03 p. 4
  - Quote: "Operating procedures are designed to reduce both the magnitude and the frequency of these stresses."
- **Q1335** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is pressurized thermal shock?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Pressurized Thermal Shock, MS-03 p. 6
  - Quote: "PTS is the shock experienced by a thick-walled vessel due to the combined stresses from a rapid temperature and/or pressure change."
- **Q1336** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What type of stress does system pressure produce on the inside vessel wall?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Pressurized Thermal Shock, MS-03 p. 7
  - Quote: "Stresses arising from coolant system pressure exerted against the inside vessel wall (where neutron fluence is greatest) are always tensile in nature."
- **Q1337** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which is one of the four plant transients with the greatest potential to cause thermal shock?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Pressurized Thermal Shock, MS-03 p. 8
  - Quote: "Plant transients with greatest potential to cause PTS include:"
- **C923** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What are the two causes of thermal shock?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Thermal Stress, MS-03 p. 1
  - Quote: "Thermal shock is caused by nonuniform heating or cooling of a uniform material, or uniform heating of nonuniform materials."
- **C924** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is the equation for thermal stress in a constrained material?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Thermal Stress, MS-03 p. 3
  - Quote: "In the simple case where two ends of a material are strictly constrained, the thermal stress can be calculated using Hooke's Law"
- **C925** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): When is a vessel usually considered thick-walled?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Thermal Stress, MS-03 p. 4
  - Quote: "If the thickness of the vessel wall is more than 5 percent to 10 percent of the vessel's radius, it is considered a thick-walled vessel."
- **C926** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What plant transients have the greatest potential to cause thermal shock?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Pressurized Thermal Shock, MS-03 p. 8
  - Quote: "Plant transients with greatest potential to cause PTS include:"
- **Q1338** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Why is ductile fracture better than brittle fracture?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Brittle Fracture Mechanism, MS-04 p. 1
  - Quote: "Ductile fracture is better than brittle fracture, because ductile fracture occurs over a period of time, where as brittle fracture is fast, and can occur (with flaws) at lower stress levels than a ductile fracture."
- **Q1339** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is brittle fracture?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Brittle Fracture Mechanism, MS-04 p. 6
  - Quote: "Brittle fracture is exhibited when metals fracture with a relatively small or negligible amount of plastic strain."
- **Q1340** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What two changes are made to reactor pressure vessels to decrease NDT?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Brittle Fracture Mechanism, MS-04 p. 2
  - Quote: "The NDT temperature can also be lowered by small additions of selected alloying elements such as nickel and manganese to low-carbon steels."
- **Q1341** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What happens to the NDT temperature of a reactor vessel during operation?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Brittle Fracture Mechanism, MS-04 p. 2
  - Quote: "Consequently, during operation the reactor vessel is subjected to an increasing fluence (flux) of fast neutrons, and as a result the NDT temperature increases steadily."
- **Q1342** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which is one of the three conditions necessary for brittle fracture?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Brittle Fracture Mechanism, MS-04 p. 3
  - Quote: "One of the biggest concerns with brittle fracture is that it can occur at stresses well below the yield strength (stress corresponding to the transition from elastic to plastic behavior) of the material, provided certain conditions are present."
- **Q1343** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): On a stress-temperature diagram, where is the NDT temperature with no flaw?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Brittle Fracture Mechanism, MS-04 p. 3
  - Quote: "The temperature at which the yield and tensile strength coincide is the NDT temperature."
- **Q1344** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which conditions tend to mitigate crack initiation?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Brittle Fracture Mechanism, MS-04 p. 4
  - Quote: "It should be noted that smaller grain size, higher temperature, and lower stress tend to mitigate crack initiation."
- **Q1345** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which is one of the five factors that determine fracture toughness?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Brittle Fracture Mechanism, MS-04 p. 4
  - Quote: "Fracture toughness is an indication of the amount of stress required to propagate a preexisting flaw."
- **Q1346** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is fracture toughness?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Brittle Fracture Mechanism, MS-04 p. 4
  - Quote: "Fracture toughness is an indication of the amount of stress required to propagate a preexisting flaw."
- **Q1347** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Where is the fracture transition elastic (FTE) point on a stress-temperature diagram?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Brittle Fracture Mechanism, MS-04 p. 4
  - Quote: "The intersection of the crack arrest curve with the yield curve (Curve B) is called the fracture transition elastic (FTE) point."
- **Q1348** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): About how far above NDT is the fracture transition plastic (FTP) temperature?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Brittle Fracture Mechanism, MS-04 p. 4
  - Quote: "The temperature corresponding with this point is normally about 120°F above the NDT temperature."
- **Q1349** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What are minimum pressurization-temperature curves based on?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Minimum Pressurization-Temperature Curves, MS-04 p. 7
  - Quote: "They are based on reactor vessel and head stress limitations and the need to preclude reactor vessel and head brittle fracture."
- **Q1350** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Where is the safe operating region on an MPT curve?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Minimum Pressurization-Temperature Curves, MS-04 p. 7
  - Quote: "Note that the safe operating region is to the right of the reactor vessel MPT curve."
- **Q1351** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is the precaution for hydrostatic testing?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Minimum Pressurization-Temperature Curves, MS-04 p. 10
  - Quote: "The precaution to be observed when performing a hydrostatic test is to make sure the pressure is consistent with plant temperatures."
- **Q1352** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which components set the limits on heatup and cooldown rates?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Heatup and Cooldown Rate Limits, MS-04 p. 13
  - Quote: "Large components such as flanges, reactor vessel head, and the vessel itself are the limiting components."
- **Q1353** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is typically required when a heatup or cooldown rate limit is exceeded?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Heatup and Cooldown Rate Limits, MS-04 p. 13
  - Quote: "Usually exceeding the heatup or cooldown rate limits requires only an assessment of the impact on the future fatigue life of the plant."
- **Q1354** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Why are soak times used?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Heatup and Cooldown Rate Limits, MS-04 p. 12
  - Quote: "Soak times are used so that heating can be carefully controlled."
- **Q1355** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): When do soak times become very significant?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Heatup and Cooldown Rate Limits, MS-04 p. 13
  - Quote: "Become very significant if system is at room temperature or below and very close to RTNDT temperature limitations"
- **C927** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is ductile fracture?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Brittle Fracture Mechanism, MS-04 p. 6
  - Quote: "Ductile fracture is exhibited when metals can sustain substantial plastic strain or deformation before fracturing."
- **C928** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What three conditions tend to mitigate crack initiation?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Brittle Fracture Mechanism, MS-04 p. 4
  - Quote: "It should be noted that smaller grain size, higher temperature, and lower stress tend to mitigate crack initiation."
- **C929** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What five factors determine the fracture toughness of a metal?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Brittle Fracture Mechanism, MS-04 p. 4
  - Quote: "Fracture toughness is an indication of the amount of stress required to propagate a preexisting flaw."
- **C930** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): How far above NDT are the FTE and FTP temperatures?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Brittle Fracture Mechanism, MS-04 p. 4
  - Quote: "The temperature corresponding with this point is normally about 120°F above the NDT temperature."
- **C931** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Where is the safe operating region on an MPT curve?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Minimum Pressurization-Temperature Curves, MS-04 p. 7
  - Quote: "Note that the safe operating region is to the right of the reactor vessel MPT curve."
- **C932** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Why are soak times used?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Heatup and Cooldown Rate Limits, MS-04 p. 12
  - Quote: "Soak times are used so that heating can be carefully controlled."
- **Q1356** (Valves): What is the purpose of construction drawings?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Fabrication, Construction, and Architectural Drawings, PR-06 p. 12
  - Quote: "The purpose of construction drawings is to provide the information necessary to build and assemble structures and systems."
- **Q1357** (Valves): Which drawing shows how the designer wants a building to appear and function?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Fabrication, Construction, and Architectural Drawings, PR-06 p. 3
  - Quote: "These drawings do not provide detailed information on how the structure or building is to be built, but rather they provide information on how the designer wants the building to appear and how it will function."
- **Q1358** (Valves): What is the main difference between a fabrication drawing and a construction drawing?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Fabrication, Construction, and Architectural Drawings, PR-06 p. 1
  - Quote: "A fabrication drawing provides information on how a single part is machined or fabricated in a machine shop, whereas a construction drawing provides the construction or assembly of large multi-component structures or systems."
- **Q1359** (Valves): Why is stating the actual dimensions on a drawing preferred over measuring a scale drawing?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Fabrication, Construction, and Architectural Drawings, PR-06 p. 5
  - Quote: "The second method is the preferred method because it reduces the chances of error and allows greater accuracy and drawing flexibility."
- **Q1360** (Valves): On a dimensioned drawing, what does a dashed line show?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Fabrication, Construction, and Architectural Drawings, PR-06 p. 6
  - Quote: "When actual dimensions are specified on a print, the basic line symbols that are illustrated by Figure 4 are used."
- **Q1361** (Valves): A dimension reads 2.50 ± 0.02. What is the maximum dimension?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Fabrication, Construction, and Architectural Drawing, Examples, PR-06 p. 16
  - Quote: "4.15 inches. The nominal length of 4.1 plus the tolerance of 0.05."
- **Q1362** (Valves): A dimension reads 2.50 ± 0.02. What is the minimum dimension?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Fabrication, Construction, and Architectural Drawing, Examples, PR-06 p. 16
  - Quote: "4.05 inches. The nominal length of 4.1 minus the tolerance of 0.05."
- **Q1363** (Valves): Where can a global tolerance for all measurements on a drawing be stated?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Fabrication, Construction, and Architectural Drawings, PR-06 p. 8
  - Quote: "Another method of expressing tolerances on a drawing is to state in the title block, or in a note, a global tolerance for all measurements on the drawing."
- **Q1364** (Valves): What do geometric tolerances state?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Fabrication, Construction, and Architectural Drawings, PR-06 p. 8
  - Quote: "Geometric tolerances state the maximum allowable variation of a form or its position from the perfect geometry implied on the drawing."
- **Q1365** (Valves): What is the preferred way to prevent step tolerances from adding up past the overall tolerance?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Fabrication, Construction, and Architectural Drawings, PR-06 p. 11
  - Quote: "This allows the unspecified, and therefor non- toleranced, dimension to absorb the errors in the critical dimensions."
- **C933** (Valves): What are the two ways dimensions can be expressed on a drawing?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Fabrication, Construction, and Architectural Drawings, PR-06 p. 5
  - Quote: "Dimensions on a drawing can be expressed in one of two ways."
- **C934** (Valves): What are the three methods of stating a tolerance on a drawing?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Fabrication, Construction, and Architectural Drawings, PR-06 p. 8
  - Quote: "Another method of expressing tolerances on a drawing is to state in the title block, or in a note, a global tolerance for all measurements on the drawing."
- **C935** (Valves): What are geometric tolerances?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Fabrication, Construction, and Architectural Drawings, PR-06 p. 8
  - Quote: "Geometric tolerances state the maximum allowable variation of a form or its position from the perfect geometry implied on the drawing."
- **C936** (Valves): Why is one dimension often left off a toleranced drawing?
  - Source: DOE-1016-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1016/2-93), Engineering Fabrication, Construction, and Architectural Drawings, PR-06 p. 11
  - Quote: "This allows the unspecified, and therefor non- toleranced, dimension to absorb the errors in the critical dimensions."

## 2026-11-05: Lesson topics (knowledge checks and key facts)

Added 142 quiz questions and 36 flashcards from the lesson topics. Every quote passed scripts/verify-quotes.py. Calculation questions use new numbers with the method the quote supports.

- **Q1366** (Motors and Generators): Why is a diesel engine not self-speed-limiting?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engines, ME-01 p. 3
  - Quote: "Diesel engines are not self-speed-limiting because the air (oxygen) entering the engine is always the maximum amount."
- **Q1367** (Motors and Generators): Why is a diesel heavier than a gasoline engine of equal horsepower?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engines, ME-01 p. 2
  - Quote: "Although a diesel engine and gasoline engine operate with similar components, a diesel engine, when compared to a gasoline engine of equal horsepower, is heavier due to stronger, heavier materials used to withstand the greater dynamic forces from the higher combustion pressures present in the diesel engine."
- **Q1368** (Motors and Generators): What is the bore of a diesel engine?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engines, ME-01 p. 17
  - Quote: "As previously stated, bore refers to the diameter of the engine's cylinder, and stroke refers to the distance the piston travels from the top of the cylinder to the bottom."
- **Q1369** (Motors and Generators): What is the stroke of a diesel engine?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engines, ME-01 p. 17
  - Quote: "As previously stated, bore refers to the diameter of the engine's cylinder, and stroke refers to the distance the piston travels from the top of the cylinder to the bottom."
- **Q1370** (Motors and Generators): An engine has a displacement volume of 150 in³ per cylinder and a clearance volume of 10 in³. What is its compression ratio?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engines, ME-01 p. 18
  - Quote: "Clearance volume is the volume remaining in the cylinder when the piston is at TDC."
- **Q1371** (Motors and Generators): Why can a diesel use a higher compression ratio than a gasoline engine?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engines, ME-01 p. 3
  - Quote: "The higher compression ratios are possible because only air is compressed, and then the fuel is injected."
- **Q1372** (Motors and Generators): Which part transforms the linear motion of the pistons into rotation?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engines, ME-01 p. 8
  - Quote: "The crankshaft transforms the linear motion of the pistons into a rotational motion that"
- **Q1373** (Motors and Generators): What is the function of the blower?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engines, ME-01 p. 12
  - Quote: "The diesel engine's blower is part of the air intake system and serves to compress the incoming fresh air for delivery to the cylinders for combustion."
- **Q1374** (Motors and Generators): What is valve lash?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engines, ME-01 p. 11
  - Quote: "Valve lash is the term given to the "slop" or "give" in the valve train before the cam actually starts to open the valve."
- **Q1375** (Motors and Generators): What do piston rings do?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engines, ME-01 p. 8
  - Quote: "These rings function as the seal between the piston and the cylinder wall and also act to reduce friction by minimizing the contact area between the piston and the cylinder wall."
- **Q1376** (Motors and Generators): What five supporting systems does a diesel engine require?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engines, ME-01 p. 12
  - Quote: "A diesel engine requires five supporting systems in order to operate: cooling, lubrication, fuel injection, air intake, and exhaust."
- **Q1377** (Motors and Generators): Why is diesel fuel kept flowing at a rate much higher than the engine burns?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engines, ME-01 p. 14
  - Quote: "Because diesel engines rely on injectors which are precision components with extremely tight tolerances and very small injection hole(s), the fuel delivered to the engine must be extremely clean and free of contaminants."
- **Q1378** (Motors and Generators): What is the difference between turbocharging and supercharging?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engines, ME-01 p. 16
  - Quote: "Turbocharging an engine occurs when the engine's own exhaust gasses are forced through a turbine (impeller), which rotates and is connected to a second impeller located in the fresh air intake system."
- **Q1379** (Motors and Generators): Why should engine intake air be as cool as possible?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engines, ME-01 p. 15
  - Quote: "The reason for ensuring that an engine's air supply is as cool as possible is that cool air is more dense than hot air."
- **Q1380** (Motors and Generators): How does the heat of combustion produce mechanical energy in a diesel?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Fundamentals of the Diesel Cycle, ME-01 p. 21
  - Quote: "First, the fuel reacts chemically (burns) and releases energy in the form of heat. Second the heat causes the gasses trapped in the cylinder to expand, and the expanding gases, being confined by the cylinder, must move the piston to expand."
- **Q1381** (Motors and Generators): What ignites the fuel in a diesel engine?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Fundamentals of the Diesel Cycle, ME-01 p. 28
  - Quote: "Ignition occurs in a diesel by injecting fuel into the air charge which has been heated by compression to a temperature greater than the ignition point of the fuel."
- **Q1382** (Motors and Generators): How many crankshaft rotations does one four-stroke cycle take?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Fundamentals of the Diesel Cycle, ME-01 p. 22
  - Quote: "the engine requires four strokes of the piston (intake, compression, power, and exhaust) to complete one full cycle."
- **Q1383** (Motors and Generators): At what speed does the camshaft of a four-stroke engine rotate?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Fundamentals of the Diesel Cycle, ME-01 p. 22
  - Quote: "In a four-stroke engine the camshaft is geared so that it rotates at half the speed of the crankshaft (1:2)."
- **Q1384** (Motors and Generators): What is valve overlap, and why is it needed?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Fundamentals of the Diesel Cycle, ME-01 p. 23
  - Quote: "The time frame during which both the intake and exhaust valves are open is called valve overlap (51° of overlap in this example) and is necessary to allow the fresh air to help scavenge (remove) the spent exhaust gasses and cool the cylinder."
- **Q1385** (Motors and Generators): When will injected diesel fuel burn?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Fundamentals of the Diesel Cycle, ME-01 p. 24
  - Quote: "The fuel enters the cylinder where the heated compressed air is present; however, it will only burn when it is in a vaporized state (attained through the addition of heat to cause vaporization) and intimately mixed with a supply of oxygen."
- **Q1386** (Motors and Generators): How many crankshaft rotations does one two-stroke cycle take?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Fundamentals of the Diesel Cycle, ME-01 p. 25
  - Quote: "But a two-stroke engine requires only two strokes of the piston to complete one full cycle."
- **Q1387** (Motors and Generators): In the handbook's two-stroke example, what lets fresh air into the cylinder?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Fundamentals of the Diesel Cycle, ME-01 p. 25
  - Quote: "But a two-stroke engine requires only two strokes of the piston to complete one full cycle."
- **Q1388** (Motors and Generators): At what speed does the camshaft of a two-stroke engine rotate?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Fundamentals of the Diesel Cycle, ME-01 p. 25
  - Quote: "In a two-stroke engine the camshaft is geared so that it rotates at the same speed as the crankshaft (1:1)."
- **Q1389** (Motors and Generators): What sets the amount of fuel each injector delivers?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engine Speed, Fuel Controls, and Protection, ME-01 p. 30
  - Quote: "The amount of fuel to be injected by each injector is set by a mechanical linkage called the fuel rack."
- **Q1390** (Motors and Generators): What happens in the governor when engine load increases?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engine Speed, Fuel Controls, and Protection, ME-01 p. 37
  - Quote: "The reduction in engine speed will be sensed by the governor flyweights."
- **Q1391** (Motors and Generators): What does a loss of lube oil pressure do to an engine with this type of governor?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engine Speed, Fuel Controls, and Protection, ME-01 p. 34
  - Quote: "This means that a loss of lube oil pressure will cut off the supply of oil to the governor and cause the governor to shut down the engine."
- **Q1392** (Motors and Generators): Which is one of the five usual protective alarms on mid-sized and larger diesel engines?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engine Speed, Fuel Controls, and Protection, ME-01 p. 40
  - Quote: "The high pressure condition indicates the engine is in poor condition."
- **Q1393** (Motors and Generators): What does high crankcase pressure indicate?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engine Speed, Fuel Controls, and Protection, ME-01 p. 40
  - Quote: "The high pressure condition indicates the engine is in poor condition."
- **Q1394** (Motors and Generators): What can high exhaust temperature indicate?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engine Speed, Fuel Controls, and Protection, ME-01 p. 39
  - Quote: "High exhaust temperature can indicate an overloading of the engine or possible poor performance due to inadequate scavenging (the cooling effect) in the engine."
- **C937** (Motors and Generators): What is the compression ratio formula for a diesel engine?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engines, ME-01 p. 18
  - Quote: "Clearance volume is the volume remaining in the cylinder when the piston is at TDC."
- **C938** (Motors and Generators): What are the bore and stroke of an engine?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engines, ME-01 p. 17
  - Quote: "As previously stated, bore refers to the diameter of the engine's cylinder, and stroke refers to the distance the piston travels from the top of the cylinder to the bottom."
- **C939** (Motors and Generators): What five supporting systems does a diesel engine require?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engines, ME-01 p. 12
  - Quote: "A diesel engine requires five supporting systems in order to operate: cooling, lubrication, fuel injection, air intake, and exhaust."
- **C940** (Motors and Generators): How many crankshaft rotations does a two-stroke diesel take per cycle?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Fundamentals of the Diesel Cycle, ME-01 p. 25
  - Quote: "But a two-stroke engine requires only two strokes of the piston to complete one full cycle."
- **C941** (Motors and Generators): What is valve overlap in a diesel engine?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Fundamentals of the Diesel Cycle, ME-01 p. 23
  - Quote: "The time frame during which both the intake and exhaust valves are open is called valve overlap (51° of overlap in this example) and is necessary to allow the fresh air to help scavenge (remove) the spent exhaust gasses and cool the cylinder."
- **C942** (Motors and Generators): Why does a diesel engine need a governor?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engines, ME-01 p. 3
  - Quote: "Diesel engines are not self-speed-limiting because the air (oxygen) entering the engine is always the maximum amount."
- **C943** (Controllers and Positioners): What happens to a mechanical-hydraulic governor on loss of lube oil pressure?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Diesel Engine Speed, Fuel Controls, and Protection, ME-01 p. 34
  - Quote: "This means that a loss of lube oil pressure will cut off the supply of oil to the governor and cause the governor to shut down the engine."
- **Q1395** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): How does heat get from one fluid to the other in a heat exchanger?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Types of Heat Exchangers, ME-02 p. 2
  - Quote: "In a heat exchanger there is no direct contact between the two fluids."
- **Q1396** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): What are the two types of heat exchanger construction?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Types of Heat Exchangers, ME-02 p. 2
  - Quote: "Although heat exchangers come in every shape and size imaginable, the construction of most heat exchangers fall into one of two categories: tube and shell, or plate."
- **Q1397** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): What separates the tube side fluid from the shell side fluid at the ends of the tubes?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Types of Heat Exchangers, ME-02 p. 2
  - Quote: "At the ends of the tubes, the tube side fluid is separated from the shell side fluid by the tube sheet(s)."
- **Q1398** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): What do baffles do in a tube and shell heat exchanger?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Types of Heat Exchangers, ME-02 p. 2
  - Quote: "The support plates shown on Figure 1 also act as baffles to direct the flow of fluid within the shell back and forth across the tubes."
- **Q1399** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): In a parallel flow heat exchanger, how do the two fluids flow?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Types of Heat Exchangers, ME-02 p. 4
  - Quote: "Note that the hottest cold-fluid temperature is always less than the coldest hot-fluid temperature."
- **Q1400** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): In which arrangement can the hottest cold-fluid temperature exceed the coldest hot-fluid temperature?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Types of Heat Exchangers, ME-02 p. 5
  - Quote: "Counter flow heat exchangers are the most efficient of the three types."
- **Q1401** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): Where are cross flow heat exchangers usually found?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Types of Heat Exchangers, ME-02 p. 6
  - Quote: "Cross flow heat exchangers are usually found in applications where one of the fluids changes state (2-phase flow)."
- **Q1402** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): What makes a heat exchanger multi-pass?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Types of Heat Exchangers, ME-02 p. 8
  - Quote: "When a heat exchanger's fluids pass each other more than once, a heat exchanger is called a multi-pass heat exchanger."
- **Q1403** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): What defines a regenerative heat exchanger?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Types of Heat Exchangers, ME-02 p. 9
  - Quote: "A regenerative heat exchanger is one in which the same fluid is both the cooling fluid and the cooled fluid, as illustrated in Figure 7."
- **Q1404** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): What does the term non-regenerative tell you about a heat exchanger?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Types of Heat Exchangers, ME-02 p. 9
  - Quote: "It is important to remember that the term regenerative/nonregenerative only refers to "how" a heat exchanger functions in a system, and does not indicate any single type (tube and shell, plate, parallel flow, counter flow, etc.)."
- **Q1405** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): Which is a common application of a heat exchanger?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Heat Exchanger Applications, ME-02 p. 12
  - Quote: "Some of the more common applications are found in heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) systems, radiators on internal combustion engines, boilers, condensers, and as preheaters or coolers in fluid systems."
- **Q1406** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): Why do radiators have fins on their tubes?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Heat Exchanger Applications, ME-02 p. 14
  - Quote: "The fins improve the efficiency of a heat exchanger"
- **Q1407** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): Why is an input fluid preheated in stages?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Heat Exchanger Applications, ME-02 p. 12
  - Quote: "Preheating in stages increases the plant's efficiency and minimizes thermal shock stress to components, as compared to injecting ambient temperature liquid into a boiler or other device that operates at high temperatures."
- **Q1408** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): What is the purpose of a steam condenser?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Heat Exchanger Applications, ME-02 p. 14
  - Quote: "It is a closed space into which the steam exits the turbine and is forced to give up its latent heat of vaporization."
- **Q1409** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): What is the hotwell?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Heat Exchanger Applications, ME-02 p. 15
  - Quote: "The bottom area of the condenser is the hotwell, as shown in Figure 9."
- **Q1410** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): What is condensate depression?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Heat Exchanger Applications, ME-02 p. 14
  - Quote: "The difference between the saturation temperature for the existing condenser vacuum and the temperature of the condensate is termed condensate depression."
- **Q1411** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): Why are condensers in large steam cycles operated at a vacuum?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Heat Exchanger Applications, ME-02 p. 18
  - Quote: "Condensers operate at a vacuum to ensure the temperature (and thus the pressure) of the steam is as low as possible."
- **Q1412** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): When securing a heat exchanger, which fluid is stopped first?
  - Source: LP-HEAT-EXCHANGERS (Heat Exchangers.docx), slide 1.25 Heat Exchanger Startup & Operation
  - Quote: "When securing a heat exchanger, first stop the hot fluid by shutting the discharge valve."
- **C944** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): What are the two types of heat exchanger construction?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Types of Heat Exchangers, ME-02 p. 2
  - Quote: "Although heat exchangers come in every shape and size imaginable, the construction of most heat exchangers fall into one of two categories: tube and shell, or plate."
- **C945** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): What are the four internal parts of a tube and shell heat exchanger named in DOE-HDBK-1018?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Types of Heat Exchangers, ME-02 p. 2
  - Quote: "At the ends of the tubes, the tube side fluid is separated from the shell side fluid by the tube sheet(s)."
- **C946** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): What is cross flow in a heat exchanger?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Types of Heat Exchangers, ME-02 p. 6
  - Quote: "Cross flow, as illustrated in Figure 5, exists when one fluid flows perpendicular to the second fluid; that is, one fluid flows through tubes and the second fluid passes around the tubes at 90° angle."
- **C947** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): What is a hotwell?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Heat Exchanger Applications, ME-02 p. 15
  - Quote: "The bottom area of the condenser is the hotwell, as shown in Figure 9."
- **C948** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): What is condensate depression?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Heat Exchanger Applications, ME-02 p. 14
  - Quote: "The difference between the saturation temperature for the existing condenser vacuum and the temperature of the condensate is termed condensate depression."
- **C949** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): Why do large steam condensers run at a vacuum?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Heat Exchanger Applications, ME-02 p. 18
  - Quote: "Condensers operate at a vacuum to ensure the temperature (and thus the pressure) of the steam is as low as possible."
- **Q1413** (Pumps): What is the purpose of the impeller?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pumps, ME-03 p. 1
  - Quote: "The vanes of the rotating impeller impart a radial and rotary motion to the liquid, forcing it to the outer periphery of the pump casing where it is collected in the outer part of the pump casing called the volute."
- **Q1414** (Pumps): What is the purpose of a diffuser in a centrifugal pump?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pumps, ME-03 p. 3
  - Quote: "A diffuser is a set of stationary vanes that surround the impeller."
- **Q1415** (Pumps): In which pump does the impeller push liquid parallel to the shaft?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pumps, ME-03 p. 5
  - Quote: "In an axial flow pump, the impeller pushes the liquid in a direction parallel to the pump shaft."
- **Q1416** (Pumps): What is a pump stage?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pumps, ME-03 p. 6
  - Quote: "A pump stage is defined as that portion of a centrifugal pump consisting of one impeller and its associated components."
- **Q1417** (Pumps): What is the purpose of wearing rings?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pumps, ME-03 p. 8
