  - Quote: "Wearing rings are replaceable rings that are attached to the impeller and/or the pump casing to allow a small running clearance between the impeller and the pump casing without causing wear of the actual impeller or pump casing material."
- **Q1418** (Pumps): What is the purpose of packing?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pumps, ME-03 p. 9
  - Quote: "Packing is material in the form of rings or strands that is placed in the stuffing box to form a seal to control the rate of leakage along the shaft."
- **Q1419** (Pumps): Why is a small amount of leakage allowed along a packed shaft?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pumps, ME-03 p. 9
  - Quote: "Stuffing boxes are normally designed to allow a small amount of controlled leakage along the shaft to provide lubrication and cooling to the packing."
- **Q1420** (Pumps): What does a lantern ring do?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pumps, ME-03 p. 9
  - Quote: "A lantern ring is a perforated hollow ring located near the center of the packing box that receives relatively cool, clean liquid from either the discharge of the pump or from an external source and distributes the liquid uniformly around the shaft to provide lubrication and cooling."
- **Q1421** (Pumps): What relationship must exist to avoid cavitation?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pump Operation, ME-03 p. 13
  - Quote: "The condition that must exist to avoid cavitation is that the net positive suction head available must be greater than or equal to the net positive suction head required."
- **Q1422** (Pumps): A pump takes suction from a tank. Pa = 30 ft, Pst = 12 ft, hf = 4 ft, and Psat = 2 ft. What is NPSHA?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pump Operation, ME-03 p. 13
  - Quote: "The condition that must exist to avoid cavitation is that the net positive suction head available must be greater than or equal to the net positive suction head required."
- **Q1423** (Pumps): Which set lists the three indications of a cavitating pump?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pump Operation, ME-03 p. 12
  - Quote: "Other indications that can be observed from a remote operating station are fluctuating discharge pressure, flow rate, and pump motor current."
- **Q1424** (Pumps): Why does throttling a pump's discharge valve help stop cavitation?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pump Operation, ME-03 p. 14
  - Quote: "Therefore, reducing the flow rate through a pump by throttling a discharge valve decreases NPSHR."
- **Q1425** (Pumps): What physical damage does cavitation do to an impeller?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pump Operation, ME-03 p. 12
  - Quote: "This physical shock creates small pits on the leading edge of the impeller vane."
- **Q1426** (Pumps): Why are most centrifugal pumps located below the level of their suction source?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pump Operation, ME-03 p. 15
  - Quote: "Most centrifugal pumps are not self-priming."
- **Q1427** (Pumps): What is the shape of a centrifugal pump characteristic curve?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pump Operation, ME-03 p. 14
  - Quote: "The lower the pump head, the higher the flow rate."
- **Q1428** (Pumps): What is pump runout?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pump Operation, ME-03 p. 14
  - Quote: "Pump runout is the maximum flow that can be developed by a centrifugal pump without damaging the pump."
- **Q1429** (Pumps): How is a centrifugal pump protected from dead-heading?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pump Operation, ME-03 p. 15
  - Quote: "One method for protecting the pump from running dead-headed is to provide a recirculation line from the pump discharge line upstream of the discharge valve, back to the pump's supply source."
- **Q1430** (Pumps): How is a centrifugal pump protected from runout?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pump Operation, ME-03 p. 15
  - Quote: "One method for ensuring that there is always adequate flow resistance at the pump discharge to prevent excessive flow through the pump is to place an orifice or a throttle valve immediately downstream of the pump discharge."
- **Q1431** (Pumps): How does the flow of a positive displacement pump differ from a centrifugal pump?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Positive Displacement Pumps, ME-03 p. 18
  - Quote: "A positive displacement pump is one in which a definite volume of liquid is delivered for each cycle of pump operation."
- **Q1432** (Pumps): A pump has two meshing spur gears revolving in opposite directions in a casing. What type is it?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Positive Displacement Pumps, ME-03 p. 22
  - Quote: "The simple gear pump shown in Figure 14 consists of two spur gears meshing together and revolving in opposite directions within a casing."
- **Q1433** (Pumps): A rotor carries vanes that move in and out to keep sealed spaces against the cylinder wall. What type of pump is it?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Positive Displacement Pumps, ME-03 p. 26
  - Quote: "The rotor carries vanes that move in and out as it rotates to maintain sealed spaces between the rotor and the cylinder wall."
- **Q1434** (Pumps): What is the main benefit of a diaphragm pump?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Positive Displacement Pumps, ME-03 p. 26
  - Quote: "The pump construction eliminates any contact between the liquid being pumped and the source of energy."
- **Q1435** (Pumps): What is slippage in a positive displacement pump?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Positive Displacement Pumps, ME-03 p. 22
  - Quote: "Slippage is leakage of fluid from the discharge of the pump back to its suction."
- **C950** (Pumps): What is the purpose of wearing rings in a centrifugal pump?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pumps, ME-03 p. 8
  - Quote: "Wearing rings are replaceable rings that are attached to the impeller and/or the pump casing to allow a small running clearance between the impeller and the pump casing without causing wear of the actual impeller or pump casing material."
- **C951** (Pumps): What is the required relationship between NPSHA and NPSHR?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pump Operation, ME-03 p. 13
  - Quote: "The condition that must exist to avoid cavitation is that the net positive suction head available must be greater than or equal to the net positive suction head required."
- **C952** (Pumps): What five changes can reduce cavitation?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pump Operation, ME-03 p. 13
  - Quote: "Decreasing the temperature of the liquid decreases the saturation pressure, causing NPSHA to increase."
- **C953** (Pumps): What is pump runout?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pump Operation, ME-03 p. 14
  - Quote: "Pump runout is the maximum flow that can be developed by a centrifugal pump without damaging the pump."
- **C954** (Pumps): How is a centrifugal pump protected from dead-heading and from runout?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Centrifugal Pump Operation, ME-03 p. 15
  - Quote: "One method for protecting the pump from running dead-headed is to provide a recirculation line from the pump discharge line upstream of the discharge valve, back to the pump's supply source."
- **C955** (Pumps): What are the three basic groups of positive displacement pumps?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Positive Displacement Pumps, ME-03 p. 18
  - Quote: "The three groups are reciprocating pumps, rotary pumps, and diaphragm pumps."
- **C956** (Pumps): What is the characteristic curve of an ideal positive displacement pump?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1018/1-93), Positive Displacement Pumps, ME-03 p. 28
  - Quote: "The characteristic curve for a positive displacement pump operating at a certain speed is a vertical line on a graph of head versus flow."
- **Q1436** (Valves): Which is one of the four basic methods of controlling flow through a valve?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Valve Functions and Basic Parts, ME-04 p. 6
  - Quote: "In general, there are four methods of controlling flow through a valve."
- **Q1437** (Valves): Which flow control method does a butterfly valve use?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Valve Functions and Basic Parts, ME-04 p. 6
  - Quote: "In general, there are four methods of controlling flow through a valve."
- **Q1438** (Valves): Which part is the primary pressure boundary of a valve?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Valve Functions and Basic Parts, ME-04 p. 2
  - Quote: "The body, sometimes called the shell, is the primary pressure boundary of a valve."
- **Q1439** (Valves): What is the purpose of the valve stem?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Valve Functions and Basic Parts, ME-04 p. 4
  - Quote: "connects the actuator and disk, is responsible for positioning the disk."
- **Q1440** (Valves): How is valve stem leakage controlled?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Valve Functions and Basic Parts, ME-04 p. 5
  - Quote: "If a valve's packing is too loose, the valve will leak, which is a safety hazard. If the packing is too tight, it will impair the movement and possibly damage the stem."
- **Q1441** (Valves): What happens if valve packing is too tight?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Valve Functions and Basic Parts, ME-04 p. 5
  - Quote: "If a valve's packing is too loose, the valve will leak, which is a safety hazard. If the packing is too tight, it will impair the movement and possibly damage the stem."
- **Q1442** (Valves): Why are gate valves not used to throttle flow?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 10
  - Quote: "Most of the flow change occurs near shutoff with a relatively high fluid velocity causing disk and seat wear and eventual leakage if used to regulate flow."
- **Q1443** (Valves): What is the main drawback of a simple globe valve?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 15
  - Quote: "The most evident shortcoming of the simple globe valve is the high head loss from two or more right angle turns of flowing fluid."
- **Q1444** (Valves): What does a globe valve backseat do?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 18
  - Quote: "The backseat design prevents system pressure from building against the valve packing."
- **Q1445** (Valves): What is a common use of a multiport plug valve?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 22
  - Quote: "Multiport valves are particularly advantageous on transfer lines and for diverting services."
- **Q1446** (Valves): In a ball valve, what shows that the valve is open?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 18
  - Quote: "A ball valve is a rotational motion valve that uses a ball-shaped disk to stop or start fluid flow."
- **Q1447** (Valves): Which valve suits fluids that must stay free of contamination, such as radioactive fluids?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 25
  - Quote: "Diaphragm valves are particularly suited for the handling of corrosive fluids, fibrous slurries, radioactive fluids, or other fluids that must remain free from contamination."
- **Q1448** (Valves): Which valve is especially suited to large flows at relatively low pressures?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 32
  - Quote: "Butterfly valves are especially well-suited for the handling of large flows of liquids or gases at relatively low pressures and for the handling of slurries or liquids with large amounts of suspended solids."
- **Q1449** (Valves): Which valve is used for relatively fine adjustments of flow?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 33
  - Quote: "A needle valve, as shown in Figure 20, is used to make relatively fine adjustments in the amount of fluid flow."
- **Q1450** (Valves): What does a reducing valve do?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 28
  - Quote: "Reducing valves automatically reduce supply pressure to a preselected pressure as long as the supply pressure is at least as high as the selected pressure."
- **Q1451** (Valves): A valve is a rubber sleeve squeezed by an external mechanism. What type is it?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 30
  - Quote: "Pinch valves are suitable for on-off and throttling services."
- **Q1452** (Valves): What is the purpose of a check valve?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 35
  - Quote: "Check valves are designed to prevent the reversal of flow in a piping system."
- **Q1453** (Valves): Why should swing check valves be kept off lines with pulsating flow?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 36
  - Quote: "Swing check valves are usually installed in conjunction with gate valves because they provide relatively free flow."
- **Q1454** (Valves): What combination makes up a stop check valve?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 40
  - Quote: "A stop check valve, illustrated in Figure 27, is a combination of a lift check valve and a globe valve."
- **Q1455** (Valves): How can a safety valve often be told apart from a relief valve?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 41
  - Quote: "Safety valves can often be distinguished by the presence of an external lever at the top of the valve body, which is used as an operational check."
- **Q1456** (Valves): What is the main difference between a relief valve and a safety valve?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 40
  - Quote: "The main difference between a relief valve and a safety valve is the extent of opening at the setpoint pressure."
- **Q1457** (Valves): What do manual actuators not permit?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Valve Actuators, ME-04 p. 44
  - Quote: "Manual actuators are capable of placing the valve in any position but do not permit automatic operation."
- **Q1458** (Valves): What is a hammer handwheel for?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Valve Actuators, ME-04 p. 45
  - Quote: "With this arrangement, the valve can be pounded shut for tight closure or pounded open if it is stuck shut."
- **Q1459** (Valves): What stops an electric motor actuator at full open and full closed?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Valve Actuators, ME-04 p. 46
  - Quote: "Limit switches are normally provided to stop the motor automatically at full open and full closed valve positions."
- **Q1460** (Valves): A pneumatic actuator closes the valve with air pressure and opens it with a spring. What is it called?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Valve Actuators, ME-04 p. 47
  - Quote: "These actuators translate an air signal into valve stem motion by air pressure acting on a diaphragm or piston connected to the stem."
- **Q1461** (Valves): How does a solenoid position a valve?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Valve Actuators, ME-04 p. 48
  - Quote: "Solenoids position the valve by attracting a magnetic slug attached to the valve stem."
- **Q1462** (Valves): Why are solenoids not used on large valves?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Valve Actuators, ME-04 p. 49
  - Quote: "However, solenoids are not practical for large valves because their size and power requirements would be excessive."
- **Q1463** (Valves): Why should valves always be opened slowly?
  - Source: LP-VALVE-FUNDAMENTALS (Valve Fundamentals.docx), slide 1.54 Manual Valve Operation
  - Quote: "Always open valves slowly to minimize system pressure transients."
- **Q1464** (Valves): What is the effect of opening a valve on flow and upstream backpressure?
  - Source: LP-VALVE-FUNDAMENTALS (Valve Fundamentals.docx), slide 1.63 Valve Position and Fluid Flow
  - Quote: "Opening a valve results in increased flow and decreased backpressure as measured upstream of the valve."
- **C957** (Valves): What are the seven basic valve parts in objective 1.3 of ME-04?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Valve Functions and Basic Parts, ME-04 p. 1
  - Quote: "Regardless of type, all valves have the following basic parts: the body, bonnet, trim (internal elements), actuator, and packing."
- **C958** (Valves): What is the primary pressure boundary of a valve?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Valve Functions and Basic Parts, ME-04 p. 2
  - Quote: "The body, sometimes called the shell, is the primary pressure boundary of a valve."
- **C959** (Valves): What does a globe valve backseat do?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 18
  - Quote: "The backseat design prevents system pressure from building against the valve packing."
- **C960** (Valves): What is the main drawback of a globe valve?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 15
  - Quote: "The most evident shortcoming of the simple globe valve is the high head loss from two or more right angle turns of flowing fluid."
- **C961** (Valves): What is a needle valve used for?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 33
  - Quote: "A needle valve, as shown in Figure 20, is used to make relatively fine adjustments in the amount of fluid flow."
- **C962** (Valves): What does a reducing valve do?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Types of Valves, ME-04 p. 28
  - Quote: "Reducing valves automatically reduce supply pressure to a preselected pressure as long as the supply pressure is at least as high as the selected pressure."
- **C963** (Valves): What is the difference between direct-acting and reverse-acting pneumatic actuators?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Valve Actuators, ME-04 p. 47
  - Quote: "These actuators translate an air signal into valve stem motion by air pressure acting on a diaphragm or piston connected to the stem."
- **C964** (Valves): How does a motor-operated valve fail on loss of power?
  - Source: LP-VALVE-FUNDAMENTALS (Valve Fundamentals.docx), slide 1.47 Electric-Motor Actuator
  - Quote: "Upon a loss of power, an MOV will fail as is."
- **Q1465** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What does the stability of a material refer to?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Properties Considered When Selecting Materials, MS-05 p. 2
  - Quote: "Stability of a material refers to its mechanical and chemical inertness under the conditions to which it will be subjected."
- **Q1466** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which term measures the ease with which a material can be worked and made into desirable shapes and forms?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Properties Considered When Selecting Materials, MS-05 p. 3
  - Quote: "Fabricability is a measure of the ease with which a material can be worked and made into desirable shapes and forms."
- **Q1467** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Why is high corrosion resistance desirable in reactor systems?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Properties Considered When Selecting Materials, MS-05 p. 2
  - Quote: "High corrosion resistance is desirable in reactor systems because low corrosion resistance leads to increased production of corrosion products that may be transported through the core."
- **Q1468** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which components make good heat transfer a major selection consideration?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Properties Considered When Selecting Materials, MS-05 p. 3
  - Quote: "Good heat transfer properties are desirable from the fuel boundary to the coolant in order that the heat produced will be efficiently transferred."
- **Q1469** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which isotopes does the handbook name as fissionable by fast neutrons?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Fuel Materials, MS-05 p. 5
  - Quote: "The isotopes uranium-238 (238U) and thorium-232 (232Th) are fissionable by fast neutrons."
- **Q1470** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What three things does fuel cladding do, according to the fuel materials chapter?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Fuel Materials, MS-05 p. 6
  - Quote: "The cladding protects the fuel from attack by the coolant, prevents the escape of fission products, and provides geometrical integrity."
- **Q1471** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What must be the first consideration in selecting a nuclear fuel?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Fuel Materials, MS-05 p. 8
  - Quote: "The nuclear properties of a material must be the first consideration in the selection of a suitable nuclear fuel."
- **Q1472** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Why is high thermal conductivity wanted in a fuel?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Fuel Materials, MS-05 p. 9
  - Quote: "High thermal conductivity allows high power density and high specific power without excessive fuel temperature gradients."
- **Q1473** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is the main cause of fuel element swelling?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Fuel Materials, MS-05 p. 9
  - Quote: "The main cause of fuel element swelling is the accumulation of two fission product atoms for each atom fissioned."
- **Q1474** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Why should fuel cladding have high thermal conductivity?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Cladding and Reflectors, MS-05 p. 11
  - Quote: "Thermal conductivity should be high to minimize thermal stresses arising from temperature differences, and the coefficient of expansion should be low or well-matched with that of other materials."
- **Q1475** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What does the handbook give as the preferred fuel cladding material for sodium-cooled fast breeder reactors?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Cladding and Reflectors, MS-05 p. 12
  - Quote: "At present, stainless steel is the preferred fuel cladding material for sodium-cooled fast breeder reactors (LMFBRs)."
- **Q1476** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which is an essential requirement for fast reactor cladding?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Cladding and Reflectors, MS-05 p. 12
  - Quote: "The essential requirements for these materials are high melting point, retention of satisfactory physical and mechanical properties, a low swelling rate when irradiated by large fluences of fast neutrons, and good corrosion resistance, especially to molten sodium."
- **Q1477** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is the purpose of a reflector?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Cladding and Reflectors, MS-05 p. 12
  - Quote: "A reflector gets its name from the fact that neutrons leaving the reactor core hit the reflector and are returned to the core."
- **Q1478** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What does a fast reactor reflector consist of, according to the handbook?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Cladding and Reflectors, MS-05 p. 13
  - Quote: "In the case of a fast reactor, neutron thermalization is not desirable, and the reflector will consist of a dense element of high mass number."
- **Q1479** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which group lists the most widely used control rod poisons?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Control Materials, MS-05 p. 15
  - Quote: "The most widely-used poisons are hafnium, silver, indium, cadmium, and boron."
- **Q1480** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What has restricted the use of hafnium in civilian power reactors?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Control Materials, MS-05 p. 15
  - Quote: "Because of the limited availability and high cost of hafnium, its use as a control material in civilian power reactors has been restricted."
- **Q1481** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Why is pure boron not used for control rods?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Control Materials, MS-05 p. 16
  - Quote: "Boron is nonmetallic and is not suitable for control rod use in its pure form."
- **Q1482** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which materials are best for slowing neutrons at low energies, below 0.1 MeV?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Shielding Materials, MS-05 p. 18
  - Quote: "At low energies (less than 0.1 MeV), low mass number materials, such as hydrogen in H2O, are best for slowing down neutrons."
- **Q1483** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What property is used to shield high energy neutrons?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Shielding Materials, MS-05 p. 19
  - Quote: "To offset this decrease in cross section with increased neutron energy, materials with good inelastic scattering properties, such as iron, are used."
- **Q1484** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What makes a good gamma shield?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Shielding Materials, MS-05 p. 20
  - Quote: "Gamma shielding is therefore more effectively performed by materials with high atomic mass number and high density."
- **Q1485** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What generally stops a beta particle?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Shielding Materials, MS-05 p. 20
  - Quote: "The beta particle can generally be stopped by a sheet of aluminum."
- **Q1486** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which design feature counteracts pellet-cladding interaction?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Nuclear Reactor Core Problems, MS-05 p. 22
  - Quote: "Fuel pellet-cladding interaction (PCI) may lead to cladding failure and subsequent release of fission products into the reactor coolant."
- **Q1487** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What can swelling of the fuel do to the cladding?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Nuclear Reactor Core Problems, MS-05 p. 25
  - Quote: "Swelling can cause excessive pressure on the cladding, which could lead to fuel element cladding failure."
- **Q1488** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is fatigue failure?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Plant Material Problems, MS-05 p. 27
  - Quote: "Fatigue failure is defined as the tendency of a material to fracture by means of progressive brittle cracking under repeated alternating or cyclic stresses of an intensity considerably below the normal strength."
- **Q1489** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which plant controls minimize cyclic stress?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Plant Material Problems, MS-05 p. 28
  - Quote: "Heatup and cooldown limitations, pressure limitations, and pump operating curves are all used to minimize cyclic stress."
- **Q1490** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What effect does work hardening have on a metal?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Plant Material Problems, MS-05 p. 28
  - Quote: "Work hardening reduces ductility, which increases the chances of brittle failure."
- **Q1491** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is creep?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Plant Material Problems, MS-05 p. 29
  - Quote: "At elevated temperatures and constant stress or load, many materials continue to deform at a slow rate."
- **Q1492** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): How is creep kept from causing failure?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Plant Material Problems, MS-05 p. 30
  - Quote: "For safe operation, the total deformation due to creep must be well below the strain at which failure occurs."
- **Q1493** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is the net effect of beta and gamma radiation on metal?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Atomic Displacement Due to Irradiation, MS-05 p. 32
  - Quote: "The net effect of beta and gamma radiation on metal is to generate a small amount of heat."
- **Q1494** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): How do fast neutrons damage a metal?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Atomic Displacement Due to Irradiation, MS-05 p. 32
  - Quote: "Heavier particles, such as protons, α-particles, fast neutrons, and fission fragments, will usually transfer sufficient energy through elastic or inelastic collisions to remove nuclei from their lattice (crystalline) positions."
- **Q1495** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): About how much kinetic energy must a struck nucleus gain in most metals to be displaced?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Atomic Displacement Due to Irradiation, MS-05 p. 33
  - Quote: "A single fast neutron in the greater than or equal to 1 MeV range can displace a few thousand atoms."
- **Q1496** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is a displacement spike?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Thermal and Displacement Spikes Due to Irradiation, MS-05 p. 35
  - Quote: "The presence of large numbers of vacancies and interstitials in the lattice of a metal will generally increase hardness and decrease ductility."
- **Q1497** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What does a large number of displacement spikes do to a metal?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Thermal and Displacement Spikes Due to Irradiation, MS-05 p. 35
  - Quote: "The presence of large numbers of vacancies and interstitials in the lattice of a metal will generally increase hardness and decrease ductility."
- **Q1498** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Why does an atom recoil when it emits a gamma ray?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Effect Due to Neutron Capture, MS-05 p. 38
  - Quote: "When a gamma-ray photon is emitted by the excited compound nucleus formed by neutron capture, the residual atom suffers recoil (sometimes referred to as the shotgun effect)."
- **Q1499** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which property does fast-neutron irradiation decrease in metals?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Effect Due to Neutron Capture, MS-05 p. 39
  - Quote: "The general physical and mechanical effects of the irradiation of metals by fast neutrons and other high-energy particles are summarized in Table 1."
- **Q1500** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Why is swelling of stainless steel a concern in fast reactors?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Effect Due to Neutron Capture, MS-05 p. 41
  - Quote: "The swelling can cause changes in the dimensions of the coolant channels and also interfere with the free movement of control elements."
- **Q1501** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What generates helium bubbles in stainless steel under irradiation?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Effect Due to Neutron Capture, MS-05 p. 39
  - Quote: "In stainless steel, trace amounts of boron undergo a (n,α) reaction that generates helium bubbles which lead to the deterioration of mechanical properties."
- **Q1502** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What do gamma and beta radiation do to organic materials?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Radiation Effects in Organic Compounds, MS-05 p. 45
  - Quote: "Ionization is the major damage mechanism in organic compounds."
- **Q1503** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): How does nylon respond to radiation?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Radiation Effects in Organic Compounds, MS-05 p. 45
  - Quote: "Nylon begins to suffer degradation of its toughness at relatively low doses, but suffers little loss in strength."
- **Q1504** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What generally happens to rubber when irradiated?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Radiation Effects in Organic Compounds, MS-05 p. 46
  - Quote: "In general, rubber will harden upon being irradiated."
- **Q1505** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which chemical bond has the least resistance to radiation decomposition?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Radiation Effects in Organic Compounds, MS-05 p. 46
  - Quote: "It is important that oils and greases be evaluated for their resistance to radiation if they are to be employed in a high-radiation environment."
- **Q1506** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is polymerization?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Radiation Effects in Organic Compounds, MS-05 p. 46
  - Quote: "This recombination of broken hydrocarbon chains into longer ones is called"
- **Q1507** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Why is aluminum unsuitable as a structural material in high temperature power reactors?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Reactor Use of Aluminum, MS-05 p. 49
  - Quote: "Generally, at high temperatures, the relative low strength and poor corrosion properties of aluminum make it unsuitable as a structural material in power reactors due to hydrogen generation."
- **C965** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is the preferred fuel cladding material for sodium-cooled fast reactors, according to DOE-HDBK-1017?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Cladding and Reflectors, MS-05 p. 12
  - Quote: "At present, stainless steel is the preferred fuel cladding material for sodium-cooled fast breeder reactors (LMFBRs)."
- **C966** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What does a fast reactor reflector consist of?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Cladding and Reflectors, MS-05 p. 13
  - Quote: "In the case of a fast reactor, neutron thermalization is not desirable, and the reflector will consist of a dense element of high mass number."
- **C967** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which materials shield low energy neutrons, high energy neutrons, and gamma rays best?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Shielding Materials, MS-05 p. 20
  - Quote: "Gamma shielding is therefore more effectively performed by materials with high atomic mass number and high density."
- **C968** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What is fatigue failure?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Plant Material Problems, MS-05 p. 27
  - Quote: "Fatigue failure is defined as the tendency of a material to fracture by means of progressive brittle cracking under repeated alternating or cyclic stresses of an intensity considerably below the normal strength."
- **C969** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What are a knock-on, a vacancy, and an interstitial?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Atomic Displacement Due to Irradiation, MS-05 p. 34
  - Quote: "The presence of interstitials and vacancies makes it more difficult for dislocations to move through the lattice."
- **C970** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What does a large number of displacement spikes do to a metal?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Thermal and Displacement Spikes Due to Irradiation, MS-05 p. 35
  - Quote: "The presence of large numbers of vacancies and interstitials in the lattice of a metal will generally increase hardness and decrease ductility."
- **C971** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): Which chemical bond is least resistant to radiation?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Radiation Effects in Organic Compounds, MS-05 p. 46
  - Quote: "It is important that oils and greases be evaluated for their resistance to radiation if they are to be employed in a high-radiation environment."
- **C972** (Brittle Fracture and Vessel Thermal Stress): What problems does swelling of stainless steel cause in a fast reactor?
  - Source: DOE-1017-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1017/2-93), Effect Due to Neutron Capture, MS-05 p. 41
  - Quote: "The swelling can cause changes in the dimensions of the coolant channels and also interfere with the free movement of control elements."

## 2026-11-05: Lesson topics (knowledge checks and key facts)

Added 80 quiz questions and 54 flashcards from the lesson topics. Every quote passed scripts/verify-quotes.py. Calculation questions use new numbers with the method the quote supports.

- **Q1508** (Pumps): What are the three common types of air compressors?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Air Compressors, ME-05 p. 1
  - Quote: "Three types of designs include reciprocating, rotary, and centrifugal air compressors."
- **Q1509** (Pumps): In a reciprocating air compressor, what opens the discharge valve?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Air Compressors, ME-05 p. 3
  - Quote: "As the piston continues upward, air is compressed until the pressure in the cylinder becomes great enough to open the discharge valve against the pressure of the valve springs and the pressure of the discharge line (Figure 2E)."
- **Q1510** (Pumps): How does a rotary slide vane compressor compress air?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Air Compressors, ME-05 p. 4
  - Quote: "The size of each cell is reduced by the eccentricity of the rotor as the vanes approach the discharge port, thus compressing the air."
- **Q1511** (Pumps): How does a centrifugal air compressor compress air?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Air Compressors, ME-05 p. 9
  - Quote: "The air becomes compressed as more and more air is thrown out to the casing by the impeller blades."
- **Q1512** (Pumps): Why are cooling systems used on air compressors?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Air Compressors, ME-05 p. 7
  - Quote: "Air coolers are used because drier compressed air helps prevent corrosion and cooler compressed air allows more air to be compressed for a set volume."
- **Q1513** (Pumps): Where is an intercooler usually located on a multi-staged compressor?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Air Compressors, ME-05 p. 7
  - Quote: "If the compressor is multi-staged, there may be an intercooler, which is usually located after the first stage discharge and before the second stage suction."
- **Q1514** (Pumps): Which of these is one of the three general hazards of pressurized air systems?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Air Compressors, ME-05 p. 9
  - Quote: "Small leaks or breaks can cause minute particles to be blown at speeds high enough to cause damage."
- **Q1515** (Pumps): Why must oil be kept out of an air compressor?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Air Compressors, ME-05 p. 8
  - Quote: "Oil introduced in an air compressor can be compressed to the point where detonation takes place in a similar manner as that which occurs in a diesel engine."
- **Q1516** (Pumps): A hydraulic piston has an area of 4 in.² and the oil pressure is 500 psi. What force is exerted on the piston?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Hydraulics, ME-05 p. 10
  - Quote: "Pressure is the amount of force on a unit area of the surface."
- **Q1517** (Pumps): In a basic hydraulic system, what does the directional control valve do?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Hydraulics, ME-05 p. 12
  - Quote: "The control valve changes the direction of oil flow, depending upon the desired direction of the load."
- **Q1518** (Pumps): What usually protects a hydraulic system from overpressure?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Hydraulics, ME-05 p. 11
  - Quote: "The pressure control box shown on Figure 8 is usually a relief valve that provides a means of returning oil to the reservoir upon overpressurization."
- **Q1519** (Steam): What drives water circulation back to the steam drum in a boiler?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Boilers, ME-05 p. 14
  - Quote: "The density difference between hot and cold water is the driving force to circulate the water back to the steam drum."
- **Q1520** (Steam): Which boiler component carries water from the downcomers to the risers?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Boilers, ME-05 p. 17
  - Quote: "Distribution headers are large pipe headers that carry the water from the downcomers to the risers."
- **Q1521** (Steam): In a boiler, what forms the combustion chamber enclosure?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Boilers, ME-05 p. 17
  - Quote: "Risers are the piping or tubes that form the combustion chamber enclosure."
- **Q1522** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): What is the purpose of a cooling tower?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Cooling Towers, ME-05 p. 23
  - Quote: "The cooling tower removes heat from water used in cooling systems within the plant."
- **Q1523** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): How does air move through a forced draft cooling tower?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Cooling Towers, ME-05 p. 21
  - Quote: "The primary difference is that the air is blown in at the bottom of the tower and exits at the top."
- **Q1524** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): What sustains the air flow in a natural convection cooling tower?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Cooling Towers, ME-05 p. 22
  - Quote: "The air circulation will be self perpetuating due to the density difference between the warmer air inside and the cooler air outside."
- **Q1525** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): What is the purpose of a demineralizer?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Demineralizers, ME-05 p. 24
  - Quote: "Demineralization of the water is one of the most practical and common methods available to remove these dissolved impurities."
- **Q1526** (Steam): What is the purpose of a steam trap?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Steam Traps, ME-05 p. 35
  - Quote: "Steam traps are installed in steam lines to drain condensate from the lines without allowing the escape of steam."
- **Q1527** (Steam): Which steam trap depends on hot water under pressure flashing to steam when the pressure is reduced?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Steam Traps, ME-05 p. 37
  - Quote: "The impulse type of steam trap is dependent on the principle that hot water under pressure tends to flash into steam when the pressure is reduced."
- **Q1528** (Steam): In a bucket steam trap, what opens the valve?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Steam Traps, ME-05 p. 36
  - Quote: "When the bucket is full, it sinks and thus opens the valve."
- **Q1529** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): How does an operator know a cartridge filter is plugged?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Filters and Strainers, ME-05 p. 41
  - Quote: "Cartridge filters have the advantage of being relatively inexpensive to install and operate."
- **Q1530** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): What is the major advantage of a precoat filter?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Filters and Strainers, ME-05 p. 42
  - Quote: "A precoat filter eliminates the problem of physically handling radioactive materials, because the filter material (called the medium) can be installed and removed remotely."
- **Q1531** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): Where are deep-bed filters usually found?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Filters and Strainers, ME-05 p. 44
  - Quote: "Deep-bed filters are usually found only in makeup water systems, where they are used to filter water after it has been treated in a clarifier."
- **Q1532** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): Why is a duplex strainer used in fuel oil and lubricating oil lines?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Filters and Strainers, ME-05 p. 45
  - Quote: "The flow may be diverted from one basket to the other, while one is being cleaned."
- **C973** (Pumps): What are the three common types of air compressors?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Air Compressors, ME-05 p. 1
  - Quote: "Three types of designs include reciprocating, rotary, and centrifugal air compressors."
- **C974** (Pumps): What are the three groups of rotary compressors?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Air Compressors, ME-05 p. 4
  - Quote: "Rotary compressor units are classified into three general groups, slide vane-type, lobe-type, and liquid seal ring-type."
- **C975** (Pumps): What is an aftercooler?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Air Compressors, ME-05 p. 7
  - Quote: "Coolers used on the discharge of a compressor are called aftercoolers."
- **C976** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): What equation relates force and pressure in a hydraulic piston?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Hydraulics, ME-05 p. 10
  - Quote: "Pressure is the amount of force on a unit area of the surface."
- **C977** (Fluid Statics and Dynamics): What does Pascal's Law say?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Hydraulics, ME-05 p. 10
  - Quote: "Blaise Pascal discovered that pressure in a fluid acts equally in all directions."
- **C978** (Steam): What is the primary function of a boiler?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Boilers, ME-05 p. 14
  - Quote: "The primary function of a boiler is to produce steam at a given pressure and temperature."
- **C979** (Steam): What does a boiler's steam drum do?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Boilers, ME-05 p. 16
  - Quote: "The steam drum separates the steam from the heated water."
- **C980** (Steam): What does a boiler economizer do?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Boilers, ME-05 p. 15
  - Quote: "The economizer uses heat from the boiler exhaust gasses to raise the temperature of the inlet feedwater."
- **C981** (Heat Exchangers and Condensers): How is water cooled in a cooling tower?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Cooling Towers, ME-05 p. 19
  - Quote: "The cooling of the water in a cooling tower is accomplished by the direct contact of water and air."
- **C982** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): What are the two groups of ion exchangers?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Demineralizers, ME-05 p. 29
  - Quote: "Ion exchangers are generally classified into two groups: single-bed ion exchangers and mixed-bed ion exchangers."
- **C983** (Steam): Where are steam traps installed?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Steam Traps, ME-05 p. 39
  - Quote: "Steam traps are installed at low points in the system or machinery to be drained."
- **C984** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): What separates filtration from demineralization?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Filters and Strainers, ME-05 p. 40
  - Quote: "Filtration is a process used to remove suspended solids from a solution."
- **C985** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): What is the intent of a backwash?
  - Source: DOE-1018-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1018/2-93), Filters and Strainers, ME-05 p. 46
  - Quote: "The intent of a backwash is to flow liquid in the opposite direction of normal flow, creating a pressure that pushes the debris off the strainer or filter."
- **Q1533** (Neutrons): Which particle has no electrical charge and is found in the nucleus?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Atomic Nature of Matter, NP-01 p. 10
  - Quote: "Neutrons are particles that have no electrical charge, have about the same mass as a hydrogen atom, and exist in the nucleus of an atom."
- **Q1534** (Neutrons): In the Bohr model, what is emitted when an electron moves to a lower allowed orbit?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Atomic Nature of Matter, NP-01 p. 3
  - Quote: "When an electron moves from one allowed orbit to another allowed orbit, the energy difference between the two states is emitted or absorbed in the form of a single quantum of radiant energy called a photon."
- **Q1535** (Neutrons): What are isotopes?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Atomic Nature of Matter, NP-01 p. 10
  - Quote: "Isotopes are nuclides that have the same atomic number and are therefore the same element, but differ in the number of neutrons."
- **Q1536** (Neutrons): A neutral atom has mass number 239 and atomic number 94. How many neutrons does it have?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Atomic Nature of Matter, NP-01 p. 10
  - Quote: "The mass number of an atom is the total number of nucleons (protons and neutrons) in the nucleus."
- **Q1537** (Neutrons): Which force holds the nucleons together against proton repulsion?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Atomic Nature of Matter, NP-01 p. 10
  - Quote: "The nuclear force is a relatively short-range attractive force between all nucleons."
- **Q1538** (Neutrons): What is depleted uranium?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Chart of the Nuclides, NP-01 p. 16
  - Quote: "Depleted uranium is uranium in which the isotope uranium-235 has a concentration less than its natural value of 0.7%."
- **Q1539** (Neutrons): What is binding energy?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Mass Defect and Binding Energy, NP-01 p. 21
  - Quote: "Binding energy is the amount of energy that must be supplied to a nucleus to completely separate its nuclear particles."
- **Q1540** (Neutrons): What happens in electron capture?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Modes of Radioactive Decay, NP-01 p. 29
  - Quote: "In electron capture, the nucleus absorbs an electron from the innermost orbit."
- **Q1541** (Neutrons): Why does a gamma ray typically accompany particle emission?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Modes of Radioactive Decay, NP-01 p. 29
  - Quote: "Many modes of radioactive decay result in a daughter nuclide that has an energy level above the ground state."
- **Q1542** (Neutrons): A nuclide lies above and to the left of the line of stability. How will it typically decay?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Modes of Radioactive Decay, NP-01 p. 29
  - Quote: "Most alpha emitters are found in the upper, right-hand corner of the chart."
- **Q1543** (Neutrons): What is the radioactive half-life?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Radioactivity, NP-01 p. 32
  - Quote: "The radioactive half-life is defined as the amount of time required for the activity to decrease to one-half of its original value."
- **Q1544** (Neutrons): A nuclide has a half-life of 7.13 seconds. What is its decay constant?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Radioactivity, NP-01 p. 32
  - Quote: "The radioactive half-life is defined as the amount of time required for the activity to decrease to one-half of its original value."
- **Q1545** (Neutrons): How does the decay of a single nuclide plot on a semi-log scale?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Radioactivity, NP-01 p. 35
  - Quote: "The decay of the activity of a single nuclide on a logarithmic scale will plot as a straight line because the decay is exponential."
- **Q1546** (Neutrons): What must be true for transient radioactive equilibrium to occur?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Radioactivity, NP-01 p. 40
  - Quote: "For transient equilibrium to occur, the parent must have a long half-life when compared to the daughter."
- **Q1547** (Neutrons): Which conservation laws apply to an elastic collision between a neutron and a nucleus?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Neutron Interactions, NP-01 p. 47
  - Quote: "The conservation principles that apply to an elastic collision are conservation of kinetic energy and conservation of momentum."
- **Q1548** (Neutrons): What identifies a particle ejection reaction?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Neutron Interactions, NP-01 p. 47
  - Quote: "Particle ejection occurs when a neutron is absorbed by a target nucleus, resulting in the formation of a compound nucleus."
- **Q1549** (Neutrons): What is critical energy?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Nuclear Fission, NP-01 p. 55
  - Quote: "Critical energy is the minimum excitation energy that a nucleus must have before it can fission."
- **Q1550** (Neutrons): In the liquid drop model, what causes the nucleus to split?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Nuclear Fission, NP-01 p. 55
  - Quote: "If the oscillations cause the nucleus to become shaped like a dumbbell, the repulsive electrostatic forces will overcome the short-range attractive nuclear forces, and the nucleus will split in two."
- **Q1551** (Neutrons): What is fertile material?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Nuclear Fission, NP-01 p. 52
  - Quote: "Fertile materials are materials that can undergo transmutation to become fissile materials."
- **Q1552** (Neutrons): Near what mass number does the binding energy per nucleon curve reach its maximum?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Nuclear Fission, NP-01 p. 55
  - Quote: "The curve of binding energy per nucleon increases quickly through the light nuclides and reaches a maximum at a mass number of about 56."
- **Q1553** (Neutrons): Why are the heaviest nuclei easily fissioned?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Nuclear Fission, NP-01 p. 55
  - Quote: "The heaviest nuclei are easily fissionable because they require only a small distortion from the spherical shape to allow the coulomb forces to overcoming the attractive nuclear force, forcing the two halves of the nucleus apart."
- **Q1554** (Neutrons): Binding energies from the curve are 809 MeV for Rb-93, 1176 MeV for Cs-140, and 1786 MeV for U-235. About how much energy is released?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Energy Release From Fission, NP-01 p. 57
  - Quote: "Therefore, in the fission process, the energy liberated is equal to the increase in the total binding energy of the system."
- **Q1555** (Neutrons): Of the 200 MeV released per fission, about how much is released some time after the fission?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Energy Release From Fission, NP-01 p. 62
  - Quote: "Of the 200 MeV released per fission, about seven percent (13 MeV) is released at some time after the instant of fission."
- **Q1556** (Neutrons): Why does an alpha particle penetrate so little?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Interaction of Radiation With Matter, NP-01 p. 67
  - Quote: "An alpha particle deposits a large amount of energy in a short distance of travel due to its large mass and charge."
- **Q1557** (Neutrons): What is the minimum gamma energy for pair production?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Interaction of Radiation With Matter, NP-01 p. 67
  - Quote: "The gamma must have an energy greater than 1.02 MeV for this to occur."
- **C986** (Neutrons): What is the Bohr model of the atom?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Atomic Nature of Matter, NP-01 p. 10
  - Quote: "The Bohr model of the atom consists of a dense nucleus of protons and neutrons (nucleons) surrounded by electrons traveling in discrete orbits at fixed distances from the nucleus."
- **C987** (Neutrons): What is the atomic number?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Atomic Nature of Matter, NP-01 p. 10
  - Quote: "The atomic number of an atom is the number of protons in the nucleus."
- **C988** (Neutrons): What is the mass number?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Atomic Nature of Matter, NP-01 p. 10
  - Quote: "The mass number of an atom is the total number of nucleons (protons and neutrons) in the nucleus."
- **C989** (Neutrons): What is mass defect?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Mass Defect and Binding Energy, NP-01 p. 21
  - Quote: "Mass defect is the difference between the mass of the atom and the sum of the masses of its constituent parts."
- **C990** (Neutrons): What is a becquerel?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Radioactivity, NP-01 p. 42
  - Quote: "A becquerel (Bq) is a unit of radioactivity equal to 1 disintegration per second."
- **C991** (Neutrons): After how many half-lives can the remaining atoms usually be assumed negligible?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Radioactivity, NP-01 p. 33
  - Quote: "The number of atoms existing after 5 to 7 half-lives can usually be assumed to be negligible."
- **C992** (Neutrons): What is transient radioactive equilibrium?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Radioactivity, NP-01 p. 40
  - Quote: "Transient radioactive equilibrium occurs when the parent nuclide and the daughter nuclide decay at essentially the same rate."
- **C993** (Neutrons): What is excitation energy?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Nuclear Fission, NP-01 p. 55
  - Quote: "Excitation energy is the amount of energy a nucleus has above its ground state."
- **C994** (Neutrons): What is transmutation?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Nuclear Fission, NP-01 p. 55
  - Quote: "Transmutation is the process of neutron absorption and subsequent decay, which changes one nuclide to another nuclide."
- **C995** (Fuel Depletion and Burnable Poisons): What is conversion?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Nuclear Fission, NP-01 p. 55
  - Quote: "Conversion is the process of transmuting fertile material into fissile material in a reactor, where the amount of fissile material produced is less than the amount of fissile material consumed."
- **C996** (Neutrons): How many neutrons are normally produced from every fission?
  - Source: LP-NEUTRONS (Neutrons.docx), slide 1.53 Neutrons Produced
  - Quote: "Normally between two and three fast neutrons are produced from every fission (most are prompt, but some are delayed)"
- **C997** (Neutrons): What is the photoelectric effect?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Interaction of Radiation With Matter, NP-01 p. 67
  - Quote: "Photoelectric effect is where a gamma interacts with an electron orbiting an atom."
- **C998** (Neutrons): What is pair production?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Interaction of Radiation With Matter, NP-01 p. 67
  - Quote: "In pair-production, a gamma interacts with the electric field of a nucleus and is converted into an electron-positron pair."
- **Q1558** (Reactor Kinetics and Neutron Sources): Which reaction is an example of an installed neutron source?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Neutron Sources, NP-02 p. 4
  - Quote: "Beryllium-9 undergoes an alpha-neutron reaction (alpha from the decay of plutonium, polonium, or radium) and becomes carbon-12."
- **Q1559** (Neutrons): How is macroscopic cross section related to microscopic cross section?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Nuclear Cross Sections and Neutron Flux, NP-02 p. 8
  - Quote: "The macroscopic cross section is the probability of a given reaction occurring per unit travel of the neutron."
- **Q1560** (Neutrons): When does resonance absorption occur?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Nuclear Cross Sections and Neutron Flux, NP-02 p. 17
  - Quote: "Resonance absorption occurs when the sum of the kinetic energy of the neutron and its binding energy is equal to an allowed nuclear energy level of the nucleus."
- **Q1561** (Neutrons): Why do heavy nuclei have more resonances than light nuclei?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Nuclear Cross Sections and Neutron Flux, NP-02 p. 10
  - Quote: "This is because heavy nuclei are complex and have more possible configurations and corresponding energy states."
- **Q1562** (Neutrons): A material has a macroscopic cross section of 0.1 cm⁻¹ for an interaction. What is the mean free path?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Nuclear Cross Sections and Neutron Flux, NP-02 p. 10
  - Quote: "This average distance traveled by a neutron before interaction is known as the mean free path for that interaction"
- **Q1563** (Neutrons): Why does the interior of a fuel pin see a lower average flux than its surface?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Nuclear Cross Sections and Neutron Flux, NP-02 p. 17
  - Quote: "Self-shielding is where the local neutron flux is depressed within a material due to neutron absorption near the surface of the material."
- **Q1564** (Neutrons): A section of a reactor has a macroscopic fission cross section of 0.1 cm⁻¹ and a flux of 10^13 neutrons/cm²-sec. What is the fission rate per cm³ each second?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Reaction Rates, NP-02 p. 22
  - Quote: "The reaction rate is the number of interactions of a particular type occurring in a cubic centimeter of material in a second."
- **Q1565** (Neutrons): A 2 MeV neutron loses an average fraction of 0.5 of its energy per collision. What is its energy after 2 collisions?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Neutron Moderation, NP-02 p. 25
  - Quote: "Sometimes it is convenient, based upon information known, to work with an average fractional energy loss per collision as opposed to an average logarithmic fraction."
- **Q1566** (Reactor Kinetics and Neutron Sources): How is a delayed neutron produced?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Prompt and Delayed Neutrons, NP-02 p. 29
  - Quote: "The delayed neutrons are emitted immediately following the first beta decay of a fission fragment known as a delayed neutron precursor."
- **Q1567** (Neutrons): What is the average energy at which prompt neutrons are produced?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Neutron Flux Spectrum, NP-02 p. 37
  - Quote: "The average prompt neutron energy is about 2 MeV."
- **Q1568** (Neutrons): What does the neutron energy spectrum of a fast reactor look like?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Neutron Flux Spectrum, NP-02 p. 37
  - Quote: "Fast reactors have a neutron energy spectrum that has the same shape as the prompt neutron energy spectrum."
- **C999** (Reactor Kinetics and Neutron Sources): What is an intrinsic neutron source?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Neutron Sources, NP-02 p. 1
  - Quote: "Intrinsic neutron sources are those neutron-producing reactions that always occur in reactor materials."
- **C1000** (Reactor Kinetics and Neutron Sources): Why are source neutrons important?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Neutron Sources, NP-02 p. 1
  - Quote: "Source neutrons are important because they ensure that the neutron population remains high enough to allow a visible indication of neutron level on the most sensitive monitoring instruments while the reactor is shutdown and during the startup sequence."
- **C1001** (Neutrons): What is a macroscopic cross section?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Nuclear Cross Sections and Neutron Flux, NP-02 p. 8
  - Quote: "The macroscopic cross section is the probability of a given reaction occurring per unit travel of the neutron."
- **C1002** (Neutrons): What is mean free path?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Nuclear Cross Sections and Neutron Flux, NP-02 p. 10
  - Quote: "This average distance traveled by a neutron before interaction is known as the mean free path for that interaction"
- **C1003** (Neutrons): What is a reaction rate?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Reaction Rates, NP-02 p. 22
  - Quote: "The reaction rate is the number of interactions of a particular type occurring in a cubic centimeter of material in a second."
- **C1004** (Reactor Kinetics and Neutron Sources): What are delayed neutrons released from?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Prompt and Delayed Neutrons, NP-02 p. 32
  - Quote: "Delayed neutrons are released from the decay of fission products that are called delayed neutron precursors."
- **C1005** (Neutrons): What is the neutron generation time?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Prompt and Delayed Neutrons, NP-02 p. 30
  - Quote: "The neutron generation time is the time required for neutrons from one generation to cause the fissions that produce the next generation of neutrons."
- **C1006** (Neutrons): At what energies are prompt neutrons born?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V1 (DOE-HDBK-1019/1-93), Neutron Flux Spectrum, NP-02 p. 37
  - Quote: "Prompt neutrons are born at energies between 0.1 MeV and 10 MeV."
- **C1007** (Neutrons): At what energies do most fissions occur in an SFR?
  - Source: ML19148A793 (ML19148A793.pdf), slide 3
  - Quote: "In SFR, moderation is avoided – no thermal neutrons; most fissions occur at higher energies (>10 keV)"
- **C1008** (Neutrons): About what share of the fission rate in a fast reactor comes from U-238 threshold fission?
  - Source: ML19148A793 (ML19148A793.pdf), slide 8
  - Quote: "Threshold fission at ~1 MeV (~10% of total fission rate in a fast reactor)"
- **Q1569** (Neutron Life Cycle): How does the effective multiplication factor differ from the infinite multiplication factor?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Neutron Life Cycle, NP-03 p. 15
  - Quote: "The effective multiplication factor, keff, is the ratio of the number of neutrons produced by fission in one generation to the number of neutrons lost through absorption and leakage in the preceding generation."
- **Q1570** (Neutron Life Cycle): Why is the resonance escape probability not significant in a fast reactor?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Neutron Life Cycle, NP-03 p. 14
  - Quote: "The resonance escape probability is not significant because very few neutrons exist at energies where resonance absorption is significant."
- **Q1571** (Neutron Life Cycle): A nuclide has σf = 2 barns, σa = 2.5 barns and ν = 3. What is its reproduction factor?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Neutron Life Cycle, NP-03 p. 14
  - Quote: "The reproduction factor is similarly modified to account for fast fission instead of thermal fission."
- **Q1572** (Fuel Depletion and Burnable Poisons): Why can a sodium fast reactor not use boron dilution for reactivity control?
  - Source: LP-REACTIVITY-COEFFICIENTS-MODULE-3 (Reactivity Coefficients Module 3.docx), slide 1.16 Control rods
  - Quote: "Contrary to light water reactors, control rods are the primary means of reactivity control, as boron dilution in sodium is not possible."
- **Q1573** (Fission Product Poisons): When will helium-3 become a significant neutron poison?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Samarium and Other Fission Product Poisons, NP-03 p. 47
  - Quote: "Helium-3 will become a significant neutron poison if significant amounts of tritium are left in a reactor during a shutdown period that lasts longer than several months."
- **Q1574** (Control Rods): What is the difference between a black and a grey absorber?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Control Rods, NP-03 p. 49
  - Quote: "A control rod that is referred to as a "black" absorber absorbs essentially all incident neutrons."
- **Q1575** (Control Rods): Why are resonance absorbers sometimes preferred to thermal absorbers?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Control Rods, NP-03 p. 58
  - Quote: "Resonance absorbers are sometimes preferred to thermal absorbers as control rod materials because they have a larger area of influence and result in a flatter flux profile."
- **Q1576** (Control Rods): An integral rod worth curve reads 40 pcm at 12 inches and 80 pcm at 18 inches. What reactivity is added by withdrawing from 12 to 18 inches?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Control Rods, NP-03 p. 58
  - Quote: "Integral control rod worth is the total reactivity worth of the control rod at a particular degree of withdrawal from the core."
- **C1009** (Neutron Life Cycle): What is reactivity?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Reactivity, NP-03 p. 22
  - Quote: "Reactivity is the fractional change in neutron population per generation."
- **C1010** (Neutron Life Cycle): What is subcritical?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Neutron Life Cycle, NP-03 p. 15
  - Quote: "Subcritical is the condition in which the neutron population is decreasing each generation."
- **C1011** (Neutron Life Cycle): What is supercritical?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Neutron Life Cycle, NP-03 p. 15
  - Quote: "Supercritical is the condition in which the neutron population is increasing each generation."
- **C1012** (Neutron Life Cycle): In a fast reactor, what causes virtually all fissions?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Neutron Life Cycle, NP-03 p. 14
  - Quote: "Virtually all fissions taking place in a fast reactor are caused by fast neutrons."
- **C1013** (Reactivity Coefficients): What are the three components of the reactivity change when sodium density falls?
  - Source: LP-REACTIVITY-COEFFICIENTS-MODULE-1 (Reactivity Coefficients Module 1.docx), slide 1.11 Coolant Temperature Coefficient
  - Quote: "When the sodium density in a sodium fast reactor is reduced, the reactivity change can be broken down into three components: spectral, leakage, and capture."
- **C1014** (Reactivity Coefficients): Why is the fuel temperature coefficient called the prompt coefficient?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Reactivity Coefficients, NP-03 p. 26
  - Quote: "This coefficient is also called the "prompt" temperature coefficient because an increase in reactor power causes an immediate change in fuel temperature."
- **C1015** (Reactivity Coefficients): What effect does radial core expansion have on reactivity?
  - Source: LP-REACTIVITY-COEFFICIENTS-MODULE-3 (Reactivity Coefficients Module 3.docx), slide 1.4 Core Geometric Expansion
  - Quote: "An increase in the radial dimensions of the core is associated with a reduction in the reactivity of the core, or a negative reactivity feedback."
- **C1016** (Control Rods): What are the sodium reactor's control rods made of?
  - Source: LP-CONTROL-RODS (Control Rods.docx), slide 1.5 Core alignment
  - Quote: "Both are constructed of boron carbide pellets"
- **C1018** (Control Rods): What is integral control rod worth?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Control Rods, NP-03 p. 58
  - Quote: "Integral control rod worth is the total reactivity worth of the control rod at a particular degree of withdrawal from the core."
- **C1019** (Control Rods): What is differential control rod worth?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Control Rods, NP-03 p. 58
  - Quote: "Differential control rod worth is the reactivity change per unit movement of a control rod."
- **Q1577** (Reactor Kinetics and Neutron Sources): On a 1/M plot, what value of 1/M marks criticality?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Subcritical Multiplication, NP-04 p. 7
  - Quote: "For a critical reactor, 1/M is equal to zero."
- **Q1578** (Reactor Kinetics and Neutron Sources): A reactor at 1000 watts has a doubling time of 2 minutes. What is its power 4 minutes later?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Reactor Kinetics, NP-04 p. 21
  - Quote: "Doubling time is the time required for reactor power to double."
- **Q1579** (Reactor Kinetics and Neutron Sources): If a stable reactor period is 26.06 seconds, what is the startup rate?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Reactor Kinetics, NP-04 p. 21
  - Quote: "Reactor startup rate is the number of factors of ten that reactor power changes in one minute."
- **Q1580** (Reactor Kinetics and Neutron Sources): What is a prompt jump?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Reactor Kinetics, NP-04 p. 22
  - Quote: "Prompt jump is the small, immediate power increase that follows a positive reactivity insertion related to an increase in the prompt neutron population."
- **Q1581** (Reactor Kinetics and Neutron Sources): A reactor has one dollar of positive reactivity. What is its condition?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Reactor Kinetics, NP-04 p. 22
  - Quote: "Measuring reactivity in units of dollars is useful when determining if a reactor is prompt critical."
- **Q1582** (Reactor Operational Physics): Why is an Estimated Critical Position calculated before startup?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Reactor Operation, NP-04 p. 24
  - Quote: "This process provides an added margin of safety because a large discrepancy between actual and estimated critical rod positions would indicate that the core was not performing as designed."
- **Q1583** (Reactor Operational Physics): Why are fast reactor reflectors not made of moderating materials?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Reactor Operation, NP-04 p. 25
  - Quote: "In fast reactor systems, reflectors are not composed of moderating materials because it is desired to keep neutron energy high."
- **Q1584** (Reactor Operational Physics): What is the reason for the stuck rod criterion?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Reactor Operation, NP-04 p. 34
  - Quote: "The stuck rod criterion is applied to the shutdown margin to ensure that the failure of a single control rod will not prevent the control rod system from shutting down the reactor."
- **Q1585** (Reactor Operational Physics): What reactor period is typical shortly after a reactor shutdown?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Reactor Operation, NP-04 p. 32
  - Quote: "The half-life of the longest lived delayed neutron precursor results in a reactor period of around -80 seconds or a startup rate of -1/3 DPM for most reactors after a reactor shutdown."
- **Q1586** (Reactor Operational Physics): Which three variables affect the amount of decay heat after shutdown?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Reactor Operation, NP-04 p. 33
  - Quote: "The amount of decay heat production after shutdown is directly influenced by the power history of the reactor prior to shutdown."
- **Q1587** (Reactor Operational Physics): About how much decay heat exists one hour after a shutdown from full power?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Reactor Operation, NP-04 p. 33
  - Quote: "This decay heat generation rate diminishes to less than 1% approximately one hour after shutdown."
- **C1020** (Reactor Kinetics and Neutron Sources): What is reactor startup rate?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Reactor Kinetics, NP-04 p. 21
  - Quote: "Reactor startup rate is the number of factors of ten that reactor power changes in one minute."
- **C1021** (Reactor Kinetics and Neutron Sources): What is doubling time?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Reactor Kinetics, NP-04 p. 21
  - Quote: "Doubling time is the time required for reactor power to double."
- **C1022** (Reactor Kinetics and Neutron Sources): What is prompt drop?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Reactor Kinetics, NP-04 p. 22
  - Quote: "Prompt drop is the small, immediate power decrease that follows a negative reactivity insertion related to a decrease in the prompt neutron population."
- **C1023** (Reactor Kinetics and Neutron Sources): What does a dollar of reactivity equal?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Reactor Kinetics, NP-04 p. 22
  - Quote: "Measuring reactivity in units of dollars is useful when determining if a reactor is prompt critical."
- **C1024** (Reactor Operational Physics): What is shutdown margin?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Reactor Operation, NP-04 p. 34
  - Quote: "Shutdown margin is the instantaneous amount of reactivity by which a reactor is subcritical or would be subcritical from its present condition assuming all control rods are fully inserted except for the single rod with the highest integral worth, which is assumed to be fully withdrawn."
- **C1025** (Reactor Operational Physics): What reactor period follows a shutdown for most reactors?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Reactor Operation, NP-04 p. 32
  - Quote: "The half-life of the longest lived delayed neutron precursor results in a reactor period of around -80 seconds or a startup rate of -1/3 DPM for most reactors after a reactor shutdown."
- **C1026** (Reactor Operational Physics): Why is a negative temperature coefficient ineffective at very low power?
  - Source: DOE-1019-V2 (DOE-HDBK-1019/2-93), Reactor Operation, NP-04 p. 29
  - Quote: "The inherent stability and power turning ability of a negative temperature coefficient are ineffective below the point of adding heat."

## 2026-11-05: Lesson topics (knowledge checks and key facts)

Added 27 quiz questions and 18 flashcards from the lesson topics. Every quote passed scripts/verify-quotes.py. Calculation questions use new numbers with the method the quote supports.

- **Q1588** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): In a sodium-cooled fast reactor, where would crystallized sodium hydride and sodium oxide collect if the sodium were not purified?
  - Source: LP-COLD-TRAPS-AND-SODIUM-COOLANT-PURIFICATION (Cold Traps and Sodium Coolant Purification.docx), slide 1.2 Cold Traps and Sodium Coolant Purification
  - Quote: "these impurities would collect in the form of crystallized sodium hydride (NaH) or sodium oxide (Na2O) at the cold points of the sodium loops"
- **Q1589** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): According to the cold trap lesson plan, what are the primary origins of impurities in sodium coolant?
  - Source: LP-COLD-TRAPS-AND-SODIUM-COOLANT-PURIFICATION (Cold Traps and Sodium Coolant Purification.docx), slide 1.2 Cold Traps and Sodium Coolant Purification
  - Quote: "originate primarily from corrosion, moisture from system component surfaces, and air intrusion into the system"
- **Q1590** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): What caused the 1987 BN-600 transient at rated power?
  - Source: LP-COLD-TRAPS-AND-SODIUM-COOLANT-PURIFICATION (Cold Traps and Sodium Coolant Purification.docx), slide 1.3 Safety Minute
  - Quote: "the incident was attributed to the drop of a chunk of impurities from the reactor roof, formed from impurities in the cover gas"
- **Q1591** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): What does the economizer do in a sodium cold trap loop?
  - Source: LP-COLD-TRAPS-AND-SODIUM-COOLANT-PURIFICATION (Cold Traps and Sodium Coolant Purification.docx), slide 1.10 Cold Trap
  - Quote: "The economizer acts as a regenerative heat exchanger and pre-heats the clean sodium re-entering the system."
- **Q1592** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): Where do precipitated impurities collect inside a sodium cold trap?
  - Source: LP-COLD-TRAPS-AND-SODIUM-COOLANT-PURIFICATION (Cold Traps and Sodium Coolant Purification.docx), slide 1.10 Cold Trap
  - Quote: "adhere to the stainless-steel mesh packing and walls within the volume of the cold trap"
- **Q1593** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): What impurity concentration level can be achieved with a sodium cold trap?
  - Source: LP-COLD-TRAPS-AND-SODIUM-COOLANT-PURIFICATION (Cold Traps and Sodium Coolant Purification.docx), slide 1.10 Cold Trap
  - Quote: "impurity concentration levels under five parts per million (ppm) can be achieved"
- **Q1594** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): As impurities build up in sodium coolant, what happens to the temperature at which impurity crystallization occurs?
  - Source: LP-COLD-TRAPS-AND-SODIUM-COOLANT-PURIFICATION (Cold Traps and Sodium Coolant Purification.docx), slide 1.15 Plugging Temperature Indicator
  - Quote: "As impurities build up in the coolant, the temperature at which crystallization occurs rises."
- **Q1595** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): Why are the inlet and outlet pressures of a sodium cold trap measured?
  - Source: LP-COLD-TRAPS-AND-SODIUM-COOLANT-PURIFICATION (Cold Traps and Sodium Coolant Purification.docx), slide 1.20 Cautions
  - Quote: "Inlet and outlet pressures of the cold trap are measured with pressure transmitters to monitor the amount of contamination retained in the cold trap."
- **Q1596** (Demineralizers and Ion Exchangers): Why can oxygen supersaturation in a sodium cold trap be a problem?
